en: The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya. 1. Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
According to the recension of the noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins of the Madhy’udeśika school, this is the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya.

The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, dwells among the Śākyas at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.

The Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, venerated, and respected; he attained the highest gain and the highest fame, and was a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal aids for the sick.
Yet, he remained unsullied therein, like a lotus by water, establishing in merit those beings who were destined for merit, and [establishing] those who were destined for the fruits [of the path].
Establishing beings in the fruits [of the path], settling beings who possess latent tendencies within those very tendencies,

distributing the nectar of immortality in no small measure to gods and humans, causing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings to attain that nectar, and having rescued them from the great abyss— the wilderness of saṃsāra with its beginningless and endless birth, old age, and death, and its impassable hells— [he acts].
Establishing [beings] in security, welfare, evenness, safety, and nirvana, having won over Aṅga, Magadha, Vṛji, Malla, Kāśi, Kośala, Kuru, Pañcāla, Cedi, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Śibi, Daśārṇa,
Cārvāka, Avanti, and others; one who has seen his own prowess through knowledge, the Self-Existent One, dwells in divine abidings, Brahma-abidings, and noble abidings.

Dwelling in Brahma-dwellings, in noble dwellings, in imperturbable dwellings, in constant dwellings, and in Buddha-dwellings; as a Victor, dwelling in the dwellings of a Victor; as a Knower, dwelling in the dwellings of a Knower;
as the All-Knowing One, dwelling in the dwellings of the All-Knowing One—furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have attained the supreme perfection of mastery over the mind.
In whichever dwellings they desire, in those very dwellings the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, abide; moreover, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are skilled in such dwellings.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī [approached] Chandā, Chandakapālā, Dāsacchandā, and Chandakamātā.

Together with five hundred Śākyan women, she approached the Blessed One, bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is rare; the teaching of the True Dharma is rare.”

"Furthermore, the Blessed One has now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, and he teaches the Dharma that leads to peace, to final Nirvāṇa, as proclaimed by the Sugata,
for the attainment of the Deathless and for the realization of Nirvāṇa.
It would be well, Blessed One, if women also might receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
The Blessed One said:
"Gautamī, may it not please you [to seek] the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Then indeed, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī—

"Indeed, the Blessed One does not grant the opportunity for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, and to attain the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Having bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she approached those five hundred Śākyan women together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, Dāsacchandā, and Chandakamātā, and said this to the Śākyan women:
"Indeed, noble ladies, the Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, receive full ordination, and become bhikṣuṇīs within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

Why then should we, noble ladies, ourselves shave our hair, don saffron robes, and mount vehicles with covered seats to follow behind the Blessed One as he travels on tour through the Kośala country?"

"If the Blessed One will grant us permission, we shall go forth; if he does not grant us permission, nevertheless, O Noble One, we shall practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One. "Very well, noble ladies," they replied to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Then the Blessed One, having stayed in the city of Kapilavastu for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour through the Kośala country.
Then indeed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, Dāsacchandā, Chandakamātā, and five hundred Śākyan women, having herself shaved off her hair and donned saffron-colored robes,
set out in vehicles with covered seats on a journey through the Kośala country to visit the Blessed One.
They followed closely behind him as he walked.

Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kośala country together with a great community of monks— five hundred monks in all— proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī in the kingdom of the Kośalas.
Having arrived there, he was dwelling right there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī approached the Blessed One, bowed her head at his feet, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"O Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is rare; the teaching of the true Dharma is rare.

And now, the Blessed One has appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, and he teaches the Dharma that leads to peace, to final Nirvana—proclaimed by the Sugata, for the attainment of the Deathless and for the realization of Nirvana."
"It would be well, Blessed One, if women also might receive the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, let it not be pleasing to you that women should have the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
5. Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī thought:
"The Blessed One truly does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Having bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she stood weeping near the gate-chamber of the Jeta Grove monastery, scratching the ground with her big toe.

Now, a certain monk saw Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī standing near the gateway courtyard of the Jeta Grove, weeping and scratching the ground with her big toe; having seen her, he approached the Venerable Ānanda and said this to him.

"Venerable Ānanda, this Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī stands weeping near the courtyard of the Jeta Grove, scratching the ground with her big toe. Go, Venerable Ānanda, and find out why Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī is weeping.
Then the venerable Ānanda approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:
"Gautamī, why do you weep? When this was said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Enough of my weeping, Noble Ānanda, for the arising of a Buddha is so difficult to encounter, and the teaching of the True Dharma is so difficult to encounter."

The Blessed One has now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha; he teaches the Dharma that leads to peace, to final Nirvāṇa, as proclaimed by the Sugata, for the attainment of the Deathless and for the realization of Nirvāṇa.
Yet the Blessed One does not grant women the opportunity for going forth and full ordination within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
"It would be well, noble Ānanda, if you would entreat the Blessed One so that womankind might likewise obtain the going forth,
the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
"Very well, Gautamī," the venerable Ānanda replied to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and having approached the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and stood to one side.
He stood to one side.
Standing there, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is rare;
the teaching of the True Dharma is rare. Yet now, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, has appeared in the world."
And the Dharma is being taught— leading to peace, leading to final Nirvana, proclaimed by the Sugata, for the attainment of the Deathless, and conducing to the realization of Nirvana.
It would be well, Blessed One, if women also might receive the going-forth, the state of a novice, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"May it not please you, Gautamī’s mother, that women should receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Then, indeed, the venerable Ānanda...
"The Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth and receive full ordination into the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Having bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:
"Indeed, Gautamī, the Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth and receive full ordination into the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
When this had been said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

"It would be well, noble Ānanda, if you were to petition the Blessed One a second time, so that womankind might likewise obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

"Very well, Gautamī," the venerable Ānanda replied to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī for a second time, and having done so, he approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and [stood to one side].
He stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is rare; [all that follows] up to the state of being a bhikṣuṇī is likewise so. When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
O Gautamī, let the mother approve the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of being a bhikṣuṇī for women within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Ānanda, it is just as if a disease-king called *kāraṇḍava* were to descend upon a well-grown barley field;
in that way, that well-grown barley field becomes defiled by a great affliction. Even so, Gautamī.
In whatever teaching the female sex also receives the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī,

that teaching becomes defiled by a great secondary affliction. Just as, Gautamī, when sugarcane is ripe, the disease-king called *mañjiṣṭhā* [appears], so too that ripe sugarcane field becomes defiled by a great secondary affliction.

In the same way, Gautamī, whatever teaching in which women obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī— that teaching becomes defiled by a great corruption. Therefore, Gautamī, it does not please me that women should have the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
9. Then the venerable Ānanda, [thinking],

"The Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata," approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:

“Indeed, Gautamī, the Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, or to attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
When this was said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

“It would be well, noble Ānanda, if you were to petition the Blessed One a third time, so that women might also obtain going forth, full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”

"Very well, Gautamī," [the Blessed One replied]. Having assented to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī for a third time, the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how many assemblies did the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas have?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas had four assemblies, namely as follows:"
"Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, regarding these four fruits of the ascetic life, namely: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit, arhatship—"
"It is possible that even a single woman from among these, dwelling heedful, ardent, and secluded, can realize [these fruits].
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, as for these four fruits of the ascetic life—namely, the fruit of stream-entry up to the supreme fruit, arhatship—"
"It is possible that even this group of women, if they dwell alone, heedful, ardent, and resolute, may realize [this] for themselves.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Indeed, Blessed One, since the previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones had four assemblies—of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—"
These are the four fruits of asceticism, namely:
the fruit of stream-entry up to the supreme fruit of arhatship. Even a woman is capable of realizing these, provided she dwells heedful, ardent, and secluded.
“Excellent, Blessed One! May women also receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

Indeed, the Blessed One’s Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has performed what is difficult to do; she was his nurse, his foster-mother, and the giver of breast milk when his biological mother had passed away. And the Blessed One is grateful and appreciative. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

"It is so, Ānanda; it is so, Ānanda. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has performed a difficult task for the Tathāgata: she was his nurse, his foster-mother, his mother after his own mother had passed away, and she was the one who gave him milk.
And the Tathāgata is grateful and appreciative. Moreover, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has also performed a difficult task for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī."
Indeed, Ānanda, it was by coming to the Tathāgata that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went for refuge to the Buddha,
went for refuge to the Dharma,
and went for refuge to the Saṅgha; indeed, Ānanda, it was by coming to the Tathāgata that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī [did so].
[1] For as long as life lasts, they abstain from taking life; [2] for as long as life lasts, they abstain from taking what is not given;
[3] for as long as life lasts, they abstain from sexual misconduct.
For as long as life lasts, she abstained from false speech;
for as long as life lasts, she abstained from drinking fermented liquors, spirits, and intoxicants.
Indeed, Ānanda, it was by relying on the Tathāgata that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī increased in faith.
She increases in virtue, she increases in learning, she increases in renunciation,
and she increases in wisdom.
For it is by coming to the Tathāgata, Ānanda, that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī knows suffering and knows its origin.
He knows cessation;
he knows the path.
11. Ānanda, when one person, relying upon another person, goes for refuge to the Buddha,
goes for refuge to the Dharma,
and goes for refuge to the Saṅgha;
Ānanda, it is not easy for one person to repay another, even if one were to attend upon them for as long as life lasts with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
even so, it would not be easy to repay.
Ānanda, when one person, having relied upon another, refrains from taking life for as long as life lasts—[that is what makes repayment difficult].
For as long as life lasts, he abstains from taking what is not given;
for as long as life lasts, he abstains from sexual misconduct;
for as long as life lasts, he abstains from false speech.
As long as life lasts, one abstains from drinking fermented liquors, distilled spirits, and intoxicants.
It is not easy for this person to repay that person;
even for the rest of their life, they would not be able to serve them sufficiently.
Namely, with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
even so, it is not easily repaid.
For, Ānanda, when one person, by relying on another, increases in faith, increases in virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom—[it is not easily repaid].
Ānanda, it is not easy for this person to repay that person;
even if one were to attend upon him for as long as life lasts with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
even so, it would not be easy to repay him.
Ānanda, when one person, by relying on another person, comes to know suffering, knows its origin, knows its cessation, and knows the path,
it is not easy for this person to repay that other person,
even if they were to attend upon them for as long as life lasts with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Even so, it does not become easy for him to repay.
12. Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "If I were to reject Ānanda, the son of Gautama, even for a third time, there would be a change in his mind;
even the teachings he has heard would lead him to confusion."

"Granted, my True Dharma shall remain for even a thousand years. Let there be no alteration of the mind of Ānanda, the son of Gautamī, and let the teachings he has heard not fall into oblivion. Granted, my True Dharma shall remain for even five hundred years."
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, it is just as if a man were to build a bridge across a mountain pass merely so that water might not overflow; even so, Ānanda, does the Tathāgata prescribe these eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs."
The nuns must, for as long as life lasts, honor, revere, respect, and worship them, and not transgress them, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.
Which are the eight? The eight weighty dharmas. (1) Weighty dharma.
13. Ānanda, a nun who has been ordained for a hundred years must bow her head at the feet of a monk ordained on that very day.
This, Ānanda, is the first heavy rule for nuns, which must be honored by nuns as long as they live and never transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
Guru-dharma 2: When a maiden who has reached eighteen years of age has completed the two years of training and fulfilled her instruction, she may expect full ordination (upasampadā) in both Saṅghas.
This, Ānanda, is the second guru-dharma which must be honored and respected by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as life lasts, just as the ocean is respected by its tides.
Ānanda, the third *gurudharma* for the bhikṣuṇīs is this:
the path of speech from bhikṣuṇīs toward bhikṣus may be either true or untrue; however, the path of speech from a bhikṣu toward bhikṣuṇīs must be true and not untrue.
Ānanda, this is the third *gurudharma* of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live, and so forth.
Regarding the fourth *gurudharma*:
the foremost seat, bed, and dwelling must be yielded by the *bhikṣuṇīs* to the *bhikṣus*.
This, Ānanda, is the fourth *gurudharma*, which must be honored and revered by the *bhikṣuṇīs* for as long as they live, and so forth.

Ānanda, a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a guru-dharma must request a half-month period of *mānatva* from the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and she must also undergo the formal reconciliation (*āhvayana*) before both communities.
Ānanda, this is the fifth guru-dharma of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as they live, and so forth.

"Ānanda, every half-month, the bhikṣuṇīs must expect to approach the community of bhikṣus for instruction. This, Ānanda, is the sixth *gurudharma* of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live," and so on in detail.
Gurudharma 7:
It is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the rains retreat in a residence where there are no bhikṣus.
Ānanda, this is the seventh gurudharma of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live, and so forth in detail.
"Ānanda, bhikṣuṇīs who have resided for eight years must seek the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) from both Saṃghas.

Ānanda, this is the eighth *gurudharma* of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as they live, and which must not be transgressed, just like the tide."
"By the ocean, Ānanda.

These, Ānanda, are the eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live; they are not to be transgressed, just as the tide is not overstepped by the ocean.
14. If, Ānanda, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī accepts these eight weighty rules and trains herself in the training so as not to commit the four offenses involving defeat."
"This is your going-forth from this day forward;
this is your full ordination; this is your status as a bhikṣuṇī.
"Very well, Blessed One," the venerable Ānanda replied, and having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:
He said:
"Listen, Gautamī, to the word of the Blessed One.
Just as if, Gautamī, a man were to build a bridge here in this mountain gorge merely for the sake of crossing over the water."

For the sake of non-transgression, even so, Gautamī, the Blessed One has prescribed eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live, and which are not to be transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
15. What are the eight? Gautamī, a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for a hundred years must bow her head at the feet of a bhikṣu ordained on that very same day.

This, Gautamī, is the first heavy rule (gurudharma) for bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live and not transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore. Thus it is for all eight heavy rules.
That very thing was reported to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:

"If indeed you, Gautamī, accept these eight weighty rules (gurudharma) and train yourself in the training for not transgressing the four rules involving defeat (patanīya-dharma), then this itself shall be your going-forth from this day forward; this shall be your full ordination (upasampadā); this shall be your status as a bhikṣuṇī."

16. When this had been said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, it is just as if there were here a young man, fond of adornment, who has washed his head and is dressed in clean garments, and he should receive upon his head a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of campaka flowers, or a garland of white lotuses, or a garland of *tṛṇamoli* grass."

In the same way, noble Ānanda, I accept these eight weighty rules with my head bowed, and I shall train myself again and again in the training regarding the four rules involving defeat so as not to transgress them.

17. Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, the female slave Chandā, Chandaka’s mother, and five hundred Śākyan women, approached the Blessed One; having arrived, she bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
18. When the bhikṣuṇīs were standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to them:
"Therefore, bhikṣuṇīs, from this day forward, you should pay homage to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī as the elder of the Saṅgha, the senior of the Saṅgha, and the leader of the Saṅgha.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having extended her joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"Blessed One, these eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs which were spoken by the Blessed One in brief—may we now hear them explained in detail?"
19. The Blessed One said:
"It is obtainable. He asked: [Is it so?]

How then, Gautamī, must a nun who has been ordained for a hundred years perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful homage toward a monk ordained on that very day?
From now on, a nun must not wait [for such honors].

When I have been ordained for a hundred years and a monk is ordained on that very day, then I shall perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful homage.

20. Now, indeed, all the bhikṣuṇīs—whether senior, junior, or of middle standing—must perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful service toward all the bhikṣus, whether senior, junior, or of middle standing.
Now, when these monks have entered the nuns' quarters,

all the nuns— whether senior, junior, or of middle standing— must perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful homage toward all the monks, whether they be senior, junior, or of middle standing.
21. Now, if a bhikṣuṇī is weak from old age or weak from illness, she should prostrate with her head at the feet of as many [of them] as she is able to reach.
For the remaining ones, having placed her joined palms to their heads, she should say:
"I pay homage to the feet of all the noble ladies."

When these bhikṣuṇīs go out from the bhikṣu-vihāra, they must salute with their heads at the feet of all the bhikṣus—whether elders, novices, or those of middle standing. Now, if a bhikṣuṇī is weak from old age or weak from illness, she should salute with her head at the feet of as many as she is able; for the remainder, she should join her palms to their heads.
Having performed [the prostration], one should say:
"I bow my head at the feet of all the venerable ones.
22. That nun, out of contempt and disdain, having addressed them as "Koṇṭa-bhikṣus" or "Ḍhossa-bhikṣus"...

Or, having considered him a physician-monk, or having considered him a fool or a simpleton, or having considered him unskilled, or having considered him ungrateful, she does not bow her head to his feet; thus she transgresses a rule of respect.

"One who desires to train and applies herself to the yoga of the Buddhas' teaching— yet that nun, out of contempt or disdain, addressing him as 'a monk who is a mere child,' or 'a monk who is a physician,' or 'a monk with a topknot,' or 'one who is not diligent, nor senior, nor of natural wisdom, nor skilled,' and having thus insulted him, speaks [to him], she transgresses a rule of respect."

86. There is no path of speech for monks toward nuns, whether by truth or by falsehood; thus it is not permitted for a monk to speak abusively to a nun, saying, "Shaven-headed woman," or "Mouth-severer.
If he speaks thus, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
87. Now, if a monk’s mother or sister has gone forth as a female renunciant and she is arrogant or haughty, [the following applies].
It is not permissible to neglect her if she is still young;
she should be told:
"O relative, if you do not train now, when will you ever train?"

"What now? When you have become aged, old, and advanced in years, it would be excellent and fitting for you that you should take up the teachings, recite them, be noble, virtuous, and desirous of training, and apply yourself to the discipline of the Buddhas.
Now, when she has indeed become old..."
She should be addressed thus:
"O relative, you are like this now; what were you like in your youth? You do not train yourself now; when will you ever train?
When you have reached the door of the assembly hall, then you will train—will you? This which belongs to you...
"Even that assembly, seeing you, would fall into misfortune through improper conduct by imitating you.
It is well for you, it is fitting for you, that you should teach, recite, be auspicious, virtuous, desirous of training, and apply yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Gautamī, this is the range of speech for nuns toward monks, whether in truth or otherwise."
Or [it may be] by means of what is untrue.
The path of speech for monks toward nuns is by means of what is true, not by means of what is untrue.

This, Gautamī, is the third heavy rule (gurudharma) of the nuns, which must be honored by the nuns for as long as life lasts, and which must not be transgressed, just as the shore cannot be overstepped by the great ocean.
Gurudharma 4.89: Now, Gautamī, the foremost meal, the foremost bedding and seating, and the foremost dwelling must be offered by the bhikṣuṇīs to the community of bhikṣus.
If anyone now prepares a meal for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, they should be told: [“This is not to be done”].
"Perform the seniority rotation.
Then, if he says, "I have no faith there, I have no confidence," he should be told,
"We do not accept [that either]."
Then he said: "Previously,
my mother or my father, or through a connection with a guild, a trade association, or a formal agreement, never before have I provided food for these venerable gentlemen."

"May the noble ladies accept it"—even if one has had as little as a single morsel of alms-food given, if the community of nuns accepts food of a hundred flavors for the community of monks, there is no offense.
90. Now, what is the "best of lodgings"?
It is when someone now gives lodging and bedding to the community of nuns.
"Give it to the senior [monk] in turn," he says.
Then, if he replies, "I have no faith there; I have no confidence," one must say, "We do not accept it either. One must say this. One must say this.
"We also do not accept it."
Then he said:

"Noble lady, bedding and seating have been given by me previously to the community of monks, whether by measure or up to the limit of the agreement. May the noble ladies accept it, at least for a single night."
If one causes a couch to be given to the community of monks, and the community of nuns accepts highly valuable bedding and seating, there is no offense.
91. What now is "the foremost monastery"?
This refers to when someone establishes a monastery for the community of nuns.
It should be said:
"Establish it as the senior succession. Then he said:
"Noble lady, I have no faith there;
I have no serene confidence," [the other] should say, "We do not accept it either."
Then he said:

"Noble lady, these monasteries have been caused to be built for them by you, whether by your mother or through some family connection; may the noble ladies accept the monastery. At the very least, having caused even a cow-dung hut or a flour-paste hut to be given to the community of monks, the community of nuns [should do likewise].
Even if she accepts a dwelling with seven stories, there is no offense.
92. These nuns, out of contempt or disdain, [address them] as "barber-monks" or "physician-monks."

Whether she is unsteady, elderly, or ignorant of the proper way, if she causes the community of monks to be satisfied with the first portion of food, the first portion of bedding and seating, or the best dwelling, she transgresses a rule of respect.
Gautamī, in this same manner, the community of monks must be satisfied by the nuns with the first portion of food, the first portion of bedding and seating, and the best dwelling.
Gautamī, this is the fourth rule of respect for the nuns, which must be honored by the nuns for as long as they live and not transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
5.93. Now, what is the procedure for a nun who has committed a *gurudharma*? She must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month and be summoned before both Saṃghas.
Now, if that nun has indeed committed a *gurudharma*, she must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month in the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha and be summoned before both Saṃghas.

If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, or thinking "she is unskilled," having fallen into a heavy offense (gurudharma), does not undergo the penance (mānatva) for half a month within the community of nuns,
nor is she summoned before both communities,
she transgresses the heavy offense.

This, Gautamī, is the fifth *gurudharma* of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as life lasts, just as the great ocean honors its shore. 6. Now, what is this? Every half-month, the bhikṣuṇīs must expect the approach of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus for the purpose of receiving instruction (*ovāda*). On the day when the *poṣadha* occurs, on that very day, the Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs—
One must go to the monks' residence.
Now, if the entire Saṃgha does not go, half of the Saṃgha must go. If half of the Saṃgha does not go, eight of those who are senior in seniority must go.

The eight senior nuns do not go [to give their consent] unless they have at least been on a month-long or fortnight-long journey; having obtained the consent of those who are eligible to give it, they may then depart.
If there is time, the stūpa must first be venerated.
Having venerated the stūpa, the consent should be given to whichever monk there is who is distinguished or well-known.
It should be said: "I pay homage to the noble Saṅgha.
The noble, harmonious Bhikṣuṇī Saṅgha bows its head at the feet of the harmonious Bhikṣu Saṅgha and requests the Dharma of approaching for instruction."
And he accepts the Poṣadha;
it should be stated a second and a third time as well. 95. Then, he says:

Thinking, "I am the elder of the Saṃgha," "I am the instructor there," or "I am the exhorter of the bhikṣuṇīs," those [bhikṣuṇīs] must also set aside these three and give their consent (*chanda*) for the remaining [members]. Having given their consent, they should go to the bhikṣuṇī residence at the time when the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has assembled for the *poṣadha* ceremony and the reciter of the Sūtras has taken up the Sūtra.

May the noble Saṃgha listen to me: today for the Saṃgha there is either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, or it is the *sandhi-poṣadha* (the junction-fast), and the lunar mansion is pure; so much of the season has passed and so much remains.
What is the prior duty of the Saṃgha?
The community of the Blessed One’s female disciples shines with few concerns and few duties. You should announce the consent and purity of those noble ladies who have not yet arrived.
When the *chanda* has been brought by the *chandahārikās*, they should ascend to the end of the assembly of elders, perform the *sāmīci* salutation, and say:
"The *chanda* has been brought by us, the *chandahārikās*, and accepted by the Venerable one named so-and-so.
At the time when the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) is seated and the reciter of the Sūtras has received the Sūtra...

"May the Saṃgha listen to me, venerable sirs. Today for the Saṃgha there is either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, or it is the *sandhi-poṣadha* (the junction-fast), or the day of the pure constellation.
So much of the season has passed, and so much remains.
What has been done by the Saṃgha previously? The community of disciples of the Blessed One shines when it has few concerns and few duties."
"Venerable ones, announce the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pāriśuddhi*) of the monks who have not arrived; and once it has been announced, report that it has been done.
Which monk shall be the conveyor of the consent for the nuns? Having been thus addressed, he should rise, go to the end of the senior monks' row, and speak.
I pay homage to the noble Saṅgha; for the entire Bhikṣuṇī Saṅgha, being united, bows its head at the feet of the united [Saṅgha],
requests instruction,
and accepts the Poṣadha.
In this way, it should be said a second and a third time.
If there is a monk who has been formally authorized as the instructor of the nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-ovādaka*) present there, he should be addressed: "Please give the instruction.
97. Now, if there is no monk at all who is the instructor of the nuns, then whoever is endowed with the twelve factors should be formally authorized.
By which twelve? Namely:
he dwells restrained by the Prātimokṣa vows, perfected in conduct and sphere of activity.
Seeing danger even in the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training; he is endowed with pure bodily and vocal actions, possesses a completely purified livelihood,
is learned in the Abhidharma, is well-versed in the Vinaya, and is capable of disciplining others in the training of higher ethics.
He is capable of training in the higher training of the mind (adhicitta-śikṣā). Tṛ. He is capable of training in the higher training of wisdom (adhiprajñā-śikṣā).
Phu.
And he becomes one whose holy life is unassailed;
that is, he becomes one who is predominantly disposed toward patience.
Hrā!
Furthermore, she does not commit any of the grave offenses (gurudharma) against the nuns;
she is pleasant in speech and endowed with the skill of eloquent expression.
One who is endowed with speech that is clear, distinct, and intelligible in its meaning,
and who is twenty years of age or more than twenty years of age—
such a person, being endowed with these twelve factors, should be formally appointed by the community as a teacher of the nuns.
98. The action must be performed by the officiating monk:

"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen to me. This monk named so-and-so is endowed with the necessary qualities. If it is the right time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha, by a formal motion (*saṃmutī*), authorize this monk named so-and-so as the instructor of the nuns (*bhikṣuṇītovādaka*). This is the proposal (*jñapti*)."

"Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me. This monk named so-and-so is being formally authorized by the Saṅgha through a formal motion (saṃmuti) to serve as the exhorter of the nuns. Those venerable ones who consent to the authorization by the Saṅgha of this monk named so-and-so as the exhorter of the nuns through a formal motion should remain silent."
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
This is the first formal motion; likewise the second and the third formal motion.
Venerable sirs, the Saṃgha has approved the monk named so-and-so as the instructor of the nuns by means of a formal authorization from the Saṃgha.
Since there is silence, it is approved by the Saṃgha; thus do I understand this.
99. Now, being one who has been so appointed, those bhikṣuṇīs must be exhorted at the proper time and not at an improper time, and in a proper place and not in an improper place.
Not in the future time;
not in the past time;
not according to one's own will.
Not distractedly;
not as a member of a faction;
not with long-winded speech.
[One] should send [a messenger] for one who wishes to arrive.
Now, what is "the wrong time"? The wrong time is when the sun has set.
And when dawn has appeared,
why is it not a proper place? A "non-place" (adeśa) is said to be in the vicinity of a brothel or in the vicinity of a gambling hall.
Near a tavern or near a slaughterhouse or prison; or in a place that is too secluded or too exposed.
What, then, is "not yet come time"? It is called not yet come time when it is the first or the second day of the lunar fortnight.
What then is meant by "not having let the time pass"?
The time that has passed refers to the fourteenth or the fifteenth day.
Rather, she should be exhorted starting from the third day until the thirteenth day.
Why is it that now consent is not given by individual choice?
A nun who is an instructor must give her consent;
rather, all must come together.
Why is it that one should not exhort the Saṃgha of nuns while it is divided? A monk must not exhort a divided Saṃgha of nuns;
rather, they must be exhorted when they are all assembled together. [6]
Why is it that you do not exhort the assembly? You must not say, "Your assembly is not yet ready to be exhorted," or "Today is not your turn to exhort the assembly.
Rather, the entire assembly should be exhorted together as a harmonious whole.
Now, since they have not been instructed with a long discourse,
they should rather be instructed in brief:
"To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,"
"The purification of one's own mind—this is the instruction of the Buddhas."
Sisters, this is the instruction; the remainder will be a formal discourse. Whoever wishes to come, let her come;
whoever wishes to listen, let her listen.
100. Now, what should be sent for one who intends to arrive?
If that monk who instructs the nuns has gone to another region, then those who are his co-residents or pupils should be encouraged by the community of nuns:
"Go and bring the noble one's bowl and robes."
Now, as they go and come, there must be no lack of provisions on the road.
When one is arriving, the community of nuns should go out to meet them for a distance of one *yojana* with parasols, banners, and flags.
Once they have entered the monastery, the community of both monks and nuns must provide them with food for seven days.
Now, if the community of nuns is poor, the community of monks must provide them with food for seven days;

at the very least, they must be honored with even a single offering of almsfood. That monk who exhorts the nuns should maintain the perception of them as daughters, and those nuns should maintain the perception of that monk who exhorts them as a father.
101. It is not permissible for that monk who exhorts the nuns to exhort them while stretching out his neck like a horse.
Rather, he should look only as far as the distance of a yoke; otherwise, they should not be exhorted.
If, however, there should ever be [an obstruction] there, such as a tuft of hair, [he may look further].
Or with eyes cast down, or with robes that have been beaten,
or with a white waistband,
or with variegated sandals.
It is not permissible to neglect her.
If she is still young, she should be corrected:
"O unrefined and unskilled woman, if you do not train now, when will you train—when you have become old, aged, and advanced in years?"
"You will have reached the age of one who has traveled the road; even this assembly of yours, seeing you and following your example, will fall into ruin through unrighteousness.
It would be good for you, and it would be fitting for you, if you were to become auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training, and apply yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas."
Now, if she is old, it should be said:
"O relative, you have now become like this; what were you like in your youth? If you do not train now, when will you train?
When you reach the entrance of the assembly hall, even this assembly of yours will see you."

"By falling into misconduct, she will meet with calamity through this [act]. It would be well for you, and it would be fitting for you, if you were to become auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training, and apply yourself to yoga within the teaching of the Buddhas. 102. Now, when that instructor of nuns has gone out for alms and sees nuns on the street with their hair curled, or otherwise styled, [he should address them as follows].
Or with eyes that are wide-open;
or with robes that have been beaten and pressed;
or with a white waist-band.
From Citrakūṭa, one should not now speak at all, even with sandals on;
lest people should criticize us, saying, "Look, sirs! This little śramaṇa is instructing his female disciple as if she were his wife.
Rather, she should be questioned.
"In which monastery does she reside?
Who is her preceptor (upādhyāyinī)?
Who is her teacher (ācāryā)? Having gone there, she should be instructed. Thus it was said.
If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, treats him as a "corner-monk" (koṇṭabhikṣu),

or as a "physician-monk" (vaidyabhikṣu), or as a "shaven-headed monk" (cūḍabhikṣu), or treats him as one who is incompetent, aged, unskilled, and lacking natural discernment, and thus does not expect to go for the fortnightly exhortation from the community of monks, she transgresses a weighty rule (gurudharma).
Thus, Gautamī, every half-month the nuns must expect to approach the community of monks for instruction.

If she does not so expect, she transgresses a heavy rule (gurudharma). This, Gautamī, is the sixth heavy rule for the nuns, which must be honored by the nuns for as long as they live and never transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
Gurudharma 7.103. Why is it now not permissible for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the rains retreat in a residence where there are no bhikṣus?
It is not permissible for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the rains retreat in villages or towns where there are no bhikṣus.

Now, if a nun is invited by her relatives living in the village, saying, "Venerable lady, please spend the rains retreat here," and there are no monks present there, yet the nun wishes to show compassion toward her relatives, she should say: "First, invite the senior assembly."
Then they said:
"We have no faith there; we have no serene confidence."
It should be said:
"I do not desire it either.
Now, if the nun possesses wealth, [she may take it].
And wishing to show compassion toward her kinsmen,
she herself should invite the monks;
once they have arrived, she should ensure that there is no lack of food for them.
They should enter the rains retreat there;
that nun, while staying there for the rains, should expect to approach those monks for instruction every half-month.
Now, when those monks have entered the rains retreat, let there be the interval between the rains.
Some danger arises and they rise up and flee.
Now, it is no longer permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to go anywhere until the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
If, meanwhile, it is safe, then they should be summoned.
Now, it is not [the case that] guests [should be invited].
Rather, one should invite those who have been previously mentioned.
When they have arrived, having honored them with food and provided them with clothing, one should give to them according to the distribution.

When invited, even if one’s own desire leads one elsewhere, there is no offense. (105) If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, regarding [the monks] as "stunted monks," or regarding them as "physician-monks," or regarding them as "shaveling monks," or regarding them as "dull, old, unskilled, and ignorant of the nature of things," enters the rains retreat at a residence where no monks are present, it is a heavy offense (*gurudharma*).

[The Buddha said: "It transgresses [the rule]. Thus, Gautamī, it is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to enter the rains retreat in a residence where there are no bhikṣus. This, Gautamī, is the seventh *gurudharma* of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live, and which must not be transgressed, just as the shore [cannot be overstepped] by the great ocean."
Gurudharma 8.106: Now, how is it that nuns who have completed the rains retreat should expect the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) from both Saṅghas?
On the very day that the invitation of the Saṅgha takes place, on that day the nuns must perform the invitation.
On the first day after the following day, at dawn, those [nuns] should go out and proceed to the bhikṣu monastery.
If the community of bhikṣus is complete, it is not permissible for all the bhikṣuṇīs to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony simultaneously; rather, one *pravāraṇā*-performer must be formally appointed.
The nun who is capable of conducting the *pravāraṇā*—
thereupon, the officiant shall perform the formal act:
"May the noble Saṃgha listen to me."
This nun, named so-and-so, is capable of conducting the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint this nun, named so-and-so, as the official who conducts the invitation ceremony for the Saṃgha. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
May the noble Saṃgha listen to me:
this nun named so-and-so is capable of conducting the Pravāraṇā ceremony.
The Saṃgha appoints this nun named so-and-so as the Pravāraṇā officer for the Saṃgha.
Whichever noble ladies approve of the nun named so-and-so being appointed by the Saṅgha as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṅgha,
let her remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let her speak.
This is the first formal motion;
in the same way, the second and third formal motions are to be stated.
"Venerable ladies, the one named so-and-so has been approved by the Saṃgha as the *pravāraṇā*-officer for the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha consents to this, since there is silence. Thus do I understand.
(108) Then, all [the nuns] must stand at the end of the row of elders (*vṛddhānta*).
Then, that *pravāraṇā*-officer must say:
The entire community of nuns invites the entire community of monks regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected:

"May the noble Saṃgha, desiring our welfare, seeking our benefit, and being compassionate, exhort us out of compassion. Knowing, seeing, and remembering, we shall act according to the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Thus a second and a third time.
Now, if the community of nuns is complete and there are many monks present, it should be said:
"The complete community of nuns invites the many monks regarding what has been seen, heard, and so forth; we shall make amends."
A second time, and a third time.
Now, if the community of bhikṣuṇīs is complete and there is one bhikṣu present,
it should be said:
"The entire community of nuns invites the noble one [to point out faults] regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; we shall make amends"—thus it is said a second and a third time.
Now, if there are many nuns and the community of monks is complete...
"Venerable ladies, many of you invite the entire community of monks to question you regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, up until we shall make amends.
This is said a second and a third time.
Now, it may be that there are many bhikṣuṇīs and many bhikṣus.
It should be said:
"The many noble ladies invite the many noble gentlemen for the *pravāraṇā* regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, up to:
'We shall deal with it according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.'"
In this same way for a second and a third time.
Now, if there are many bhikṣuṇīs and only one bhikṣu is present:
It should be said:
"The many noble ladies invite the noble one for the *pravāraṇā*; we shall deal with whatever is seen, heard, or suspected according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.
This is to be repeated a second and a third time.
Now, if there is only one nun and the Saṃgha is complete,
it should be said:
"I, [name], invite the Saṃgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the noble Saṃgha exhort me; I shall act accordingly. Thus a second and a third time. Now, if there is only one bhikṣuṇī:
If there are many monks present,
one should say:
"I, [name], invite the many noble sirs to speak of what they have seen, heard, or suspected."
"May the noble ladies instruct me so that I may act according to the Dharma.
This is to be said a second and a third time.
Now, if there is only one nun present...
There is one monk; he should say:
"I, named so-and-so, invite the noble one regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."

"May the noble one, desiring my welfare, seeking my benefit, compassionate and full of pity, instruct me out of compassion; knowing, seeing, and remembering, I shall act according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.
Thus a second and a third time.
If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, or thinking "he is a dull-witted monk," [does not heed her].
Whether he is regarded as a "physician-monk," or a "tonsure-monk," or as one who is incompetent, aged, unskilled, and lacking natural discernment— if,
after having spent the rains retreat, he does not expect the invitation from both Saṃghas, he transgresses a weighty rule (gurudharma).
Thus, Gautamī, bhikṣuṇīs who have completed the rains retreat must request the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) from both Saṅghas.

This, Gautamī, is the eighth weighty rule (*gurudharma*) for bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by bhikṣuṇīs for as long as life lasts, and not transgressed, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.

Gautamī, these are the eight *gurudharmas* for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, respected, and worshiped by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live; they are not to be transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
They are like the *pārājika* rules.
[The first is: sexual intercourse.

111. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣuṇīs: "Therefore, bhikṣuṇīs, from this day forward, you should regard Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī as the elder of the Saṅgha, the senior of the Saṅgha, and the leader of the Saṅgha.
"Blessed One, these four dharmas leading to downfall which have been taught by the Blessed One after his direct realization—Blessed One, may we hear them in detail?"
The Blessed One said: "It is permitted, Gautamī.

For a faithful daughter of good family who perceives five reasons, it is sufficient to point out the discipline (vinaya) and sufficient to maintain the discipline just as in the discipline for monks."
113. This is one occasion, Gautamī, when the Tathāgata was dwelling in Śrāvastī.

Then, [the question arose] regarding the Elder Śāriputra, up to: "What indeed, Blessed One, is the cause, what is the reason, by which, upon the passing away of some Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, the teaching remains long-lasting and the True Dharma remains long-lasting," as it is set forth in the Bhikṣu-vinaya.
This was one occasion, Gautamī, when the Tathāgata was staying at Vaiśālī. [The story of Yaśikā] is related in detail as the first origin.
Therefore, Gautamī, a bhikṣuṇī also must train in this very same rule.
The second origin of the matter concerning two Licchavi youths;
the third, that there is no renunciation of the training for a bhikṣuṇī;
the fourth, that there is no formal act of revealing weakness.
The origin of the story concerning Nandika is the fifth;
the origin of the story concerning Markaṭī is the sixth.
Therefore, Gautamī, the bhikṣuṇīs should train in this very matter in detail.
114. Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs.
