If she, thinking, "I will not disclose this to others so that others may not know of it," [conceals it],
this nun becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained;
[the rest as before].
"Knowing" means she should know it herself, or hear it from another, through a reliable sight or hearing.
"A grave offense" (*duṣṭhullām āpattiṃ*) means that one of the various [eight] grave offenses has been committed or transgressed;
"she should not announce it to others" means she should not speak of it.
"Alone" (*ekāye*) means by herself.
"Among the great multitude" means among two or three;
"in the midst of the Saṃgha" means within a complete Saṃgha;
"fallen" means she has fallen from the holy life (brahmacarya).
"Dead" means deceased;
"seated and dejected" means having entered the state of a householder;
"fallen away from this Dharma and Vinaya" means having gone over to the sphere of other sectarians.
Then that nun might say to the nuns:
"Venerable ladies, I indeed knew that the nun named so-and-so had committed and repeatedly practiced a grave offense."
Thinking, "I shall not tell others so that no one else may know of this," that nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Beyond" (pāra) is said to be the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna);
[and so on] as far as "designation" (prajñapti).
133. This nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhulla-āpatti) at sunrise, yet she does not form the intention to conceal it.
At the time when the sun is about to rise, she forms the intention to conceal it; thus, at the breaking of dawn, this nun becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense.
In this manner, two sessions and eight recitations are to be performed,
as prescribed for concealment in the Bhikṣu-vinaya.
Now, suppose that nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhullā āpatti).
Now, she must inform another person.
If she is a female pupil (antevāsini) or a co-resident (sārdhavihāriṇī) and sees [the offense],
yet conceals it out of attachment, thinking, "If I report this now, the nuns will expel me," she becomes guilty of a Pārājika offense.
This nun sees another nun committing an offense. She then informs the others: "I have seen the nun named so-and-so committing a grave offense.
[The other nun thinks: "I see that if she reports this, she will now be expelled by the nuns; therefore, I too shall conceal it."
She too sees that if she were to report it, both would be expelled; thus, she conceals it.
She also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. In this way, as many as conceal it, all become *pārājika*.
This nun sees another nun committing a grave offense;
she informs others, saying:
"The nun named so-and-so has committed a grave offense."
She then said,
"You have committed a wrong by informing me;
do not inform anyone else either," and she incurs a *thūl'-accaya* offense.
If this nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhullāpatti),
she must inform yet another nun;
however, if she is fierce or acts with violence, she may see [the situation] and [act accordingly].
"If [the nun] obtains equanimity, thinking, 'May this not cause an obstacle to my life or an obstacle to my holy life,' there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, knowing that another nun has committed and indulged in a grave offense (duṣṭhullāpatti), should conceal it..."

She must not report this to others among the great assembly of monks when there is a disturbance. When that nun has fallen away from the nuns—having died, passed away, despaired, or departed from this Dharma and Vinaya—then a nun might say to the nuns: "Venerable ladies, I indeed knew that the nun named so-and-so had committed and repeatedly indulged in a grave offense."
If she thinks, "I shall not inform others;
let no one else know of this," that nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer to be lived with.
Pārājika Dharma 8: Following One Who Has Been Expelled 134. The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come forth...
[The] usual formula [applies]. Wandering from various monasteries, he eventually resided at Kauśāmbī in the Ghoṣitārāma.
At that time, the venerable Chandaka committed one or another offense among the five classes of offenses.
He was addressed by the monks: "Venerable Chandaka, do you see this offense?
He then said:
"I do not see it; do you all see it either?"
"Let them see her fallen!
What indeed is the use of this wicked woman to me?
The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, if this Chandaka suppresses any one of the five classes of offenses and does not perceive that offense..."
Therefore, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act of suspension against him for his failure to see an offense.
The Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension against him;
he does not share in the enjoyment of the Dharma nor in the enjoyment of material goods with them.
Now his mother was residing in another bhikṣuṇī monastery;
he went there and said,
"Sister, I have been suspended by the Saṃgha."
"He does not share with me either the enjoyment of the Dharma or the enjoyment of material things.
She then said,
"Venerable Chanda, you are not capable [of this]."
"I shall share with you both the enjoyment of the Dharma and the enjoyment of material things.
She then shared with her both the enjoyment of the Dharma and the enjoyment of material things.
Thereupon, she was addressed by the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Noble lady, this noble Chandaka has indeed been suspended by the complete Saṃgha according to the Dharma and Vinaya; he has not yet performed the act of atonement.
Noble lady, do not follow after this monk.
The Blessed One said:
"O noble ladies, as long as I am not free from fault, who else will follow this monk?
I myself shall follow this monk."
"Why should I not comply with this? Why should I not follow this?
Those bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī then reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said: "If this nun Chandakamātā continues to support the monk Chandaka, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed reparation,
then go and, three times in private, three times in a group, and three times in the midst of the Saṃgha, admonish her for the relinquishing of this matter."

Then she was addressed at Kuvega: "Is it true, noble lady Chandakamātā, that you continue to associate with the noble Āryachandaka, who has been suspended by the harmonious Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed penance?
She replied:
"Yes, I am so addressed at Kuvega."

"Noble Chandakamātā, do not follow the noble Āryacchandaka, who has been suspended by the complete Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed the act of atonement.
Indeed, Noble Chandakamātā, that which a friend should do for you—one who desires your welfare, seeks your benefit, and acts as your friend—is this: they depart after speaking one word;
two words remain. Desist! [She replied: 'I will not desist.'"
In this manner, it should be done a second and a third time.
Thus, an inquiry should be made before the great assembly in the midst of the Saṅgha until she says, "I do not desist.
Those bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Blessed One, the noble Chandakamātā has been approached three times in private, three times before the great assembly, and three times in the midst of the Saṅgha for the relinquishing of this matter, yet she does not relinquish it.
The Blessed One said, “Summon Chandakamātā.”
She was then summoned,
and the Blessed One said:
"Is it true, Chandakamātā?"
"Thus indeed you associate with the monk Chandaka, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed the act of atonement.
You have been approached three times in private, three times in a group, and three times in the midst of the Saṃgha for the purpose of relinquishing this matter, yet you do not relinquish it.
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Chandakamātā!

Indeed, Chandakamātā, in many ways I have censured difficult speech and spoken in dispraise of difficult speech; yet you, it seems, are harsh and abrasive, perverse, and one who grasps what is contrary to the Dharma."
"Chandaka-mātā, this is not the Dharma;
this is not the Vinaya; this is not the teaching of the Teacher.
One must not act thus; one must not do thus."
For one who acts in this way, there is no increase in wholesome qualities.
And now, knowing this, you side with a monk who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.

Therefore, it is not permissible for one who knows to side with a monk who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, as long as he has not performed the act of reconciliation.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "Gautamī, assemble as many bhikṣuṇīs as there are who dwell in dependence upon the city of Kauśāmbī,
until the training rule has been prescribed."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself, or hear it from another, through a formal act of seeing or a formal act of hearing.
"By a complete *saṃgha*" means by one that is not divided.
"By means of the Dharma and Vinaya, through not seeing an offense, through not making amends for an offense, and through not relinquishing three types of views—
he is 'suspended,' meaning he has been made subject to non-association;
he is 'not reinstated,' meaning he has not been restored."
"She should associate" means she should associate with him either through the enjoyment of material goods or through the enjoyment of the Dharma.
That nun should be addressed by the nuns in this way:
"Venerable lady, this monk has been [suspended] by the harmonious Saṃgha."
The full passage continues as before:
if she should accept that very same matter and not relinquish it— namely, that she follows a suspended monk—
that nun is like Chandakamātā.

"By the nuns" means by the Saṃgha, by a group of many people, or by a single individual; she is to be exhorted and admonished up to three times. Three times in private among a group of many people, and three times in the midst of the Saṃgha, she is to be told:

"Is it true, O so-and-so, that you continue to follow one who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed the act of atonement?"
He says, "It is raw.
Then she should be told:
"Noble lady, do not side with the monk named so-and-so, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya."

"Whatever indeed should be done for you, O [Name], by a friend who desires your welfare and seeks your benefit, she does that for you. That friend has addressed you with one remaining word: 'Desist! You replied, 'I will not desist. This was said a second and a third time... (and so on).
Even in the midst of the Saṅgha, if she should, up to three times, be told, "Renounce this matter," and she renounces it, that is well;
but if she does not renounce it, this nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Regarding the term *pārājika*: it is the designation for the manifestation, disclosure, exposition, analysis, clarification, and making plain of a *pārājika* offense.

137. This nun, being exhorted and admonished three times in private regarding a matter that ought to be relinquished, does not relinquish it; she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (vinayātikrama) for each word [spoken].

Being exhorted and admonished three times in the midst of the community, if she does not relinquish the matter that ought to be relinquished, she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline for every single word.

If one consents to the formal motion (*jñapti*) in the midst of the Saṃgha, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*). When the first proclamation (*vācā*) has been made, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline; when it has been proclaimed a second time, one incurs a grave offense (*thūl'-accaya*).
When the second speech is superimposed, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*);
when that speech is removed, one incurs a grave offense (*thūl'-accaya*).
When the third speech is superimposed, one incurs a grave offense.
When she has been expelled, she becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense;
that is, when she has fallen into a *pārājika* offense.

And those transgressions of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*) and grave offenses (*thūl'-atyaya*) which occurred during the great assembly in the state of agitation or within the midst of the Saṅgha—all of these are suspended, and only one heavy offense remains.
If this [nun] is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense,
but desists in the interim, she should be made to undergo the formal act (*kārāpayitavyā*) regarding the five remaining categories of offenses.
Now, how is that which is "worthy of relinquishment" (*pratiniḥsargārha*) to be understood?
"Did you say, 'Will you follow such-and-such a suspended monk, even though he is not fit to be followed'?
"I did not follow him; I am following him now, and I shall follow him. In this way, it is fit to be relinquished. What then is that which was not fit to be relinquished?

"I shall comply with the monk named so-and-so who has been suspended. Having now complied, [he thinks] "I do not comply" or "I shall comply"—this is to be regarded as being unworthy of relinquishment.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

If a nun, knowing that a monk has been suspended by a unanimous Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and has not yet performed penance, should continue to associate with him, that nun is to be addressed by the other nuns as follows:
"Venerable lady, this monk has indeed been suspended by a unanimous Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and he has not yet performed penance;
do not associate with this monk."
And if that nun, being thus addressed by the nuns,
should persist in that matter and not relinquish it, that nun is to be formally exhorted and admonished by the nuns up to three times for the relinquishment of that matter.
If, while being exhorted or admonished up to three times, she relinquishes that matter, that is good.
And if she does not desist from it, this nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Summary verse: sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, and killing.
False association, the eightfold matter,
concealing faults, and following one who has been suspended.
The category is fulfilled.
The *pārājika* offenses are concluded. [Now follows] the *saṃcaritra*.
138. Regarding the act of matchmaking (*saṃcaritrakarma*), everything concerning the monks is literal; as the Blessed One has said:

"If a nun should engage in matchmaking—whether she conveys a woman’s intention to a man, or conveys a man’s intention to a woman, whether for marriage or for a lover—even if only for a momentary union."

Furthermore, this dharma is one involving an initial offense; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, meaning that the remainder depends upon the Saṃgha, and the means of deliverance is achieved by relying solely upon the Saṃgha.
This is the second *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharma.
The groundless [charge] and the two [cases of] what is non-existent are to be treated in the same manner as for the monks,
up until that which the Blessed One said.

If a nun, out of malice, anger, and resentment, being displeased, should groundlessly charge a pure nun who is free from offense with a *pārājika* offense, thinking, "Perhaps I might cause her to fall away from the holy life," and if at a later time, whether she is interrogated or not, that legal case is found to be groundless— [this constitutes an offense].
If a nun, being at fault, persists in her fault and says, "I speak out of malice," this too, in this category,
is an offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṃgha (saṃghāvaśeṣa) committed immediately, even if it is merely a slight matter.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun, being malicious, out of malice, angry, and displeased, should, on account of some minor point or mere fragment of another matter, accuse a nun who is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense with a *pārājika* offense."
"Perhaps I might cause her to fall from her celibate life. Later on, when she is being questioned or exhorted, that legal case becomes something entirely different;
and of that different legal case, she grasps at some mere fraction or particle of a point, and the nun persists in her fault through her own fault.
"I say," this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* Dharma 4:
*Ussayavāda* (Groundless Accusation).
139. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a nunnery and a dwelling for non-Buddhist ascetics situated between two walls.
That rag-robe fell there in the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra; at that time,
there was a resident bhikṣuṇī named Sthūlanandā.
She then said,
"O heretics, make this rag-robe!
You are shameless and devoid of modesty, having fallen away from shame and dread of blame."

The noble ladies, being endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, saw them entering and exiting at both the proper and improper times, and their minds became afflicted. They then said, "This is the rainy season; when the rains have passed, we shall do it then."
She then said,
"Do it right now!
But they did not do it.
Then she reviled them: "You who have fallen from long life, lost your lifespan, whose hopes are shattered, you who have fallen away from the gods like donkeys of a carriage—you will not do it!
How can you be naked?
You are shameless and without modesty; you are ruined by a lack of shame and modesty, possessing false views, and cast down into ruin."
"Make this patched garment.
They then said, "O daughter of Itikitika, you who are nourished by *vaḍaḍiṅgara* [food], you ascetic woman! If you die, we will not make this patched garment.
She then went and reported this to Āsande.
Having reported all of this, he said, "Long-lived one, act in such a way that those rags (*kaṇṭhā*) are made. The attendants were faithful and devout; they then said, "Summon the *miśrasthā*."
They were then summoned.
Those attendants said:
"O sons of Itikitikā! You naked heretics, fallen from the state of the gods, you donkeys for vehicles, you who have been cast down by false views!"
"Go and make that rag-robe!
You are shameless and lack modesty, whereas the noble ladies are endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame.
When they see you entering and exiting at all hours, both by day and by night, it will cause a disturbance in the minds of those noble ladies who lead the holy life. Then, by those attendants...
Appointed against their will, they were made to work;
by day they raised up a wall,
and at night it was washed away by the rain.
Now, as they were performing their work for three months, that time passed. They then said,
"We shall do the clay-work for this nun, the daughter of Itikitika, who is well-nourished by *vaḍaḍiṅgara*."

The lay followers (upāsakas) were complaining: "See, householders! Your object of veneration, the female ascetic (śramaṇikā), thinking 'I have power,' has made us perform labor for three months against our will. The lay followers reported this matter to the family-visiting nuns (kulopikā bhikṣuṇīs), and the nuns in turn reported it to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Call Nandā."
She was then summoned:
"Is it true, Nanda?
and so forth.
Until they have become completely purified.

Furthermore, if a nun should dwell speaking with praise [of herself] among householders or wanderers, for a day or even for a moment, at least together with monastery attendants or novice monks, this too is an offense involving immediate transgression.
"Furthermore, if a nun" means one who has received full ordination.
"Should dwell with contentious talk" means they should engage in quarreling.
"With householders" means with laypeople. "With wanderers" means from the Gautamas down to the matted-hair ascetics.
"During the day" means during the daytime of the sun.
"For a moment" means for that instant, for that brief duration. "At least by the monastery attendants" means by those who serve the Saṃgha.
If one should dwell together with those designated as novices (śramaṇoddeśaka), that is, from those who are fifteen years of age up to those who are seventy,
this too is an offense involving immediate transgression (prathamāpattika) entailing formal meeting of the Saṃgha (saṃghātiśeṣa).
The Saṃgha is said to mean those eight *pārājika* rules.
This offense among them is with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) and requires remedial action (*sapratikarma*).
"Saṃghātiśeṣa" is the designation for the disclosure, the manifestation, the opening up, the analysis, the making clear, and the exposition regarding an offense that is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.

If this nun announces it at a royal household or at a seat [of authority], it is a thullaccaya; if she causes it to be built, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa. If she announces it at the house of a lay follower or at the house of a faithful family, it is a violation of the Vinaya.

If one reproaches [another] who is striving for restraint, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya; even a monk who reports [the matter] to the royal court incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya if he reproaches one who is striving for restraint.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun should dwell as one who speaks with excessive familiarity, whether for a day or for a moment, with householders or wanderers, or at the very least with monastery attendants or novice monks, this is an offense; it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* dharma, an offense entailing immediate confession.
(Saṃghātiśeṣa Dharma 5)
[Section] 141. The Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī. Now, at that time, there was a nun named Rāṣṭrā.
She had a sister named Rāṣṭrapālā who was married in a wretched village; she was not yet married off,
and she sent word.
"Noble lady, come to the kingdom if you wish to see me alive. She went there, and she passed away.
Then her brother-in-law lamented:
"Noble Rāṣṭrā, now that your sister has passed away, who will look after this boy? Who will attend to this house of mine?
We must attend to Noble Rāṣṭrā."
Then it occurred to her, "Indeed, evil winds are blowing.
Having gone out, she came to Śrāvastī and said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Venerable ladies, I have been made to fall away from the holy life.
They said, "What? Or how?"
He relates this very matter in detail:
the nuns report this circumstance to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in turn reports it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Summon Rāṣṭrā.
She was then summoned.
All of that was asked in detail, up until [the reply]: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"And yet, you travel along a road without a nun. Therefore, it is not permissible [to do so]; thus the training rule has been prescribed.
This is the origin of the matter."
The bhikṣuṇīs were traveling along a road.
Now, another bhikṣuṇī—graceful, beautiful, young, and inspiring—took a breath or let out a sigh, stepped off the path, and sat down. At that moment, a caravan of men was approaching.
She was surrounded by them,
and they said to her:
"Noble lady, you are gracious, beautiful to behold, young, and in the prime of your youth."
Sensual pleasures are to be enjoyed;
why then have you gone forth?
"What is this disillusionment of yours?
He replied, "I have gone forth."
They said, "Tell us first, for until they have surrounded you and are holding [the bowl] for you, those nuns have gone to another village. Then,
remorse arose within her.
She informed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, indeed, there is an offense for one who acts against her will. 143. This is the origin of the case: nuns were traveling along a road.
Now, another nun was ill;
she crossed over to another village without the other nuns.
She then felt remorse and reported her remorse to Mahāprajāpatī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"There is no offense in the case of one who is ill."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "Gautamī, assemble [the nuns]. [The usual formula follows.
"Whatever nun should travel along a road without another nun, even as far as to another village, except at the proper time—herein, this is the proper time: when the nun is unwilling [to go]."
Or if she is ill;
this is the occasion here.
This rule also entails an offense upon its first commission.
"Again, a nun" means— as in the previous formula—
a nun who is alone, without a companion.
The journey along the road is three *yojanas* or two *yojanas*,
or at the very least, the distance between villages.
"Against her will" means she is obstructed by the carcass of an elephant, the carcass of a horse, the carcass of a cow, or the carcass of a human.
Regarding "one who is ill": she is either weak from old age or weak from disease.
The Blessed One has withdrawn the rule for one who is ill; there is no offense for her.
This is the occasion in this case.
Now, when these nuns travel along a road, as long as they remain within the boundary (sīmā), even if they travel a great distance, there is no offense.
But if they now go from one village to another, or from one city to another, or cross a wilderness path,
they must cross while remaining within arm’s reach (hastapāśa) of one another.
If they go beyond the reach of the hand,

even by as little as four finger-breadths, they incur an offense of transgression requiring confession (*deśanāgāmi-vinayātikrama*). If they go one and a half cubits or two cubits, they incur a grave offense (*thūl'-accaya*).
Now, if one nun comes and stands within the boundary, she incurs a grave offense (thūl'-accaya). If another comes and crosses this boundary, all those who cross in this manner incur a grave offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
If a nun should travel along a road in the company of another nun, even as far as to the next village, except at the proper time;
herein, the proper time is when the nun is unwilling [to go] or is ill.
This is the rule here:
this dharma is an offense upon the first commission,
even for staying one night in another village.
144. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.
There, at that time, was the son of a smith who was endowed with faith and serene confidence.
His wife, named Śuklā, was the daughter of a smith; she was gracious and beautiful to behold.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself at the proper time and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Walking for alms in regular order, he went to that man's house and stood at the doorway.
At that moment, the man was eating.
Turning back as she was serving,
she stood there, thinking, "Lest he, upon seeing the Blessed One, rise up in agitation. Then it occurred to him, "Why indeed does she stand here turning back?"
The Blessed One also emitted those rays of light out of a desire to convert [the beings]; by that light he was looked upon,
and by that [light] the Blessed One was seen.
Then he said:
"Ah! Is it really true that you are obstructing my access to the Blessed One? You are one who desires my misfortune!"
"You do not desire my welfare," she said;
"I do not wish harm upon my noble husband;
I am propitiating the Blessed One."
"But rather, do not rise upon seeing the Blessed One while you are still in a state of agitation. Then she thought: "Fie upon my life as a householder!
For here I am, thinking that I shall do what is pleasing [to him]."
Having been addressed with unpleasant words,
she then said, "Noble son, I am going; I shall go forth into the religious life."
Then he said:
"In which teaching?
He replied:

In the past, Ānanda, these very Śākya women were six courtesans right here in Śrāvastī.

While he was walking for alms, he was addressed by those courtesans:
"Now this ascetic enjoys sensual pleasures himself,
yet he speaks in dispraise of sensual pleasures.
With these words, they— intent on mockery and intent on harassment— threatened him with various ill-spoken phrases and scattered burning coals over him from their bowls.

Then, Ānanda, that pratyekabuddha, touched by painful sensation and experiencing harsh and bitter feelings, being oppressed in both body and life, rose up right there in the air and, without further clinging, attained final nirvāṇa;
and his own previously established fire-element pervaded his body.
Then those courtesans, being terrified, thought: "An evil deed has been accumulated by us;
much demerit has been produced, for such a highly fortunate seer has been harassed."
"Therefore, this will be experienced by us as suffering; know that you shall now feel remorse. Then, having taken possession of his body, they constructed a stupa.
They honored him with parasols, banners, and flags;
they honored him with flowers, incense, and perfumes;
and they made this aspiration:
"In the future, may we please such a Teacher as this;
may we also obtain those five qualities which he has obtained."
Because they committed those evil deeds, these women were reborn in the hells; there they experienced suffering for many thousands of years.
Ānanda, it was while laughing that these foolish commoners committed the evil deed, the consequence of which—even with tearful faces—they now experience as suffering.
That she performed this worship and gave rise to remorse,
and that she made the aspiration for the future time: "May we please such a Teacher as he who is the possessor of these qualities."
"We too shall attain those [states]," they thought,
until they became those who attain final nirvana there through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
"Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse?"
"And how shall I uphold it?
The Blessed One said, "Therefore, Ānanda, you should uphold this Dharma-discourse by the name 'The Great Exposition of Causes' (Kāraṇavaipulya). Thus he spoke.
157. Now, when the city of Kapilavastu was besieged by Virūḍhaka, some of the bhikṣuṇīs remained hidden within the city while others went outside;
thus, the bhikṣuṇīs were separated from one another.
Regarding their remorse,
the Blessed One said:
"In that case, there is no offense for one who is unwilling and whose city has been besieged."
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on a journey,
and among them there was a bhikṣuṇī who was weak from old age.
"Weak with illness" means: "We have been separated from our caravan";
thus the nuns have transgressed.
Now, having become remorseful,
they reported their remorse to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī then reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, there is no offense for one who is unwilling."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs until they have all become purified.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī should dwell apart from another bhikṣuṇī for even one night, except on an authorized occasion, [she commits an offense]."
In this regard, these are the exceptional circumstances: a nun is ill, or she is besieged during a siege of a city;
these are the exceptional circumstances here.
"Any nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"Without the nuns" means alone, without a companion. "Should she dwell apart for even one night" means until sunrise, except in special circumstances.
In this regard, there is this exception: when a nun is unwilling [to go],
or is weakened by old age, or weakened by illness, or when there is a siege of the city— namely,
when that city is besieged by a hostile army.
Even if a bhikṣuṇī runs out from within the city to the outside, or enters from the outside into the city—
even if she enters— there is no offense.
However, if that bhikṣuṇī, while the sun is still up, remains apart from the other bhikṣuṇīs and causes dawn to break [in separation], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If the sun has set and they have not yet departed, she incurs a *thūl'-accaya* offense when the dawn breaks. Within the nuns' dwelling or elsewhere, everyone must remain within arm's reach of one another.
Three times during the night, mutual contact must be maintained.
It should be touched with the hand,
but certainly not all at once;
rather, if one does not provide access during each watch— specifically during the first watch— one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

If he does not give it during the middle watch, he incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*); if he does not give it during the last watch, he incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline;
if he gives it at all times, there is no offense.
Now, if it is a two-storied building, one [nun] shall descend by the lower story and the other by the upper story;
they must descend three times during the night.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
Furthermore, if a nun should dwell apart from other nuns for even a single night, except at the proper time; herein,
the proper time is when the nun is ill,
or when the city is besieged— this is the proper time in this case.
This dharma is also one involving an initial offense, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 7: Unpermitted. 158. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, in Rājagṛha, there was another man belonging to a group of non-soldiers whose wife, named Sudinnikā, was young, gracious,
and beautiful to behold;
she had now passed away.
That woman desired the man; her brother-in-law wished to have sexual union with her;
that woman said to other women:
"Venerable ladies, I have no desire for this man;
moreover, my brother-in-law wishes to take me as his wife.
Another woman said:
"Do you wish to be released? She then said, "I do."
She said,
"Go to Śrāvastī;
there now lives a bhikṣuṇī named Kālī."
She will cause you to go forth.
She has now run out and gone to Śrāvastī.
She went to the nuns' quarters and asked,
"Which is the cell of the noble Kālī? Another pointed it out to her, saying, "This is it."
Having approached her, she said,
"Noble lady, I wish to go forth. She was then made to go forth and received full ordination by her.
Then that man searches for [them], thinking, "I will mix them," but he does not find them;
then he hears this:
"In Śrāvastī there is a female ascetic named Kālī;
she has ordained her. Then that man, traveling by stages, went to Śrāvastī and inquired.
"What is the nunnery here?
[Being asked thus,] another pointed it out,
saying, "This is it," and he entered there.
He asked until he said, "Who is the noble Kālī? She then replied, "I am.
He then said:
"The time has come for the Noble One to ordain my wife, whom you have not released.
She then said,
"How could that be, O Long-lived One?"
He then said,
"From Rājagṛha. She then said:
"You have entered our city, O Caṇḍāyu," said the one named Sāntevāsinī.
"Bring the outer robe; while you wear this Caṇḍāyu, I shall have you bound with a collar."
Then that man, being afraid, thought,
"Lest this nun, being bold and talkative, should cause me to be bound.
That man complained and retreated, and having gone outside, he informed a great crowd of people about the bhikṣuṇīs.
"Look, sirs! This female ascetic ordains my wife without her being released, and she even threatens me with imprisonment!
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Summon Kālī.
She was then summoned.
All of this was asked,
and [the reply was] "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"You have committed a misdeed, Kālī!
How is it that you ordain one who has not been authorized by her preceptors?
Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain one who has not been authorized by her preceptors."
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Behold, Blessed One, how this Kālī was liberated through her presence of mind in the present moment,
and that man, terrified, fled away."
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣuṇīs, it was not only now that Kālī was liberated by her presence of mind;
this man, too, was terrified and fled."
On another occasion as well, she was liberated by this very same presence of ready wit,
and this man, being terrified, fled away. Long ago, O bhikṣuṇīs, this very city was Vārāṇasī.
This woman was walking at night carrying a girl upon her shoulder when a lion appeared before them;
seeing it, the girl then began to weep.
That woman struck the girl with a slap of her palm and said, "One lion was eaten by you; now you wish to eat this one as well.
The lion saw this.
Thinking, "This woman is such a crow-like, talkative eater;
she will devour me," he flees in fear.
A monkey came before him and asked the lion,
"O son of the king of beasts, where will you go? The lion replied:
Fear has come upon me.
The monkey asks:
"What kind of fear?"
The lion explained in detail and said:
"It should not be spoken in this way."
"You are a lion, O king of beasts!
Who shall strike you?
Come here; turn back!"
He did not wish to go;
the lion was seized by the monkey by the hair,
who said, "Come here!"
Upon seeing her, the girl wept.
The woman said to her, "Do not weep, girl;
who brought this man here, seizing him by the hair?"
"Now, eat whatever you desire.
The lion thought,
"Let it not be that this was merely a prearranged signal."
In this very way, he gives what is fit and what is unfit;
she too eats it.
Since I have already fled once, why am I turned back again?
Then, having shaken off that monkey, he fled;
a deity spoke this verse:
"This wisdom has arisen in the present."
This has not arisen for long;
see how the fear of the lion was dispelled by eloquence.
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣuṇīs, it may occur to you that she was some other woman;
it should not be viewed in this way."
This very woman was that Kālī.
Monks, it might occur to you that she was some other girl;
it should not be viewed in this way.
This very Sudinnikā was that girl.
Monks, it might occur to you that Siṃha was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
This very man was that lion;
even then, she was liberated by this present eloquence of hers,
while this man, being terrified, fled away.
159. Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs until they have become completely purified.
Should any bhikṣuṇī ordain one who has not been authorized by those who grant authorization, this is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense, entailing immediate confession."
"Furthermore, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasaṃpannā*).
"Without being authorized by those who should authorize her" refers to the following: for an unmarried girl, the mother and father are the ones to authorize;
for a married woman, the mother-in-law and father-in-law, as well as the husband and brother-in-law, are the ones to authorize.
"Should ordain" means she should confer full admission (*upasampadā*).
If that nun ordains one who has not been authorized by those who grant authorization, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
if she imparts the training, she incurs a *thūl'-accaya* offense.
If she confers full ordination [on a woman who has not been permitted], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. When someone seeking the going-forth arrives, she must be asked:
"Have you been permitted by those who grant permission?
If she says, "No," [she may not be ordained].
If she is unmarried, she should be told:

"Come after you have obtained permission from your mother and father. If she is married, she should be told: "Come after you have obtained permission from your husband, your brother-in-law, your mother-in-law, and your father-in-law."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should ordain one who has not been authorized by those who should authorize her, this too is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense, an immediate transgression. This is the eighth *saṃghātiśeṣa* rule."
[Vadhyā 160] The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. There was a market town named Mallakalya belonging to the Mallas.
Now, at that time, the wife of another wrestler was committing adultery with another man;
he said to her,
"Asuka, desist!"
"Therefore, there is a fault;
therefore, I shall not do such and such an unwholesome thing to you.
But she, being wicked, did not desist.
"I shall die;
I will not, however, desist from this fault.
Having said this, he took the woman caught in adultery and brought her before the seat of justice.
"I desire, sirs, that she be obtained according to their own law.
But what is the own law of those Mallas? It is that a woman who commits adultery with another man [is forfeited]."
Having performed the distribution of gifts for seven days before both assemblies of kinsmen, she was torn apart by a saw in front of them.
The court officials said:
"Let her be given; receive your own property."
Then that man, having led her home, said:
"O daughter of Itikitikā, give whatever you have and whatever you do not have;
for seven days I shall tear you apart with pincers before both assemblies of your kinsmen."
Then, having assembled the community of kinsmen on both sides and prepared food, drink, edibles, and delicacies, she wept.
The women said, "What is the use of weeping? It was you yourself who acted in such a way that you must now experience this suffering."
She then said,
"I will not do it; I am going to die."
"Rather, I weep because they will tear me apart with a pair of scissors before the assembly of kinsmen on both sides. Another said:
"Do you wish to be released? She replied, "I do."
He said,
"Go to Śrāvastī;
there is a nun named Kālī."
She will cause you to go forth.

Having heard her words, she ran out—whether the people were eating, drinking, or distracted—in whatever manner possible; then, by asking from person to person, she gradually arrived at Śrāvastī and inquired.
"What is the nunnery here?
Another pointed it out to her; she then entered and asked.
Who is the noble Kālī?
She was described by another as "this one."
She approached her and said,
"I wish to be ordained by the Noble Lady.
She then replied:
"Have you been authorized by those who authorize?
She then asked,
"But who, Noble Lady, are the ones who authorize?"
He said:
For an unmarried girl, it is her mother and father;
for one who is married, it is her mother-in-law and father-in-law, as well as her husband and brothers-in-law.
She said:
"In that case, I am authorized;
when I have been well-released and thoroughly released by Gopāṭika."
He said, "O mother of sons, you were well-released; you were truly well-released when you were released into the care of Gopāṭikā.
She was then caused to go forth and was ordained by her.
That man searches,
thinking, "I will split it with a small hoe," but he does not find one;
then he hears [the following].
In Śrāvastī there was a nun named Kālī. She ordained her [disciple],
who, having come to Śrāvastī, asked:
"What is the nunnery here?
"It is this one," they told him, and so on;
he then entered there.
The noble lady named Kālī said:
"What should be done?"
When he had arrived, [the husband] said to the noble lady, "I wish to have my wife, who has not been given up, ordained. She then asked,
"Where are you from?"
He said:
"From the time of the *āmalaka* fruit.
He said: [Yes].
"You are Caṇḍāyu the thief; you are a prowler who has entered Śrāvastī with the intent to spy.
Do you not know that the people of Śrāvastī are constantly hostile and as fierce as *āmalaka* fruits?
Then she summoned her female disciple.
"First bring the monastic robe; while this Caṇḍāyu is still wearing her tattered garment, I shall have her bound in the royal palace.
That man saw that this female ascetic was indeed audacious, talkative, and bold.
"I shall have him bound!
Now this man grumbles and withdraws;
that man now grumbles before the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs and the great multitude of people.
"Look, sirs! This female ascetic ordains my wife even though she has not been released by me, and she threatens me with imprisonment. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Then the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Kālī!
How is it that you, knowing her to be one who should be executed, known [to be such], and subject to punishment by her kinsmen, still attend to her?"
Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain a woman who is known to be liable to execution, recognized as such, and subject to punishment by her kinsmen.
This is the very case in point.
There was a town of the Śākyas called Śākyavāna.
In this very way, it should be done in detail:
as long as another [woman] was likewise ordained by me,
I received a disciplinary penalty for that.
"Go; I do not venture to ordain you.
Then she approached various other bhikṣuṇīs, but none of them ordained her, until finally she was ordained by the heretics.
That man searches,
thinking, "I will split it with a small hoe," but he does not find one.
He heard that she had been ordained by the heretics in Śrāvastī;
he then said,
"Now that daughter of Itikitikā has met with a very great destruction in this very life."
The daughter of the lay follower, having been ordained by the heretics,
no longer seeks out or inquires after [the Buddha];
she now suffers because of that state of being a heretic, on account of that state of being a heretic.
Now those heretics, who are poorly taught and unrighteous,
drink rice-water and they drink the rinsing of the cooking pot.
Naked, shameless, and fearless, even those desiring women defile them.
That woman said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Alas, our going forth is fraught with delusion; we have fallen into a pit."
I have fallen into hell; I have fallen into a precipice;
deliver me!
Have compassion for me!
Lift me up!
Have compassion for me!
"Ordain me!
But they did not wish to do so;
she then approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"It is permitted."
Whatever censure was directed there has now fallen upon the heretics.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble them; thus they shall become purified."

If a nun, knowing that a woman is condemned to death, recognized as such, and subject to punishment by her kinsmen, should ordain her—except at the proper time—this being the proper time: she was formerly a follower of another sect;
this rule is also a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense involving immediate transgression.
162. "A nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another. "To be executed" means to be put to death.

"Known" means known by both groups of kinsmen, namely the maternal side and the paternal side. "Subject to the penalty of kinsmen" refers to those called kinsmen: Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Ambaṣṭhas, Vaidehas, Bhaṭanas, and Kuṅkumālas.
Some are cut into pieces with a cow-horn;
some are wrapped in insects or *kāliñja* plants and burned;
and some have a jar of sand tied around their necks and are cast into the water.
The heads of some are blown apart; the ears and noses of some are cut off;
and a heated plowshare is thrust down the stream into the mouths of others.
The Mallas cremate [the body] with cow dung; the Śākyas with straw;
the Kṣatriyas, having wrapped it in reeds, burn it;
and the Abhīras throw it into water after tying a jar around its neck.
The heads of the Śakas and Yavanas are blown away;
their ears and noses are cut off;
or a heated plowshare is thrust into the opening of their wounds.

"One should cause to attend" means one should cause to go forth and cause to receive full ordination. "Except at the proper time" refers to a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense. "Except at the proper time"—in this regard, this is the proper time: [the time of illness, etc. (as previously specified).
She has previously belonged to another sect.
"Those of other sects" refers to:
the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Nirgranthas, Ājīvakas, Treḍaṇḍikas, Mākandikas, Gudugudukas, Gautamas, Dharmacintakas, Vṛddhaśrāvakas, Dakatṛtīyakas, and so on, up to the Prajñaptis.

If that nun, knowing and being aware that a woman is subject to execution, known [to be so], and has incurred the penalty of her kinsmen, nevertheless grants her the going forth, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
if she gives her the training, she commits a *thūl'-accaya*;
if she confers full ordination upon her, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "If a nun, knowing that a woman is condemned to death, recognized as such, and subject to punishment by her kinsmen, should ordain her—
except at the proper time."
In this regard,
the exception is as follows: if she has previously belonged to another sect,
this rule constitutes an immediate offense.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 9:
Crossing a River Alone.
163. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Then, while many women were bathing in the river Ajirāvatī,
the nun Sthūlanandā arrived at that very spot.
Having set aside her robes in one place, she waded across using her arms.
Then those women said,
"The noble Sthūlanandā is coming.
Having rested for a moment at the water-vessel, she returned once more.
The women said,
"This noble lady Sthūlanandā has arrived;
the noble lady has acted with excessive restlessness."
"How is it that you cross by means of your arms?
Then those women were censured.
The monks heard this matter.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One, until the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression, Nanda."
"And yet you are crossing the river all alone!
Therefore, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to cross a river without [another woman].
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:"
"Summon the bhikṣuṇīs, Gautamī, until they have become thoroughly purified.
Whatever bhikṣuṇī should cross a river without another bhikṣuṇī, this rule is also one involving an initial offense.
'Whatever bhikṣuṇī' means one who has received full ordination."
"Without a nun" means alone.
"River" means that which flows outside the boundary and reaches outside the boundary. "Should cross" means she should go from this shore to the other shore.

This rule is also one involving an immediate offense. To the extent that these bhikṣuṇīs cross rivers, they must cross within arm's reach of one another; if they cross beyond arm's reach, it is a grave offense (thūl'-accaya).
They become far removed by a great distance [from the offense], which is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*; or, if one stands in the middle while others cross over, it is a *thūl'-accaya*.
As long as they continue in this manner one after another, they all incur a *thūl'-accaya*.
These bhikṣuṇīs bathe in the river; they should bathe within the reach of one's hand. If they bathe beyond the reach of one's hand, they commit an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should cross a river without another nun,
this too is an offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṃgha (saṃghātiśeṣa), entailing immediate transgression.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 10: On One Who Has Been Suspended. 164. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
There, a nun named Kālī went on a tour of the villages.
While she was away, the community of nuns performed a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepanīyakarman*) against her female pupil.
Having completed her tour of the villages, she returned.
She then said:
"Noble lady, the Saṃgha has performed an act of suspension against me;
they do not share with me either the enjoyment of the Dharma or the enjoyment of material goods."
She then said,
"Be silent until the nuns have assembled.
She then said:
"Summon the noble ladies!
Whenever she returns from her travels through the villages at one time or another,
she then distributes the *vaibhaṅgika* (distribution of goods) to the bhikṣuṇīs."
When those nuns were told, "Assemble," they assembled very quickly, thinking, "She will give us some distribution of goods.
She then said:
"Let the noble Saṃgha listen to me."
This is the nun named so-and-so;
the Saṃgha has performed the act of suspension against her.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha restore the nun named so-and-so.
This is the formal motion.
Let the noble community of nuns hear me:
this nun is named so-and-so.
The Saṃgha has performed the act of suspension against her.
The Saṃgha now reinstates that nun named so-and-so.
Noble ladies, whichever of you approves of the Saṃgha reinstating the nun named so-and-so, let her remain silent; whichever does not approve, let her speak.
This is the first formal proclamation.
Thus, by three proclamations, the noble ladies have formally restored this nun named so-and-so;
the act of suspension has been performed by the Saṃgha.
"It is agreeable to the Saṃgha because it is silent; thus do I understand this.
Then, because she was bold, talkative, and arrogant, no one rejected her.
Thereupon, those nuns, being distressed, said:
"What, then, is this?
others said;
"We too do not know."
The bhikṣuṇīs should report this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reports it to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Summon Kālī;
let her be questioned on this very matter.
She said:
"Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"It is a transgression for you, Kālī, that knowing a bhikṣuṇī has been suspended by the complete Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and has not yet performed penance, you [should act thus]."
Without having performed the preliminary duties and without having looked back upon the community of nuns, you are reinstating [the nun];
therefore, this is not permissible.
[The usual formula]... Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Assemble [the nuns] until they have become completely pure."
Furthermore, if a nun, knowing that another nun has been suspended by a unanimous Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and that she has not yet performed the act of atonement,
has not performed the preliminary duties,
and has not obtained the consent of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha—
If she herself withdraws [the robe],
this rule is one of immediate offense (*prathamāpattika*).
"A nun" means one who is fully ordained by both Saṃghas.
"She, this nun, knowing" means:
either she knows by herself or she has heard it from another;
"a nun by a complete Saṃgha" means by one that is not divided.
"According to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya" means: when there is an offense, [one acts] by not seeing it, and by a non-Dharmic procedure.
"Because of not relinquishing three views," means that he has been suspended and deprived of communal life;
"not having made amends" means that he has not been reinstated.
"Without having performed the preliminary duties" means that the nuns remain in their natural state, having neither informed [the Sangha] nor requested permission.

This rule also extends as far as the formal designation.

She reviles the Saṅgha and leads the Saṅgha into a wrong course; "the noble Saṅgha follows favoritism," she says,

Relying on faults and relying on delusion, he thinks that I should be reviled and censured.

yet she does not relinquish it."

And if that nun, being thus addressed by the nuns, should persist in taking up and adhering to that very matter,

If, being exhorted or admonished up to three times, she relinquishes that matter, that is good.

this matter is to be dealt with up to the third time... [as before] ...until this nun, having been exhorted and admonished three times regarding the matter that ought to be relinquished, does not relinquish it.
With each utterance, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

If she has been deprived [of the robe], there is a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).

Those who act in violation of the Vinaya in private, those who do so among a great multitude, and those who do so in the midst of the Saṃgha.

How is it subject to relinquishment?

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Furthermore, a nun becomes one who reviles the Saṃgha;
she speaks thus:
"He acts out of favoritism."
Venerable ladies, the Saṃgha is prone to hatred, the Saṃgha is prone to fear,

If, relying on malice, fear, or delusion, she thinks that she should revile or abuse [another] by relying on [the authority of] the Saṃgha,
that bhikṣuṇī should be addressed thus by the bhikṣuṇīs:

The Saṅgha does not act out of favoritism; the Saṅgha does not act out of malice;

The Saṅgha does not follow delusion;
nor does the Saṅgha, relying on desire, ill-will, fear, or delusion, consider that the Noble One should be reviled or censured.

"Only the noble ones, relying on desire, or relying on hatred, fear, or delusion, think that the Saṅgha should be reviled, provoked to anger, or censured. Noble lady, desist from reviling the Saṅgha!
If, being thus addressed by the bhikṣuṇīs, that bhikṣuṇī persists in taking up and adhering to that very same matter, [she is to be dealt with according to the rule].
If she does not relinquish it,
that nun is to be exhorted and admonished by the nuns up to three times for the relinquishment of that matter.
While being exhorted and admonished up to three times...
If he should relinquish that matter, that is good; if he should not relinquish it,

If she does not desist,

that nun is to be exhorted and admonished by the nuns up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter. If, while being exhorted or admonished up to three times, she relinquishes that matter, that is good.
If she does not desist from it, but persists in taking up and adhering to that very matter,
this too is an offense subject to a third admonition;
[this applies when] two [nuns] dwell in association.
170. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, these two bhikṣuṇīs, Nandā the Śākyan girl and Uttarā the daughter of Māsoraka, lived in close association through physical contact and they lived in close association through verbal contact.
They dwell in association through physical and verbal contact;
they conceal one another's faults.
How is it that they now dwell in association through physical contact?
Why now do they conceal each other's faults? One conceals the fault of another, and another conceals the fault of yet another.
Those nuns are addressed by the other nuns thus:
"Venerable ladies, do not live in physical contact; do not [live] in verbal contact; do not [live] in both physical and verbal contact;
do not conceal each other's faults."
Though they were addressed once, they did not desist; though addressed a second and even a third time, they still did not desist. The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One in detail. [Pejāla... pejāla... Furthermore, there were two nuns living together in close association.
Those nuns who conceal each other's faults should be addressed by the other nuns in this way:
"Noble ladies, do not live in such close association with one another, concealing each other's faults."
Noble ladies, dwell separately.
For you who dwell separately, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected,
not decline.

And if those nuns, being thus addressed by the other nuns, should relinquish that matter, that is well. But if they do not relinquish it, those nuns are to be exhorted and admonished by the other nuns up to the third time for the relinquishment of that matter.
If, being exhorted or admonished up to three times, they should relinquish that matter, that is good;
but if they do not relinquish it and persist in adopting and maintaining that very matter,
this rule is also one that applies up to the third time.
Furthermore, there were two bhikṣuṇīs who lived in close association, namely Nandā the Śākyan girl and Uttarā the daughter of Māśoraka.
They lived in association through bodily contact, verbal contact, and both bodily and verbal contact.
"Concealers of faults" means concealers of offenses.
Those bhikṣuṇīs— just as Nandā the Śākya maiden and Uttarā the daughter of Māśoraka—
should be addressed by the community of bhikṣuṇīs, by the Saṃgha, or by a group of many people, or by a single bhikṣuṇī, in this manner:
Venerable ladies, do not live in close association,
covering one another's faults;
[and so on].
They remained having taken up and grasped that very matter—
that matter with which they lived in association and concealed each other's faults.
"Those nuns" refers to Nandā the Śākyan girl and Uttarā the daughter of Māṣoraka.

And if they do not desist from it, this too is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, up to the third [formal] act;
[the rest is] as before,
up to the formal rule (*prajñapti*).

Likewise, when she consents to the formal motion (*jñapti*) in the midst of the great assembly of the Saṃgha, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

"I shall prepare a meal for the noble ladies. Then, as those women were preparing the food, they said,

and from what remained of her eating, she prepared whatever kind of food it was.

the bhikṣuṇīs said,

She eats and she drinks;
she causes [others] to know [the need for] a bowl and a robe;

Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī, having requested [alms] for the sake of others, causes [something] to be purchased for herself—a bowl, or a robe, or food, or soft food, or medicinal requisites for the sick—[she commits an offense]."
This is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

"Any nun" refers to one who is fully ordained. "For the sake of others" means having requested on their behalf, having requested for the sake of the Saṅgha’s meal, or refreshment, or a drink of rice-gruel.
If one should cause [another] to procure for oneself a bowl, or a robe, or food, or soft food, or medicinal requisites for the sick, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Rather, one should inform only the person for whose sake one requests them.
Now, if she causes a garment to be lost for the sake of food, or a drink, or a gruel-drink, by requesting it and then giving it away as a gift to be shared;
or if she provides bedding and seating, or gives it for the rainy season or the winter—
she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This nun causes the Saṃgha to be provided with a meal;
it should be given as something relinquished, released, and not withheld.
If there is anything remaining there—whether rice, soup, or even anything edible or consumable—it must be shown [to her].
If he takes it and goes away, one should remain indifferent;
but if he says, "I give this to the Noble One," [one should accept it].
It should be said:
"No, give it to the Saṃgha."
Then he says, "It has been given by me to the Saṃgha;
I give it to the Noble Lady," and she accepts it.
There is no offense;
for a monk as well, it is exactly the same, though there is an offense consisting of a transgression of the rule.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun, having requested [donations] for the sake of others, should have a bowl, a robe, food, soft food, or medicinal requisites for the sick purchased for herself,
that is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pācattika). This is the fourteenth offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

They said, "Let us pass the bowls around. Then they asked,

There are four alms-bowls as requisites;
if they keep more than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
This is now the fixed limit for a nun regarding the possession of alms-bowls.
Even if a monk uses many bowls after having made a selection [of them], there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should make a hoard of bowls, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*."

The offense involving forfeiture and expiation (niḥsargika-pācattika) 16: On relinquishing [the robe], 177. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
There was a nun named Sthūlanandā who neither washed, nor sewed, nor dyed her robes.
Now, her outer robe (saṃghāṭī) was soiled with filth and torn to pieces; she left it in the dwelling-place, saying, "Whoever wishes may take it."
Now there was another nun named Jetā who wore coarse robes. She was addressed by the nuns:
"Noble lady, wash this outer robe, sew it, beat it, and wear it."
Then Sthūlanandā said, "Noble lady, bring this outer robe; it is mine.
Look, noble ladies, nothing at all can be placed in the shelter."
The entire monastery was filled with those who had been expelled;
then that woman, being audacious, talkative, and bold, snatched away her outer robe (saṃghāṭī).
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One [of this matter]. Thereupon the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, having either deposited or caused to be deposited an old outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) in a nunnery, should say, 'Let whoever wishes take it,' [this is not an offense]."
If, after having spoken thus, she herself should subsequently take it up, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*. "A nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*) means one who has received full ordination; [the rest is] as before.
"In the nunnery" means in the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇīs.
"Saṃghāṭī" means a robe. "Having laid it down" means by herself.
"Having caused [it] to be deposited" means by another.
"Let her who desires it take it" means that afterwards she herself should take it; [if she does so], it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

If this nun, having deposited or caused a robe to be deposited in the nuns' quarters, says, "Let her who desires it take it," and someone else has already taken it, it is not permissible to snatch it away.
If she seizes it, it constitutes an offense requiring relinquishment (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
Now, if it has not been taken possession of by anyone and she herself has need of it, even if she takes it, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if miscellaneous minor requisites have been deposited and they have been taken possession of by someone else, it is not permissible to seize them.
If one seizes [an item], one commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

If a monk, having deposited a bowl, a robe, sandals, or even minor or very minor requisites in a monastery for monks, says, "Whoever wishes may take it," if it has been taken by someone, it is not permissible to seize it back.
One incurs a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*) by seizing [an object].
However, if it has not been taken by anyone and that person himself is the one seeking it, there is no offense even if one takes it.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, having deposited or caused to be deposited an old outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) in a nun’s dwelling, says, “Let whoever wishes take it,” and afterwards takes it herself,
that is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pācattika*). This is the seventeenth rule concerning offenses of expiation involving forfeiture.
178. "To sew. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, another bhikṣuṇī had washed an old saṃghāṭī that was extremely soiled; having sewn it and spread it out in the sun, she set it in the wind to dry.
A fire broke out and her outer robe was burned. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The full passage] as far as the Blessed One said:
"In this way, you have worn out an old outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) but neither repair it yourself nor cause it to be repaired. Therefore, it must indeed be repaired or caused to be repaired."
This is the origin of the matter:
those nuns—daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Mallas, and daughters of the Licchavis, who were delicate—were becoming exhausted while washing heavy outer robes (saṃghāṭī).
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One; then the Blessed One said:
"In that case, I authorize [it] for six or five nights."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...the Blessed One said:

"If a nun, having sewn or caused to be sewn a new outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), does not join it together herself or cause it to be joined together for more than five or six nights while she is not ill, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pācattika*)."
"Again, a nun" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"An old outer robe" (*purāṇasaṃghāṭī*) refers to an old garment (*purāṇacīvara*).
"Outer robe" (*saṃghāṭī*) refers to one that is double-layered (*dvipuṭā*).
"Having sewn out" means by oneself;
"having had sewn out" means by another.
"Beyond" means more than five or six nights; it does not mean exactly five or six.
Now, indeed, for more than six nights, one should not have [a robe] sewn oneself, nor have it sewn by another;
if one has it sewn, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
[The rest is as before.]
As far as the designation goes:
now, if a nun’s outer robe (saṃghāṭī) becomes soiled, if it is light, it should be washed in that very manner.
It is not permissible to unpick [the robe].
Now, if it is a *sārikā* (a type of patch or seam), having unpicked it again and again, it must be washed; then, having applied new fastenings, it must be placed in the sun.
Having gathered it together and placed it in a basket, a bowl, or a tray, one should step over it with a piece of wood or a piece of stone;
it is not permitted to let it remain scattered.
Now, if there is no vessel available, one should place it in one spot and step over it with a brick or a piece of stone.
Thereafter, she should be reunited with the robe by a female disciple, or by a fellow-student nun, or she herself should reunite it.
Now, if she is weak from old age or weak from illness, even if she reunites it after a long time, there is no offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:

If a nun, having sewn together or caused to be sewn together old outer robes (*saṃghāṭī*), does not re-sew them herself or cause them to be re-sewn for more than five or six nights while she is not ill, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*;
this is the eighteenth *niḥsargika-pācattika* rule,
having spoken thus [to the nun] who is undergoing training.
179. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, there was another *śikṣamāṇā* who was to be ordained;
she then said to the nun Sthūlanandā:

She said,

and she said,

She felt ashamed;

until the Blessed One said:

"A nun" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"A *śikṣamāṇā*" refers to one who has undertaken the training.
"If you give me a robe, then I will ordain you.
"A robe" means: what is called a robe includes woolen cloth, cotton, and so on, up to the *saṃkakṣikā* (breast-covering).

"She takes that robe" means: just as the nun Thūlanaṇḍā [acted], she should not herself confer full ordination; if she does so, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense. This is the rule. First, this nun takes the robe from a *śikṣamāṇā*.
"I shall ordain you. She should then be established [in the precepts].
Now, if she is unable to do so—whether due to weakness from old age or weakness from illness—another person should be requested to assist.
She should be told: "Having taken this robe, provide her with attendance.
If she does not wish for it, that robe must be returned [to her], and she should be told:
"Go and receive full ordination wherever you desire."
If that nun, having taken a robe, neither sets it aside nor returns the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
For a monk as well, it is a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:

If a nun, having spoken thus to a *śikṣamāṇā*: "If you give me a robe, then I will grant you full ordination," and having accepted her robe, does not grant her full ordination, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense; [this is] the nineteenth [offense], regarding the wearing of heavy robes.

184. Regarding the transition: The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.

The bhikṣuṇīs set out for their alms-round. They said, "Come, Noble Lady, let us go for alms-food."
She said,
"I will go as soon as I take my outer robe.
Then she searched for her own outer robe, but she did not see it.
Then it occurred to her: "The noble lady must certainly have put on her outer robe;
it is fitting that the noble lady go having put on my outer robe.
She then said:
"Go, you noble ladies; I will not go. Why? [She said this because] the noble lady had gone after putting on her outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*). Then they said:
"Put on your outer robe, noble lady, and come.
She replied, "I cannot do so, noble lady; you are my teacher and one worthy of my highest veneration."
She did not go;
she was deprived of her meal and excluded.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One; then the Blessed One said,
"Call Bhadrā here."
She was then summoned, and when she had replied, "It is true,
Venerable Sir," the Blessed One questioned her about all of this in detail.
"Since you indeed perform the transfer of robes in this manner,
it is a *duṣkṛta* for you, noble lady.
Therefore, it is not permissible to perform the transfer of robes."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: [peyālam] ... up to ...
"Whatever nun should effect the transfer of a robe, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
"Whatever nun... [and so forth]. "Robe" (*cīvara*): a robe is defined as the outer cloak (*saṃghāṭī*) up to the bathing cloth (*dakaśāṭikā*).
"Exchanging" (*saṃkramaṇa*) means one for another.
This is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule.
Now, it is not permissible for a nun to put on her outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) without having informed her pupil.
If she puts it on, she must say: "I have put on this outer robe."
If you enter having put on my outer robe (saṃghāṭī),
then if there is an extra robe, she should be told:
"This outer robe has been put on by me for you."
"If you enter with this robe-cloth, you shall enter. Now,
if a nun is washing, sewing, or dyeing her outer cloak (saṃghāṭī),
and if she is capable [of doing so], a share must also be given to her.
She should be told:
"Stay right here; today I shall share my alms-food with you.
The monk should also speak in this way.
If she does not speak [of it], she incurs an offense of transgression of the Vinaya.

Pācattika Dharma 72: On the Robe of a Śramaṇa. 185. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Rāṣṭrapāla, my nephew,

The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Gartodara, Gartodara’s mother, and Gartodara’s father had gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Gartodara’s father and mother had gone forth among the Śākyas, while Gartodara had gone forth among the heretics.

Now, wrapped in a hand-kambala and shivering from the cold, making the sound "khaṇa-khaṇa" while playing his lute of teeth, he arrived at the monastery. Women are affectionate by nature; she then said:
"Son Gartodara, are you cold? He then replied, "Yes."
She gave him a fragrant, well-washed upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) as a cloak.
Having put it on, he went to a tavern and sat there drinking.

People then complained: "What [use] is this banner of a seer given to these people of wrong views, who have fallen into ruin, who are like donkeys in their vehicles, and who have fallen from the state of a *surā* (wine) ascetic? This was heard by the nuns.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...
until the Blessed One said:
"Call Gartodaramātā.
She was then summoned,
and everything happened exactly as before.
The Blessed One questioned her at length,
until she replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "It was a transgression for you, O mother of Gartodara."
"Therefore, it is not permissible to give a saṃghāṭī robe with one's own hand to a householder or a wandering ascetic.

[the usual formula] until "they shall become purified."
If a nun should give a standard robe with her own hand to a layman or to a wandering ascetic, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"If a nun" means one who has received full ordination.
"To a layman" means to a householder.
"Of the wandering mendicant" refers to [the category] ending with the matted-hair ascetics of the Gautama clan.
"With one's own hand" means hand to hand.
"The robe of a śramaṇa" means the banner of the sages.
One incurs a *pācattika* offense, as prescribed in the rule.
It is not permissible to give a monastic robe (*śramaṇacīvara*) with one's own hand to a householder or to a wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*).
Now, if there is a nun who has performed meritorious deeds, and women now request a piece of saffron cloth for the sake of an auspicious rite for a boy or a girl:
It is not permissible to give [the robe] with one's own hand; it must be given by means of a *kalpiyakāraka* (an attendant who prepares things deemed allowable).
If a monk gives a *śramaṇacīvara* (monk’s robe) with his own hand to a householder or a wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*), he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Now, even if the monk has performed meritorious deeds, [the robe] must still be given by means of a *kalpiyakāraka*.
It is not permissible to give a large cloth;
rather, a piece of rag should be given.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun should give a monk’s robe with her own hand to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, it is a *pācattika*.
186. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.

When a nun has an inner robe made, it must be made according to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure: four spans in length, using the span of a Sugata;

Pācattika-dharma 73 and 74:
"An inner room" refers to that which has been permitted by the Blessed One.
"Having it made for a bhikṣuṇī" means that she herself should either make it or have it made by another.
In this regard, the measurement is as follows: "length" refers to the longitudinal extent;

"width" refers to the transverse extent, which is four spans (*vitasti*) by the span of a Sugata—that is, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha. One should have it made no more than that; beyond this measurement, cutting [the excess] constitutes a *pācattika* offense.
As far as the designation [of the robe-measure] is concerned:
if that nun makes it long according to the standard measure, but makes it excessive in width,
whether she does so herself or causes it to be done, there is an offense of completion upon its finishing.
When it is finished, one incurs a transgression of the Vinaya that must end with its use.
Likewise, if one makes it crooked, or makes it long when it should be of the proper measure,
or makes it of the proper measure at the ends while making it excessive in the middle.

If one makes it standard in the middle and excessive at the ends; or if one measures it as double [the size] but it shrinks when wet, and one measures it when it has shrunk thinking, "It will expand when dry"; or if one expands it when it is dry thinking, "It will expand when wet"—one incurs a *pācattika* offense. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
When a nun has an inner robe made, it must be made according to the proper measurement. Herein, this is the measurement: four spans in length, using the span of a Sugata.
If one should cause it to be made more than two spans across, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
