The Bathing Robe (dakaśāṭikā), Chapter 188. The setting is Vaiśālī.
Now, Bhadrā Kāpileyī went to the river Sarpiṇikā to bathe.
Having set aside her robes, she descended to bathe.
Five Licchavi youths, their hearts bound by passion for her, stood on the riverbank,
desiring to behold Bhadrā’s slender limbs.
She then said, "Long-lived one, go, go, while I am crossing.
They then replied,
"No."
"We wish to see the noble lady's slender body.
She then said,
"Long-lived one, what is the use of seeing this putrid body, with its nine openings constantly discharging impurities?"
"Proceed until I have crossed over.
They then said,
"No, indeed not."
"We wish to see the noble lady's slender limbs.
When they did not go and a long time passed,
she, considering them to be blind fools, crossed over with one hand extended in front and the other behind her.
Seeing her naked, they fainted and fell;
hot blood issued from their mouths,
and having passed away, they died.
This was the occasion... [and so on] ... until the bhikṣuṇīs said to the Blessed One:
"Behold, Blessed One, how these five Licchavi youths, their minds bound by passion, have fainted and fallen for Bhadrā!
The Blessed One said,
"It is not only now that they have fainted and fallen for Bhadrā with their minds bound by passion."

At other times as well, their minds were bound to Bhadrā; at other times too, Blessed One, and at other times too, so it was with the bhikṣuṇīs. Long ago, bhikṣuṇīs, in the past—at a time when there were thirty abodes—an apsaras named Bharaṇī was reborn in one of those abodes.
Gracious and beautiful to behold, she outshone all other apsarases;
she outshone all other apsarases, shining, glowing, and radiating with splendor.
Five sons of the gods had their hearts bound to her.
And Śakra, the Indra of the gods,
had Mātali as his charioteer and Jaya as his driver.
Vijaya;

They then said:
"We cannot divide this into five parts;
instead, let us compose a verse.
Whoever among us is most thoroughly convinced by it shall take possession of it."
Śakra, the lord of the gods, speaks this verse:
Whether standing or sitting, one finds no comfort on a seat;
But when one lies down, one finds comfort—when desires abandon me. [1]
Mātali the charioteer spoke this verse:
"O Lord of Gods, you are happy indeed that you obtain such happiness while asleep;
for desires always strike me down, like the sound of a drum at the head of a battle."
The devaputra Jaya spoke this verse:
"Just as when a drum is being beaten, there arise waves again and again, so too do desires always strike at me, like a current of wood driven along. [3]
The divine son Vijaya spoke this verse:
"For a log being carried along, there may occasionally be an attachment;
but for me, my eyes are always wide open like those of a moth. [4]
The divine son Khāṇu spoke this verse:
"All you gentlemen are happy, for whom verses come to mind;
as for me, indeed, I do not know whether I live or die. [5]
Those sons of the gods said:
"You have made an excellent choice;
let this Bharaṇī be yours—she who is beautiful in every limb. [6]
The Blessed One said:

it should not be viewed in this way."
She was that very apsaras Bhadrā;
those other sons of gods were these same five Licchavi youths. Even then, their minds were bound to her.
Even now, their minds remain bound to her.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked:
"Blessed One, as the ripening of what karma is Bhadrā so pleasing, beautiful to behold, of noble birth, of great renown, of great wealth, and one who attains realization so swiftly?"

Then the Blessed One addressed Bhadrā Kāpileyī: "May it be inspired in you, Bhadrā, to deliver a discourse concerning your own former lives to the bhikṣuṇīs. Then Bhadrā, recollecting her manifold former births, addressed the bhikṣuṇīs.
Long ago, sisters, in times past, there was a city named Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśī.
At that time, there was a certain poor woman who was summoned by the wife of a merchant to have her hair adorned.
She was arranging the hair for that merchant’s wife.
Since the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not appear [in this world], Pratyekabuddhas arise;
then a Pratyekabuddha named Śuṇṭhika, wandering for alms, entered that house for food.
The Pratyekabuddha remained silent; no one spoke to him. Then that woman said to the merchant’s wife:
"Give him alms.
That merchant's wife, looking upward, said:
"Who would give alms to one who is so ill-favored and of such little consequence?"
She said:
"These who are pleasing in body are not desired; those who are pleasing in mind are desired."
"I will not give it to him.
Then that poor woman said, "Noble daughter, give me [the food]; I shall give to him that which was to have been given by you as my meal today."
She then commanded:
"Whatever food you receive today, take it and either throw it into the water or give it to him.
She then obtained that food.
Having thus made an offering with her hand out of faith toward that Pratyekabuddha,
the Pratyekabuddha departed right then and there through the air.
Seeing this, she was satisfied, elated, and joyful, and she entered her home.
The merchant saw the seer departing through the air from his house;
then, having entered the house, the merchant asked,
"Has any seer entered here?"
He said,
"I have entered.
He said:
Something was given to him;
he said,
"No."
The guild-leader was deeply distressed, thinking, "Such a worthy recipient of offerings, who has entered my house, has not been honored by this poor woman.
Then the guild-leader said to that woman,
"Give me this merit which you have accumulated today."
"I shall give you abundant gold and bullion. She then said: "All wealth, grain, gold, and silver are subject to exhaustion;
but the fruit of merit given to the Munis is never exhausted in any way. [7]
If I were otherwise than this, I would be called poor by others;
because of not seeing such as these and because of not sharing my enjoyments,
may I be freed from ugliness and possess an abundance of enjoyments.
Do not live dependent on others, being subject to the families of others. [9]
And thus shall I walk, O Hero, as you walk;
likewise shall Sītā be free from passion, liberated from the bonds of existence. [10]
Having given food to the seer, I am joyful and delighted, well-established in the next world and free from deficiency. [11]
Having passed away from here, I shall be reborn in the delightful Nandana grove; there I shall roam amidst the throngs of gods.
At the proper time, I gave food as an offering to the Well-Accomplished One for the sake of abandoning suffering. [12]
Then that wife was dismissed by the merchant;
that poor woman was installed as the Bhaṭṭārikā.
"Sisters, you might think that she was some other poor woman, but it should not be viewed in this way."
"I myself was that poor woman.
Because I honored that Pratyekabuddha with alms-food with a devout mind, through the ripening of that karma, I have become beautiful. [The rest as before.]
Moreover, sisters, it was not by this alone that I planted roots of merit whereby I became gracious, beautiful to behold,
and swift in realization;
on another occasion as well, I planted roots of merit.

189. Sisters, in the past, in a former time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a certain woman placed a copper wheel in a basket, scattered flowers over it, covered it with a cloth from Kāśi, and offered it to the Blessed One Kāśyapa. Having made the offering, she made this aspiration:

Having covered the wheel of the chariot, complete with its hub and rim, with a fine cloth, I shall indeed bear witness to those dharmas that were witnessed by the best of sages; I too shall bear witness to that Dharma.
Now, on account of some business, she had been reprimanded by her husband, and she was consequently filled with longing.
He said:
"Fie upon this female state! The female sex is contemptible."
"I shall go and hang myself.
Taking a rope, she went out;
and not far from there, seeing the stūpa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, she was filled with faith.
Adorned with ornaments, clothed in garments from Kāśī, and her limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, she thought:
"I shall die;
I shall perform an offering at the stūpa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa."
With a serene mind, she removed those ornaments, scattered them over the stūpa, covered it with a garment from Kāśī, and anointed it with sandalwood paste; then she made this aspiration:
"In a future time, may I please such a Teacher as this, and may he teach me the Dharma, and may I understand the Dharma he teaches."
Having hanged herself there, she passed away and was reborn in the abode of the Thirty-three.
Surrounded by a retinue of thousands of apsarases, she remained there for the duration of her lifespan; then, passing away from there, she was reborn among humans.

She was born into a brahmin family of the Kāpila clan in Vaiśālī; her kinsmen gave her the name Bhadrā. Having no desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure, she went forth from home and became a renunciant, whereby she brought about the destruction of all taints (*āsrava*).
She who, with a devout mind, offers to the Blessed One Kāśyapa garments from Kāśi and fresh ointment—
that woman of Kapila pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One, the Teacher. Then the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, one must indeed make what is called a *dakaśāṭikā* (bathing robe).
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"Behold, Blessed One, how this Bhadrā went forth together with the Elder Mahākāśyapa!"
The Blessed One said:
"It is not only now that these two have gone forth;
at another time as well, these two went forth."
"At another time also, Blessed One; at another time also, O Bhikṣuṇīs.
Long ago, Bhikṣuṇīs, in a past age, four royal sages (rāja-ṛṣis) took up residence in a potter’s family:
Khāṇuvarṇa among the Kaliṅgas, and Bhārgava among the Gandhāras."
Nimi was the king of the Videhas, and Ugrasena was a kṣatriya. [13]
These four royal sages, possessed of fierce splendor and great strength, stayed for one night in the family of a potter. Having approached the potter, they asked him:
"What did you see, or what did you hear, that you announced your renunciation?"
The great king of the Kaliṅgas, a bull among men, who was the color of a withered stump, being questioned by the potter, spoke these words: [14]
O woman, the second [note], from which delight comes, having arrived, fastens the conch shell fashioned with superior gold as a bond. From where [does it come]? From where has delight come?
Having seen and heard the fault of association,
I practice the life of a mendicant.
The great king Bhārgava, a bull among men of the Gandhāras, being questioned by Kumbhakāra, spoke these words: [16]
But the female birds, for the sake of a corpse,
fly down in great numbers;
they run about for the purpose of food.
Having seen that, I practice the life of a monk. [17]
Then King Nimi, the great king of Videha and lord of Mithilā, being questioned by the potter, spoke these words: [18]
Alas! I see that very woman, who was once like a cloud in complexion and as smooth as if anointed with oil,
now lying broken on the ground for the sake of a fruit.
Having seen this, I am filled with agitation; I shall practice the life of a monk.
The great king Ugrasena, a bull among kṣatriyas, being questioned by the potter, spoke these words: [20]
In the midst of such splendor, you beheld that bull endowed with a body whose hump was moving and colored;
yet, for the sake of desire, you were shattered by him.
Seeing him broken, I practice the life of a mendicant. [21]
All these gods have gathered together like a blazing fire at night;
I too shall go forth into homelessness.
Having abandoned all delightful sensual pleasures.
The potter’s wife said:
"This is the very time; there is no other, for there is no instructor outside of this [community]."
"I too shall go forth;
my little sons, where will they go? [23]
They do not know the raw from the cooked, nor the salty from the unsalted; like fledglings released from a man's hand, these foolish children are ignorant and lack wings. [24]
I have gone forth following him who has gone forth;
I follow him as he wanders.
King Nimi was the Bodhisattva; Śārisuta was Kaliṅga;
Ugrasena was Maudgalya; Ānanda was Bhārgava; Kāśyapa was the potter; and Bhadrā was that potter-woman. [26]
At that time also, both of these were renunciants;
even now, both of these are renunciants.
Now the Blessed One permitted bathing cloths for the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs then made bathing cloths from the robes of the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, it is not permissible to make a water-strain cloth from a garment as it was originally received. Thus, the training rule was prescribed: when a bhikṣuṇī has a water-strain cloth made, it must be made according to the proper measurements.
In this regard, the measurement is as follows:
in length, it is four spans according to the span of a Sugata.
If one should have it made more than two spans across, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
"Bathing-cloth" refers to that which was permitted by the Blessed One.
"Having it made" means that she should either make it herself or have it made by another.

"Authoritative" means: here the authoritative measure is four spans (*vitasti*). "By the span of the Sugata" means: the Sugata is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; his span is equal to two and a half feet of a bed-leg across. If one causes it to be made beyond that, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
Now, if they bathe in a secluded spot or a bower without a bathing-cloth (*daka-śāṭikā*), there is no offense.

If a monk bathes without a bathing-cloth (*dakaśāṭikā*), he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. However, if he bathes in a secluded place (*nikuñja*) without a bathing-cloth, there is no offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
When a nun has a bathing cloth made, it must be made according to the proper measurements. Herein, these are the measurements: four spans in length.
With a span of the Sugata as the measure,
two [spans] across;
if one should cause it to be made beyond that, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
Pācattika-dharma 76, Kaṭhina 190. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā was requested by the community of nuns:
"Noble lady, are you able to beg for cloths on behalf of the community?
She then replied:
"It is possible.
She then went to some poor families and said,
"O you of great merit, are you able to give a cloth for the Saṅgha?"
They said, "Noble lady, we shall understand; you will come again.
She came again and again.
They said,
"We shall know, we shall know.
Then she spoke.
"If you wish to give, then give!
The time for the Saṃgha's robes is passing away. What shall we do? you say.
They did not give it then,
and the time for the robes passed.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on until the Blessed One said:
If a nun, out of a weak expectation regarding robes, should cause the Sangha’s *kaṭhina* suspension to pass by, it is a *pācattika*.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"Weak" means lacking the capability.

"Regarding 'expectation for a robe' (*cīvarapratyāśāya*): 'robe' (*cīvara*) refers to [garments] from *kāla* down to *kṣaumunikā*. 'The kaṭhina-spreader of the Saṃgha'—if one should cause it to pass beyond [the limit], that is, cause it to exceed [the time], it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the formal rule (*prajñapti*)."
Now this nun is being encouraged: "Noble lady, will you be able to request the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha?
If she is capable, she should take up the task.
Having made an effort, one should not beg from families that are weak;
rather, one should beg from those who are capable— whether they be fathers, sons, brothers, sisters, or relatives by birth or kinship—
and once those who are capable of giving have been requested, they should be informed [of the situation].
Then they say, "We shall know, we shall know," and she should be told:
"Either give it or refuse it, for the time for the robes is passing.
Now, if she is unable [to provide them], that nun should be encouraged for the sake of the Saṃgha's removal of the kaṭhina.

If, having encouraged [the donor], one neither asks for it oneself nor causes it to be asked for, nor informs the community of nuns that it has not been obtained, one incurs a *pācattika* offense. Furthermore, if a monk, out of a weak expectation regarding robes, causes the community’s *kaṭhina* suspension to pass by, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, out of a weak expectation regarding robe-material, should cause the Sangha's *kaṭhina* spreading to be postponed, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*). Phu.
Pācattika Dharma 77:
Concerning the Carrying of Robes.
191. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Then those nuns, having come to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One while dressed in their inner and outer robes, were overtaken by a fire as they were departing;
their robes were burned.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
This is precisely why you do not now wear this robe for wearing;
therefore, a robe for wearing must indeed be worn.
This is the origin of the matter.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Now, those bhikṣuṇīs— daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Mallas, and daughters of the Kolitas— who had gone forth from delicate backgrounds,
were becoming exhausted while carrying their heavy outer robes (saṃghāṭī).
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī...
[as before] ...until the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I allow it for one who is ill.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble [the nuns]."
[The full passage] as before, up to:
"Whatever nun who is not ill does not wear her robe for wearing, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
'Whatever nun' means one who is fully ordained."
"A robe for traveling" refers to the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) up to the bathing cloth (*dakaśāṭikā*). "One carries it" means that it should be taken wherever one goes.
"Not being ill" is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill.
If this nun, when not ill, does not carry her robe for use, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
However, there is no offense if she is now worshipping a *caitya*, walking the *caṅkrama*, or going within the boundary (*sīmā*).
A monk, too, if he does not carry his robe for use, incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill does not wear her customary robe, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
This is the seventy-eighth rule concerning offenses of expiation.
192. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, daily food was being brought from the family of Bhadrā Kāpileyī’s kinsmen.
She cooked it in the monastery and ate it.
Now her sons and brothers arrived;
they had gone to visit Bhadrā.
She said to the others, "You shall eat. They then said, "We shall eat. Thereupon, she gave it to them.
He said:
"This is indeed delicious!
Where did you get this?"
She said,
"It was brought from your house. They replied:
"In our house, food is not cooked so deliciously.
She replied,
"How could your auspicious slave-girls know how to do it?"
"How should they be protected? [They replied: "In this very way, they make the household utensils crack. Then, having gone home, they beat those female slaves with sticks and whips.
"Itikitikā’s daughters, we give you such a quantity of requisites, yet you make them useless!
They, weeping, said:
"Noble lady, she will kill us!"
The bhikṣuṇīs heard of this matter; [the rest is] as before.
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, noble lady.
Therefore, it is not permissible to cook, cause to be cooked, roast, or cause to be roasted any hard food or soft food that has been brought by another."
This is the origin of the matter.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, those bhikṣuṇīs—both daughters of the Śākyas and daughters of the Kolitas—were walking for alms.
They receive food that has been kept overnight;
rice that has been kept overnight; and soup that has been kept overnight.
They ate stale vegetables and stale boiled beans; having eaten them again and again, they vomited.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī...
[peyāla] ...up to: "Is it permissible, Blessed One, for a nun to eat while remaining silent?"
The Blessed One said, "It is possible.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"[These rules] shall remain until they have been thoroughly purified."

If a nun, having repeatedly cooked or caused to be cooked, roasted or caused to be roasted, or boiled or caused to be boiled food— whether hard or soft— that was brought from elsewhere, eats or consumes it while not being ill, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Again, a bhikṣuṇī" refers to [the standard formula].
"Brought from elsewhere" means brought from a village or brought from a city.
"Solid food" means solid food; "soft food" means soft food.
"Having cooked" means by oneself; "having had cooked" means by others.
"Having roasted" means by oneself;
"having caused to roast" means by others;
"having boiled" means by oneself.
"Having caused to be woven" means by others.
"Not being ill" is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill. What, then, is intended here by "illness"?

Whether she is weak from old age, or weak from illness, or vomits after eating, or becomes unwell— this is what is intended here by "illness. If that nun, out of greed for flavor, should repeatedly cook or cause to be cooked alms-food that has already been brought to her, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
Now, when it has become cold, it is permitted to warm it;
however, one must not do so with a large pan or a small pot.
Rather, it should be warmed with a copper vessel, a bronze vessel, or a brass bowl.
If a monk cooks for himself, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
However, if he has it cooked by a kitchen attendant, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if the alms-food has become cold and he warms it, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "If a nun, having received hard food or soft food from another, should again cook it or have it cooked,
roast it or have it roasted, or boil it or have it boiled, and then eat or consume it while not being ill, [she commits an offense]."
Or [if she does so], it is a pācittika offense. Hā.
Pācattika Dharma 79:
On the Water-Fan.
193. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Gartodara, Gartodara’s mother, and Gartodara’s father went forth from the household life into homelessness.
Gartodara’s father and Gartodara’s mother had gone forth among the Śākyas, while Gartodara went forth among the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthikas).
Gartodara’s father ate his meals, while Gartodara’s mother stood before him fanning him and holding a water-pot.
He then began to speak of various past deeds of hers that were unpleasant to her;
she then struck him on the head with her water-pitcher.
And he was struck on the head with the handle of the fan; you who are not clever, not mature, unskilled, and ignorant of human nature— even now you speak what should not be spoken.
She was seen by the bhikṣuṇīs,
and they said to her:
"Noble lady, do not do this."
"This foremost assembly cannot be treated in such a manner.
She then said:
"Indeed, this man is incompetent, unskilled, and ignorant of the proper way; even now he speaks those things which ought not to be spoken."
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression, Gartodaramātā."
This is not the Dharma; this is not the Vinaya.
That you now attend upon a monk while he is eating with water and a fan—therefore, it is not permissible to attend upon him with water and a fan.
As far as the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should attend upon a monk while he is eating by fanning him with water, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Regarding the phrase "if a nun": one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
[The full] passage:
"A monk" means one who has received full ordination. [The full] passage:
"Eating" means any kind of solid food or soft food, whether consisting of the five groups of food or mixed with the five groups of food.
"To serve with a fan" means: if she holds a water vessel or provides a breeze with a fan, it is a *pācattika* offense,
according to the established rule.

If that nun carries a water-pot but does not fan herself, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. If she fans herself but does not carry a water-pot, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If she does both, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Neither case constitutes an offense.
This offense applies to one monk with one nun;
however, if there are now many monks, there is no offense.
Now, if a nun’s father or brother is a monk, even if he fans her while she is eating, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should attend upon a monk while he is eating by fanning him with water or a fan, it is a *pācattika* offense. 0.
Pācattika Dharma 80: Eating Garlic 194. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.

and he said:

and he said:
"If they eat, why do they trample [the crops]?"

If a nun should eat garlic, it is an offense of expiation.

Furthermore, whatever else there may be that is garlic—all garlic is not permitted;
it is not permitted raw, nor is it permitted cooked.
Liver is not permitted;
anything at all is not permitted for internal consumption.
However, if a nun has a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury, she is permitted to smear it [with ointment].
Having smeared it, one must not remain standing in an open area where others approach;
rather, one should stay in a secluded place until the news has spread.
After washing [the hands], one should depart.

"If a nun should eat garlic, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). 1.

[71] Transferring, [72] the robe of a śramaṇa,

Pācattika Dharma 81: Giving.
[Number 195] The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. A sister of the bhikṣuṇī Rāṣṭrapālā had passed away.
Now she would give various kinds of hard and soft foods to those nephews after having eaten them herself;
people then complained, "Look, sirs! This female ascetic gives away to householders what was given out of faith!"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She said:
"Go and summon Rāṣṭrapālā.
She was then summoned.
The Blessed One questioned all of that in detail;
he replied, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible to give hard or soft food with one's own hand to a householder. This is the origin of the rule."
Gartodara, Gartodara’s father, and Gartodara’s mother went forth from the home life into homelessness. Gartodara’s father and Gartodara’s mother had gone forth among the Śākyas;
Gartodara had gone forth among the heretics.
When he approached Gartodaramātṛ, she gave him a bowl filled with various kinds of fried cakes.
Taking it, he went to a tavern; there he ate some himself and offered some to others. They then said:
"Where did you obtain this? He then said,
"Make no noise!"
The Śramaṇīs of the Śākyas are worthy of offerings;
we too are worthy of offerings from them;
we too are worthy of offerings from them.
Now people were complaining; the nuns heard of this matter.
[The usual formula] ... as far as the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, O mother of Gartodara."
Therefore, it is not permissible to give solid food or soft food to a householder or a wandering ascetic.
Then the Blessed One—
[the usual formula]— up to [the conclusion].
If a nun should give hard food or soft food with her own hand to a householder or to a wanderer, it is a *pācattika*.
"If a nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"To a householder" means to a layperson.
"Of the wandering mendicant" refers to [the lineage] ending with the matted-hair ascetics of the Gautama clan.
"With one's own hand" means hand to hand,
or vessel to vessel.
"Solid food" means whatever is solid food;
"soft food" means whatever is soft food.
Should she give it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittika).
Now, if someone comes to a nun—
whether it be a blood relative or a brother—
and she has something to give him, it is not permissible for her to give it with her own hand.
It should be given by means of a *kalpiyakārī* (one who prepares things for use).
Now, if there is no *kalpiyakārī*, it should be said:
"Therefore, take it yourselves and eat."
Then, if he sees that this person is greedy for flavors and eats everything,
having had him accept as much as was relinquished, [he should give] the remainder.
He should be told,
"Gopā!
Then, having placed him on the ground, he should be told.
"Take it and eat.
Now, if a renunciant comes, it is not permissible to give hard food or soft food with one's own hand;
it must be given through a *kalpiyakārin* (an attendant who prepares what is allowable).
Now, if there is no one who prepares what is permissible, [one may say]: "Take this very thing and eat it. Then he says:
"O kinsman, why do you behave toward us as if we were outcasts?"
It should be said:
"In that way, you have gone forth into a poorly proclaimed teaching.
Now, when he goes to another village, he is permitted to have a permissible task performed for him.
Therefore, eat yourselves and accept [the food] from us.
Now, if he knows [them to be] "greedy for flavors"— the rest is as before.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should give hard food or soft food with her own hand to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
The Blessed One was dwelling at Kauśāmbī.
The nun Chandakamātā entered the royal harem of the king.

She provides collyrium, counter-collyrium, emetics, purgatives, sudation therapy, nasal medication, surgical treatment, and medicinal drugs;

"This is not the life of renunciation; this is the practice of a physician.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on until the Blessed One said:
"Summon Chandakamātā. She was then summoned,
and the Blessed One said:
"Is it true, Chandakamātā, that you make your living by the science of medicine? "Yes, Blessed One.

"Chandaka’s mother, that was a misdeed!
Therefore, it is not permissible to make one's livelihood by means of the science of medicine. Then the Blessed One [spoke].
[The usual formula] ... up to ... Furthermore, if a nun should make her livelihood by means of medical science, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Medical science" means the science of snakes, the science of poisons, and so forth, up to the movements of the planets.
If she makes her livelihood by that means, it is a *pācattika* offense;
this is the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
It is not permissible for a nun to practice medicine.
It is possible to teach [this]:
if a monk makes his livelihood through the science of medicine, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should make her livelihood by means of the science of medicine, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

"Whatever nun" is as before.
"Householder" means a layperson.
"Parivrājaka" refers to those ranging from the Gautamas to the Jaṭilas.
"The science of medicine" refers to the knowledge of snakes, the knowledge of poisons, up to the movements of the planets.
"One should cause the body to recite the science of medicine" means one should instruct it.
As far as the designation is concerned:

If a monk teaches the science of medicine, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

"If a nun should teach the science of medicine to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, it is a *pācattika* offense."
Pācattika Dharma 84:
Service for Laypeople 198. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.

Recite and study!"
Apply your minds thoroughly;
in this way, you will have rendered me a service. Indeed, it is thus that we too shall render you a service.
Then, having ascended to the upper story, they took cotton; some prepared it for treatment,
others carded it,
and others spun it.

they took bundles of thread and approached the female lay devotee.
"Upāsikā, a favor has been done.

"This is my favor to you, noble ladies: having eaten from my hand, you should recite, study, and apply yourselves to yoga within the teaching of the Buddhas. When the nuns heard what had been said disparagingly by that female lay devotee, they reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... as far as the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression, O bhikṣuṇīs."
Therefore, it is not permissible to perform domestic services for householders. ... [down to] ...

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī" means one who has received full ordination.
"Gṛhī" means a householder. "Vaiyāpṛtya" means that one should perform service, such as spinning or carding wool, up to and including weaving,
grinding, pounding, cooking, or sewing.

Pācattika Dharma 85:
On Eating Together. 199. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā approached another family at midday while it was cloudy.

She then entered there suddenly and without being announced.

Now that man was agitated and distressed; the king was making him perform this task, thinking, "First, I will have him investigate this female ascetic, the daughter of Itikitikā. She, for her part, was terrified.
She spoke to the fleeing bhikṣuṇīs: "Noble ladies, I have been made to fall away from the holy life. [The bhikṣuṇīs] reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on as before.
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda; how is it that you, knowing this, approach a family where a meal is being prepared during the day without having first announced your arrival?
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call together the nuns, Gautamī. [The usual formula]... down to:
Whatever nun, knowing a family that provides food, should go there during the day without having previously informed them, it is a *pācattika* offense."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"Family" refers to families such as those of Brahmins and so forth.
Where there is a woman and a man, a cooking pot and a small jar, a pestle and a mortar, a winnowing basket and a measure of barley—this is the last household.
"Eating together" means that the woman is the food for the man, and the man is also the food for the woman.

"To enter uninvited" means: it is a *pācattika* offense, as defined [in the rules], to enter until such time as one has been invited. Now, when it is known that this is a family where food is shared, it is not permissible for one who has not previously informed them to enter uninvited.
If there is a gatekeeper, one must speak to him.
If he says, "I am entering," and [the other] says,
"Do not enter," one must not enter.
Then he said:

If they remain silent, it is not permitted to enter.

If even a monk approaches [such a family] without prior notice, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

Association 200. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.

Pācattika Dharma 87:
Swearing an Oath 201. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā quarreled with the other nuns.
Whenever she was defeated, she would then prostrate herself, saying:
"Homage to the Blessed One! I swear by the feet of the Blessed One!"
I swear by the saffron robes;
I swear by the end of suffering:
if I speak thus.
May I not die while wearing the saffron robes;
may I not bring about an end to suffering;
may I not go to the destination of one who has killed his mother.
I go to the destination of one who kills his father; I go to the destination of one who kills an Arhat;
indeed, I go to the destination of one who is ungrateful.
I go to the destination of one who betrays a friend; I go to the destination of one who reviles a noble person;
I become a denizen of hell.
"I go to the realm of animals; I become a hungry ghost.
May it also be so for Bhadrāyaṇī, who spoke thus to me."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She said: "Go and summon Nandā.
Then the Blessed One questioned her about all of this in detail.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, Nanda,” and so on, until the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun should dwell using oaths—whether referring to herself or referring to another—there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). ...
"Should dwell using oaths" means she should make a formal oath.
"I swear by the feet of the Blessed One, the Blessed One;
all as before.
Up to: if that nun swears an oath referring to herself or another, it is a *pācattika*.
A monk who swears incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should dwell while swearing—whether referring to herself or to another—it is a *pācattika*."
Pācattika Dharma 88:
Weeping. 202. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā quarreled with the other nuns;
whenever she was defeated, she would strike herself with her fingernails, slaps, and fists,
and beat her own belly.
Balabalā wept.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"Is it true, Nanda, that you are quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs?
[And so on]...
up to: you are crying out 'Help! Help!'?"
"Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "It is a transgression for you, Nanda; this is not the Dharma," and so forth, until: "Therefore, it is not permissible to weep after having struck oneself."
Then indeed, the Blessed One said: "Up to the point that they shall be completely purified—whichever nun, having struck herself, should weep, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
"Again, a nun" is as before.
"Having killed herself" means by means of sticks, or stones, or by whatever other means.
"Should she weep," means that if she should shed tears, it is a *pācattika* offense;
this is the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
That nun harms herself but does not weep; she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
If she weeps but does not strike, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
if she both strikes and weeps, she incurs a *pācattika* offense;
if she neither strikes nor weeps, there is no offense.
If a monk, having struck himself, weeps, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, moreover, having struck herself, should weep, it is a *pācattika*. (8)
Pācattika Dharma 89:
Kṣiyati 203. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, regarding Sthūlanandā, the nun Jetā was highly praised by the families.

That nun Jetā, being virtuous, approached the families with a graceful deportment—graceful in her advancing and retreating, in her looking ahead and looking aside, in her drawing in and extending [her limbs], and in her wearing the outer robe, bowl, and monastic robes; she was neither agitated nor arrogant.
Her speech is not fickle, not talkative, and not scattered;
it is pleasing, whereby gods and humans are inspired with faith and perform acts of service toward her.
They greeted her, rose up for her,
and invited her to accept alms-bowls, robes, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
yet the nun Sthūlanandā was neither perfected in decorum nor perfected in dignified deportment, wearing robes that were soiled and filthy.
With breasts that were split and gaping, hanging down like swollen testicles, with swollen buttocks, they were arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, and loose-lipped in speech;
they showed her no respect and did not invite her.
Then she said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Look, noble ladies! Noble Jetā, who was praised by my own families, speaks ill of me.
She then said:
"This is not so, Noble Lady; I am not speaking dispraise of the Noble Lady. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Then the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda.
[The rest is as before.]

"Since you indeed fall into the practice of censuring others based on what was wrongly heard and wrongly understood, it is therefore not permissible for you to fall into the practice of censuring others based on what was wrongly heard and wrongly understood.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call them together, Gautamī, until they have become completely purified.
Furthermore, if a nun should speak thus to other nuns: 'When I, noble ladies, approached such-and-such a family...'"
If, out of ill-will toward a certain named bhikṣuṇī regarding the Blessed One, one should charge her with an offense based on what was wrongly heard or wrongly understood, it is a *pācattika*.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained.

"Should speak thus to the nuns" refers to how the nun Sthūlanandā said: "Venerable ladies, such-and-such a family," where "family" means a kṣatriya family, a brahmin family, a royal family, or whatever [other] families there may be.
Furthermore, there are other families;
thus, for example, as in the case of the nun named Jetā,
[the phrase] "the Blessed One has malice" refers not to the ten grounds for anger which are improper occasions for provocation.

"Without proper basis" means: by what has been wrongly heard or wrongly understood, not by a formal act of seeing (*darśana*), nor by a formal act of a *śramaṇa*. If a nun should charge another with an offense on the grounds of such [fault], she commits a *pācattika* offense; this is the rule (*prajñapti*).
It is not permissible for a nun to charge another with an offense based on what has been wrongly heard or wrongly understood.
If she does so, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
Even a monk, by means of what is wrongly heard or wrongly understood, incurs the offense of censure and commits a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, if a nun should speak thus to nuns: 'Venerable ladies, when I approach such-and-such a family...'"

If, because of a slight hearing or a misunderstanding of the words "the Blessed One harbors resentment and lacks confidence toward the nun named so-and-so," one should fall into the offense of reproach, it is a *pācattika*. 9.
Pācattika Dharma 90:
Regarding Stinginess Toward Families. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā, having dressed herself at the very break of dawn and taken her bowl and robes, stood at the gate-chambers of great families.
To the monks as they were entering, she said:
"Let the noble ones enter; let the noble sirs enter; it will be accomplished for our sake."
"First, having given the foremost alms-food to you who are the first, we shall afterwards consume it ourselves.
Do not go to other families;
for it is not accomplished by others."
Then, being ashamed, they will withdraw.

This same procedure should be applied to the bhikṣuṇīs. Likewise, when wandering mendicants, parivrājakas, ājīvakas, nirgranthas, and even those who contemplate the Dharma enter, [the same protocol applies].
As they were entering, she reviled them:

"O Caṇḍāyus, you who have lost hope, whose hopes are shattered, you who are ruined by liquor, you donkeys, naked ones, shameless, lacking modesty, holders of false views, and fallen ones—enter! Is it for your sake that success is achieved?"
"Having first given you the foremost alms-food, I shall afterwards consume it myself;
do not visit other families,
for success is not achieved through other [means]."
Then, being ashamed, they would withdraw;
thus it created an obstacle for all who were wandering for alms.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The] usual formula... up to where the Blessed One said:
"Call Nandā."
She was then summoned;
the Blessed One questioned her about all of that in detail.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, Nanda, that you act with such stinginess toward families.”
"Therefore, it is not permissible that you practice stinginess regarding families;
therefore, it is not permissible to practice stinginess regarding families.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call them together, Gautamī. [The usual formula applies] up to:
"Whichever nun should practice stinginess toward families, it is a *pācattika* offense."

"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained. "Stinginess toward families" means she should create an obstacle; this is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*), as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) extends.
It is not permissible for a nun to practice stinginess toward families.
He commits a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk or a nun asks, one must speak of actual virtues.
However, if outsiders ask, and one makes a frown [of disapproval] thinking, "Lest they cause me to adopt wrong views," there is no offense.
If a monk also acts with stinginess toward a family, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should act with stinginess toward a family, it is a *pācattika*. [End of section 16]. Summary verse:
[81] He gives; [82] he treats medically; [83] he causes to recite; [84] service for householders; [85] eating together; [86] social association.
[87] He utters curses; [88] he weeps; [89] he dwells [in resentment]; [90] out of envy for the family.
The ninth section is completed.
Pācattika Dharma 91:
In the presence of.

205. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Gartodara, Gartodara’s mother, and Gartodara’s father went forth from the household life into homelessness... [as before] ...until that old man was eating.
Gartodaramātā was serving [him].
Then he began to speak of certain past deeds of hers—those faults involving an abundance of women—which were unpleasant to her.
She then said:
One with a fierce lifespan;
one who is neither a youth nor an elder;
one who is unrefined, unskilled, and ignorant of the nature of things.
Even now you speak what should not be spoken.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [The rest as before.]
"Up to: 'Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
'It was a misdeed on your part, Mother Gartodara.'"
[The usual formula applies.
Therefore, it is not permissible to revile or abuse a monk to his face.
Then the Blessed One [proceeded] until [the rules] became completely purified.
If a nun should revile, incense, or abuse a monk face-to-face, it is a *pācattika*.
"A nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"Face-to-face" means within earshot of both parties.

"Should revile" means: she should provoke with the syllables *a*, *śa*, and *e*, and she should scold and abuse [him], saying, "O savage! O fool! O old man! O unskilled one! O you who do not know the nature of things! This is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
It is not permitted for a nun to revile, provoke, or scold a monk face-to-face.
If she reviles, becomes angry, or abuses [him], it is a *pācattika*.
Now, if a nun’s father, brother, or kinsman has gone forth [into the religious life],
and he is agitated, arrogant, and unconcentrated, she may then speak to him.
Now, it is not permissible to speak by means of intimidation;
rather, one should cause him to understand through wisdom.
If he is a youth, he should be addressed as follows:
"O kinsman, if you do not train now, when will you train?
When you have become worn out and old? Then, indeed, when one has become an elder, one should speak."
"If you do not train now, when will you train? It will be when you have arrived at the entrance of the maṇḍala.
It is not permissible for a monk to revile nuns in their presence, saying, "shaven-headed woman," "prostitute," and so forth...
If that nun reviles a monk in his presence, it is a *pācattika* offense. //1//
Pācattika Dharma 92:
Less than twelve years [of seniority].
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, nuns who had been [ordained] for one year, two years, up to six years were taking on pupils;
yet they neither exhorted nor instructed them.
They grew like *indragava* oxen, they grew like jackal kids.
Being deficient in proper attire and deficient in proper deportment, they did not know how one should behave toward a preceptor (upādhyāyinī),
how one should behave toward a teacher (ācāryā),
or how one should behave toward elder and senior nuns (bhikṣuṇī).
How [should one act] in a village? How in the forest? How in the midst of the Saṃgha?
"How should one practice regarding the wearing of the outer robe, the alms bowl, and the robes?
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī...
[as before] ...until the Blessed One said:
"Summon those bhikṣuṇīs.
They were then summoned,
and the Blessed One questioned them about all of this in detail.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“In that case, it is not permissible to ordain one who has fewer than twelve years of standing in the rainy-season retreat.”
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the nuns until they have all gathered.
"Furthermore, if a nun who is less than twelve years [of standing] should ordain another, it is a *pācattika* offense."

"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "Less than twelve years" means: a nun who is less than twelve years [old] is called "less than twelve years"—that is, one who has less than twelve rainy seasons (*udakavarṣa*) and less than twelve full years (*saṃvatsara*). A nun who has less than twelve rainy seasons but completed twelve full years is also "less than twelve years."
One who is less than twelve years [from conception] in water-years, yet more than twelve years in full years, is a nun of less than twelve years.
If she was ordained in the winter and is ordained by means of that twelfth year, she is a nun of less than twelve years until the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) has been performed.
A nun of less than twelve years is one who has not yet completed her twelfth year since ordination.
Thus she was ordained in the summer or during the rains;
thus she was ordained during the first invitation ceremony (*purimikā varṣopanāyikā*);
or she confers ordination before the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) has been performed.

If one who was ordained during the later *varṣopanāyikā* confers ordination before two *pravāraṇā*s have been performed, she is a nun of less than twelve years’ standing. One who has completed twelve rainy seasons (*udakavarṣa*) but whose full year is not yet complete is a nun of twelve years’ standing. One who has completed twelve years is a nun of twelve years’ standing.
A nun who has completed twelve years of rainy-season retreats (*udaka-varṣa*) and twelve full years;
a nun who has completed twelve years of rainy-season retreats and more than twelve full years;
one ordained during the winter who is ordained by means of that twelfth year after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has been performed—such a nun is one who has completed twelve years.
In this way, she is ordained during the summer or the rainy season;

in this way, having been ordained at the first invitation ceremony (*purimikā varṣopanāyikā*) and having completed the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), she ordains others as a nun who has fulfilled twelve years.

Having been ordained at the second invitation ceremony (*paścimikā varṣopanāyikā*), she ordains others by means of that twelfth year after two invitation ceremonies have been performed; thus she is a nun who has fulfilled twelve years.
If one should ordain [a girl] who is less than twelve years old, it is a *pācattika* offense.
If that nun ordains [a girl] who is less than twelve years old, it is a *pācattika* offense; if she causes her to go forth, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
A monk also, if he ordains [a boy] who is less than twelve years old, incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has fewer than twelve years of seniority should ordain a candidate, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
Pācattika Dharma 93:
Anaṅgopetā. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One has prescribed a training rule:
it is not permitted to ordain one who is less than twelve years old.
Now, at that time and on that occasion, the nuns of the group of six were exactly twelve years old.
Now they were ordaining and initiating them,
yet they neither exhorted nor instructed them;
[and so on].
"As for how one should practice regarding the wearing of the outer robe and the carrying of the alms bowl—
the nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...until she was summoned."
The Blessed One asks all of that in detail, [to which they reply],
"Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain one who is not endowed with the requisite qualities.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"[The rules] shall remain until they are completely purified."
If she has completed twelve years but is not endowed with the [necessary] qualities (*anaṅgopetā*), and she ordains [a candidate], it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).

"Having completed twelve years" is as explained in the first rule of training (*śikṣāpada*). "Not endowed with the qualities" means that one who is "endowed with the qualities" (*aṅgopetā*) is one in whom the ten qualities exist, as follows: [listing of the ten qualities].
She is restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa vows. [1]
One becomes learned in the Abhidharma. // 2 //
She becomes one who is learned in the Vinaya. (3)
She becomes capable of establishing [others] in the training of higher ethical discipline. // 4 //
She becomes capable of establishing [others] in the training of higher mind. // 5 //
She becomes capable of establishing [others] in the training of higher wisdom. // 6 //
She is capable of restoring one who has fallen into an offense, or of causing her to be restored. // 7 //
She is capable of withdrawing herself from calamities, or of causing others to withdraw from them. (8)
She is capable of attending to the sick herself or of having them attended to by others. // 0 //
She is twelve years old, or more than twelve years old. Ḷṃ.
She in whom these ten factors are found is said to be "endowed with the factors.
By the opposite, she is "not endowed with the factors.
If one who is not endowed with the factors should ordain [a woman], it is a *pācattika* offense.
... [as before] ... up to the formal rule:
if she ordains one who lacks the requisite qualifications, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one confers full ordination, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a monk who is not endowed with the [required] limbs also allows one to go forth or confers full ordination, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If she has completed twelve years [of training] but is not endowed with the requisite qualities, and yet she ordains [a candidate], it is a *pācattika* offense. // 3 //
Pācattika Dharma 94:
On Not Being Authorized. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One has prescribed a training rule:
"One who is twelve years old and endowed with the [required] qualities should be ordained.
Now, those nuns who are twelve years old and endowed with the qualities are ordaining others.
Now the bhikṣuṇīs were complaining:
"She is indeed twelve years old, yet it is not known whether she is endowed with the [required] characteristics or not."
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said: "She must request permission for ordination."
The formal act (karma) must be performed by the karma-maker.
Let the noble Saṃgha listen to me:
if it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, this nun named so-and-so is twelve years of age and endowed with the [necessary] qualities.

She should request the formal authorization for ordination from the Saṃgha. The noble lady, the bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so, who is twelve years of age and endowed with the requisite qualities, requests the Saṃgha for the formal authorization for ordination.
It is pleasing to the Saṃgha, because of its silence; thus do I understand this to be.
Now she should request thus:
"I pay homage to the noble Saṃgha.
I, the bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so, am twelve years of age and endowed with the [required] qualities."
"I, [name], request the Saṃgha for authorization to attend upon [the teacher].
It would be well indeed if the noble Saṃgha would grant me authorization to attend upon [the teacher]. In this manner should a bhikṣuṇī make her request.
The motion: Let the noble Saṃgha listen to me.
This nun, named so-and-so, is twelve years of seniority and endowed with the requisite qualities.
She requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to ordain others.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant permission for the nun named so-and-so, who has twelve years of standing and is endowed with the [required] qualities, to ordain others.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Let the noble Saṃgha listen to me.
This nun, named so-and-so, is twelve years of seniority and endowed with the requisite qualities. She requests from the Saṃgha authorization for ordination.
The Saṃgha grants authorization for ordination to this nun, named so-and-so, who is twelve years of seniority and endowed with the requisite qualities.

Whichever noble ladies approve of the granting by the Saṃgha of the authorization for the nun named so-and-so— who has twelve years of seniority and is endowed with the [required] qualities— to ordain others,
let her remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let her speak.
This is the first formal motion;
likewise the second and the third formal motion.
The Saṃgha has granted the authorization for ordination to the nun named so-and-so, who is twelve years of age and endowed with the required qualities, O noble ladies.
It is pleasing to the Saṃgha because it is silent; thus do I understand this.

Now, indeed, until they have become completely purified—even if she has completed twelve years and is endowed with the [required] qualities—if she ordains one who has not been formally authorized, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Endowed with the factors" means that a bhikṣuṇī becomes endowed with the factors by means of ten factors;
the remainder is as before.
"Unauthorized" means that she is indeed unauthorized if she is not authorized.

If she is not endowed with the necessary qualities and has not been formally authorized, and they nevertheless perform the ritual for her— failing in the motion (*jñapti*), failing in the assembly (*gaṇa*), failing in the proclamation (*anuśrāvaṇā*), and being defiled by one or another of the secondary defects of the ritual—
then she is thus unauthorized. If one should ordain her— that is, confer full admission (*upasampadā*)— it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
If that nun ordains one who has not been authorized, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika);
if she causes her to go forth, she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (vinayātikrama).
Therefore the Blessed One said:
Even if she has completed twelve years and possesses the [required] limbs, if she ordains one who has not been formally authorized, it is a *pācattika* offense. //4//
Pācattika Dharma 95: Regarding the Unvirtuous. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
That nun Kālī, the daughter of a Licchavi, who was ordained three years ago,
has completed her training;
yet she opens the other monasteries with keys and master-keys and stays there together with householders and wandering ascetics.
She was ordained by her;
now the nuns are complaining:
"Why has she been ordained—she who is immoral, a thief of bolts, and keeps male companions?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She said: "Go and summon Kālī.
She was then summoned.
The Blessed One questioned her at length until she replied, “Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, Kālī.”
"Kālī, this is not the Dharma so long as you continue to ordain one who is immoral, a backbiter, and a companion to men.
Therefore, it is not permissible, knowing her to be so, to ordain one who is immoral, a backbiter, and a companion to men.
Now, the Blessed One [spoke] until they became completely purified."
If a nun, knowing that a woman is immoral, has broken her vows, and is accompanied by a man, should ordain her, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"Of bad character" means one who has failed in morality or has transgressed the precepts.
"One who picks locks" means one who opens the doors of monasteries belonging to others by means of picks and master-keys.
"One who has male companions" means...
"She lives in close association with householders and wandering mendicants.

"Should she ordain [her]" means: should she confer full admission (upasampadā), it is an offense of expiation (pācattika), as far as the formal rule (prajñapti) extends. Now, regarding her who lives in close association with householders and wandering mendicants: she is not permitted to be ordained.
However, if she is now able to fulfill the holy life (brahmacarya), she may be ordained after having been separated from that association.
If a monk, knowing that a novice (śrāmaṇera) is immoral and associated with women, should confer full ordination upon him without having him removed, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, knowing [a woman] to be immoral, one who keeps the bolt raised [at night], and one who has a male companion, should admit her into the order, it is a pācattika. //5//
Pācattika Dharma 96:
A Girl Less Than Twenty Years of Age.
210. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now, the nuns were ordaining girls who were only ten or twelve years old; they were lacking in discernment and not perfected in proper conduct. They did not know how to behave toward their preceptor, nor how to behave regarding the wearing of the outer robe, the bowl, and the religious garments.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"Summon those bhikṣuṇīs."
They were then summoned.
The Blessed One questioned them about all of that in detail, until they replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain a maiden who is less than twenty years of age.
Furthermore, until they have become completely purified,
if a nun should ordain a maiden who is less than twenty years of age, it is a *pācittika* offense.
"Less than twenty years old" means: less than twenty years of water (rainy seasons), less than twenty years [of age], is "less than twenty years old.

One who has less than twenty years of water but has completed twenty years [of age] is "less than twenty years old. One who has less than twenty years of water but is more than twenty years [of age] is "less than twenty years old."
If one born in the winter season is ordained by that twentieth year before the *pravāraṇā* has been performed, she is less than twenty years of age. The same applies to one born in the summer season.
Likewise, if one born during the first *varṣopanāyikā* (the first rains-retreat) is ordained by that twentieth year, she is less than twenty years of age.
She was born during the later *varṣopanāyikā* (the later rainy-season retreat); he confers full ordination upon her when she is twenty years old,
yet she has not performed the two *pravāraṇā* ceremonies and is less than twenty years of age.

If all [the nuns], perceiving her to be less than twenty years of age, confer full ordination upon this girl who has become a *kumārī* and is actually less than twenty years of age, they all incur a *pācattika* offense;
