There are six cases where it is a *pācattika* offense,
up to the formal rule (*prajñapti*). Now,

if a nun has a fellow resident or a pupil who is overly familiar with her, she should either separate herself from that person, cause them to be separated, or speak in praise of wandering forth on pilgrimage.
Now, if she is weak from old age or weak from illness, she should be separated from the other bhikṣuṇīs;
she should be told:
"There will be a separate salutation to the caitya."
There will be the sight of monks.
When we were young, we wandered about in this manner.
Furthermore, if a monk does not remove a resident disciple who is longing for worldly things, nor causes him to be removed, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is an attendant does not remove, nor cause to be removed, her dependent from such calamities—even by as little as five or six *yojanas*—it is a *pācattika* offense.
This is the 109th *pācattika* dharma."
Furthermore,
while the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī,
a nun named Sthūlanandā, who was not endowed with the requisite qualities, gave formal ordination.
She did not instruct them nor did she discipline them;
they grew like Indra-cows, they grew like auspicious goats,
and so forth.

"How indeed should one proceed regarding the wearing of the outer robe, the bowl, and the robes? Then that nun was addressed by the other nuns: "But what is the use of attending upon a noble lady who lacks the necessary qualities? This noble lady should be spoken to and instructed in this way.
She then said:
"Why are these women of the Bhadrāyiṇī group causing envy by attending upon my assembly?
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on,
until the Blessed One said:
"It was a transgression for you, Nanda, that you should thus fall into the practice of reproaching others. Therefore, it is not permissible to fall into the practice of reproaching others.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Call them together, Gautamī,
until they have become completely purified.
Furthermore, if a nun, being addressed in this way by the nuns..."
Furthermore, regarding one who has been ordained by a noble nun who is not endowed with the [eight] requisites:

if, having been told, "The noble lady should speak and instruct her thus," she should fall into a state of reproach, it is a *pācattika* offense. "A nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"By the nuns" means by the Saṃgha, by a large group, or by a single individual. Furthermore, "for a noble lady who is not endowed with the limbs" refers to one who is endowed with the ten limbs;
she is one who is restrained by the Prātimokṣa vow. [1]
[2] He becomes one who is learned in the Abhidharma; [3] he becomes one who is learned in the Abhivinaya;
and so on, up to...
And she must be twelve years old.
She for whom these ten factors are not present is one who lacks the necessary parts (*anaṅgopetā*).
If she should speak so as to cause him to fall into a state of reproach, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*), up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).

If this nun, being admonished by the nuns, should fall into the state of reproach, saying, "Why [should one be concerned] about a nun who is not endowed with the requisite qualities (anaṅgopetā) having been ordained? she commits a *pācattika* offense. If a monk, being admonished by the monks, should fall into the state of reproach, saying, "Why [should one be concerned] about a venerable one who is not endowed with the requisite qualities having been ordained? he incurs a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:

If a nun, being addressed thus by other nuns—"What indeed is the use of a woman who lacks the necessary qualities (anaṅgopetā) having been ordained?"—should fall into a state of resentment (*kṣiyā-dharma*), it is a *pācattika* offense. 9.
Pācattika Dharma 110:
Not to dismiss.
224. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Then another *śikṣamāṇā* said to Sthūlanandā,
"Noble Nandā, please grant me full ordination.
She replied:
"Certainly, I shall ordain you," she said;
but she became embarrassed,
neither ordaining her nor dismissing her.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [The usual formula applies]... up to: "Call Nandā before you."
She was then summoned; she was questioned on all of those very points, to which she replied,
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda.
Furthermore, whichever nun should speak thus to a *śikṣamāṇā*:"

If, having said, "When you have completed the preliminary training (pūraśikṣā), then I will ordain you," she neither confers the full ordination nor dismisses her, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). "The nun" means one who is fully ordained;
[the rest is as before].
"A trainee" (śikṣamāṇā) is one who has practiced the training for two years according to the eighteen rules.
"She should speak thus" means as the nun Sthūlanandā did; [if she says], "I will ordain you," she should indeed be ordained.
Now, if she is not capable herself, another should be requested.
But if she neither attends to [the preceptor] herself, nor requests another, nor dismisses [the candidate], saying, "Go,
receive full ordination wherever you wish," [she commits an offense].
If that nun, having said to a *śikṣamāṇā*, "I will have you ordained," subsequently neither ordains her nor releases her from the obligation, it is a *pācattika* offense. //10//
Pācattika Dharma 111: Vehicle 225. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Then Bhadrā Kāpileyī, having mounted a carriage drawn by four horses, was going to her kinsmen's home. People then complained, saying, "Look, sirs! This female ascetic has great desire!"
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
[the matter was then brought before the Buddha] until it was fully resolved.
"Whichever nun should mount a vehicle, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
This is the origin of the matter:
the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, those daughters of the Śākyas, the Koliyas, and the Licchavis—who were naturally delicate—had gone forth into the religious life.
Walking on foot, they grew weary.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so forth,
until the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I allow it for one who is ill.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Whatever nun, not being ill, should mount a vehicle, that is a *pācattika* offense."

"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "Not ill" is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill. "Illness" means being weak from old age, or weak from disease, or naturally delicate such that she is unable to come on foot—this is the illness intended here.
Regarding vehicles: an elephant vehicle, a horse vehicle, a camel vehicle, a cow vehicle, a donkey vehicle, a boat vehicle, a palanquin vehicle, and a wheeled carriage as the eighth.
If she should mount one, it is a *pācattika* offense.
It is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to mount a vehicle.
Where camels or oxen are yoked,
one should instead mount a woman's vehicle;
where female camels or female oxen are yoked, there one should mount.
Now, if she is unconscious and does not recognize whether it is a woman or a man, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if she crosses from one side of a boat to the other, there is no offense.
Or, if the boat is traveling upstream or downstream, she should resolve upon the condition: "May I not die."
If a monk who is not ill mounts a vehicle, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya; however, there is no offense if he does so for a valid reason. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun who is not ill should mount a vehicle, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika Dharma 112, Chapter 226. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.

Bhadrā Kāpileyī went to her kinsmen’s home carrying an umbrella and wearing fastened sandals; people then complained, saying, "Look, sirs! Even now this female ascetic, though she has gone forth, still possesses great desire."
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible [to use] a parasol or sandals."
This is the origin of the matter:
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, those Śākya maidens who had gone forth as nuns were being scorched by the heat as they were walking along.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...until the Blessed One said: "In that case, I allow it for one who is ill. [As before.]
Whatever nun, not being ill, should wear a sunshade and sandals, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Whatever nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*). "Not being ill" is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill.
What, then, is intended here by "sickness"? Is it one who is weakened by old age, or weakened by disease, or naturally delicate?
Or is it one who is able to go [but] is scorched by the heat?
"Parasols and sandals": a parasol is called a *bhūrja*-parasol, a *tāla*-parasol, a bamboo parasol, a leaf parasol, or a cloth parasol.
Sandals are called those with a single sole or those that are double-soled.
"Should keep" means he should use them; [if he does so], it is a *pācattika* offense.
As far as the designation is concerned:
if that nun, not being ill, carries an umbrella but does not wear sandals, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
if she wears sandals but does not carry an umbrella, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If one carries both [the handle and the canopy], it is a *pācattika* offense; if neither, there is no offense.
If a monk also carries an umbrella made of *picumastaka* (castor-oil plant) or the like, or one that is folded or lacks a handle, he incurs a transgression of the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill should wear a parasol and sandals, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika Dharma 113.
[Monk 227: The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Now, Bhadrā Kāpileyī was going to her family home.
Their beds were spread and re-spread with double and triple layers of coverlets, and they were ascended by means of ladders.
Wanderers (caraka) and mendicants (parivrājaka), as well as nuns (bhikṣuṇī), entered for the sake of alms;
seeing this, they grumbled.
"Look, my dear, even now this female ascetic still has such great desire!
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, who said,
"Go and summon Bhadrā."
She was then summoned.
The Blessed One questioned her about all of that in detail, to which she replied,
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In this way, you sit down upon or lie down upon a couch or a seat that exceeds the proper measure.
Therefore, it is not permissible to sit down upon or lie down upon a couch or a seat that exceeds the proper measure."
Now, indeed, until they have become completely purified:
whatever nun should sit down or lie down on a couch or a chair that exceeds the proper measure, it is a *pācattika*.
"Whatever nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"Exceeding the proper measure" means exceeding the eight-finger-breadth measurement of the Sugata.
"On a couch or a chair" refers to fourteen couches and fourteen chairs. "Or should sit down" means to sit upon them.

"Or she should lie down" means she prepares a bed; it is an offense of expiation (pācittika) according to the formal rule. If that nun, having sat down once, remains sitting for the entire day, she incurs one offense of expiation.
If she sits down again and again, there are as many *pācattika* offenses as there are times she does so.
If she sits or lies down after burying [the bed] in the ground so that it exceeds the prescribed measure, there is no offense.
A monk who sits or lies down on a couch or a chair that exceeds the prescribed measure incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should sit down or lie down on a bed or a bench that exceeds the proper measure, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). //2//
Pācattika Dharma 114:
Sharing One Bed. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, those nuns of the group of six made their beds using a single sheet for both the mattress and the coverlet;
they broke the frames, tore the slats, and tore the four-cornered supports.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
When they had been summoned, they were questioned;
they replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
It is a transgression for you, O bhikṣuṇīs, as far as [the following].
Whatever bhikṣuṇī should arrange a shared bed with one who uses the same covering and wearing of robes, it is a pācattika.
"Whatever bhikṣuṇī" means one who has received full ordination.
"Having a single covering" means having a single bed-covering;
"having a single upper garment" means having a single cloth;
"bed" refers to a couch for the lame, a bench for the lame, and so forth, up to mats, straw mats, and the like.
"Should arrange" means she should do so.
This constitutes a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule:
it is not permissible for a nun to arrange a shared bed.
Furthermore, one should sleep alone on a couch. On three benches, two people may sleep; they should extend their legs in such a way that their knees do not touch one another's.
On a mat, one should sleep alone.
When it has been designated for use by three people lying down crosswise, they should lie on separate individual mats, just as on a square couch or a seat.
Now, if there is a bedding made of grass and so forth, it is not permissible to step upon it too heavily;
rather, it must be arranged evenly and securely with separate individual mats.
Now, when it becomes cold, having each made their own inner garments, one *saṃcelī* (upper robe) must be made.
If a monk also makes a bed together [with a woman], he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun should arrange for a shared bed, it is a *pācattika* offense. //3//
Pācattika Dharma 115:
Departing. 229. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā, having reserved bedding and seats in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, departed on a journey.
When visiting nuns arrived,
those nuns were made to vacate the bedding and seats belonging to the Saṅgha in that monastery according to seniority.
Then those bhikṣuṇīs complained:
"Why does she now set out on a journey while obstructing the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha?
One must not depart without having relinquished the bedding and seating."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She said: "Call Nandā.
She was then summoned.
This very point was questioned, up until: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda, that you set out on a journey without having relinquished the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha."

Therefore, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to set out on a journey without having relinquished the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha. Indeed, [this rule shall remain] until they have become thoroughly purified. Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī sets out on a journey without having relinquished the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha, it is a pācattika offense.
"Any nun" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Beds and seats belonging to the Saṃgha" refers to a bed, a chair, a mattress, a square cushion, a bolster, or a pillow.
"Without having relinquished" means without having returned them.
"If she should set out on a journey," meaning if she goes elsewhere, it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule.
It is not permissible for a nun to set out on a journey without having relinquished the communal bedding and seating.
If she does set out, she must say: "I am relinquishing the bedding and seating that has been left behind."
If one departs without having made a formal exit, one incurs a *pācattika* offense.
Now, if a monastery consists of a single dwelling and one sets out on a journey without having made a formal exit, one incurs a transgression of the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Pācattika Dharma 116:
Entering. 230. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, while Gartodara’s father was bathing him in his own monastery,
Gartodara’s mother went to the monastery unannounced;
having entered, she massaged his back.
He looked at her,
and then he said,
"Ah, this is indeed a woman!"
She then said, "Gartodara’s mother is not at fault. What exactly is the offense here? Now, I used to bathe her on one occasion and on another occasion as well."
He then said, "Formerly I was a householder; now I am a renunciant.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call Gartodaramātā.
She was then summoned, and the Blessed One questioned her about all of that in detail.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “On another occasion as well, I shall bathe you.”
He then said:
"It is a transgression for you, Gartodaramātṛ, that you approach in this manner, knowing [the situation], yet without having been informed beforehand or invited.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said: "Therefore, it is not permissible... [and so on].
If a nun, knowing that a monastery contains monks, should approach it beforehand without having informed them or being invited, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"A nun" means one who has received full ordination.
"Containing monks" means, at the very least, where there is even a single monk present.
"A monastery" means either a forest hermitage or one near a village.
"Not previously informed" means not having been announced;
"not invited" means not having been summoned.
"Should approach" means she should enter,
as in the case of the nun Gartodaramātā.
[This is] an offense of expiation (*pācattika*), and so forth, up to the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
Now, when these nuns go to the courtyard, they should stand at the gateway and announce:
"I pay homage, Noble One; we shall enter.
Then that monk must inform the other monks so that the monks do not become exposed.
If they are far apart due to work with clay or work with bricks,
and they are not crowded together, it should be said:
"Wait a moment, sisters."
Having approached those monks, he should say to them:
"Venerable sirs, please put on your lower robes and clothe yourselves; the nuns are entering.
And this should not be said by one who is unskilled or ignorant of the proper custom.
"Do not enter hastily!
Then indeed it should be said:
"O monks, do not enter while remaining at a distance."
Now, if they enter without having announced themselves, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
When they place one foot inside, they incur an offense of transgression against the discipline (vinayātikrama);
when they place the second foot inside, it is an offense of expiation.
For that very reason, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*) if one enters [the nunnery] without having first informed [the nun].
A monk (*bhikṣu*) who enters a nun’s dwelling (*bhikṣuṇī-upāśraya*) without being announced also incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline.
Rather, standing at the gateway, one should snap one's fingers.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, knowing that a monastery belongs to a community of monks, should approach it without prior notification and without being invited, it is an offense of expiation. (Rule 3)
Pācattika Dharma 117,
[Section] 231: The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, some bhikṣuṇīs, while wandering on tour through the Kośala country, arrived at a village settlement to take up residence. There, they were addressed by another woman whose husband was away:
"Prajāpatī, give us shelter."
She then said,
"Noble lady, my husband has gone abroad;
he might return unexpectedly."
Then they said,
"Who indeed will know whether he will come or not?
Now, the shelter had been given by her to those nuns who had returned.
That man returned at an improper time;
having now eaten and drunk, he was oppressed by his afflictions and lay in amorous union with his wife.
Then those bhikṣuṇīs were awakened by that sound.
Now, those who were not yet free from passion experienced a perception of non-contact.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [peyāla] ...until the Blessed One said:
Then he had those bhikṣuṇīs summoned; once they were summoned, the Blessed One questioned them about all of that in detail.
"Is it so? "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"And yet, knowing this, you still take up a bed in a family where food is shared, intruding upon their space."
Therefore, it is not permissible. This is the very case that arose: the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.

Now, while the bhikṣuṇīs were wandering on tour through the Kośala country, they arrived to stay at a certain village dwelling. They then searched throughout the entire village but could not find any house that was without men.
They then retreated to the street, and at night a wind and rainstorm arose.
They became harassed and distressed.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize [this] during times of wind and times of rain.
This is the origin of the matter.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī."
When the nuns had arrived at the street, the women informed them:
"Enter this house, enter this house; there is danger here from thieves."
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"No; no training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One."
It is not permissible to have a bed prepared in a house with a man present. There, those nuns were harassed by rogues during the night; one among them was led astray from her celibate life.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize [this] for as long as there is a time of suspicion regarding men.
Furthermore, if a nun, knowing it to be a family where food is shared, should make her bed in such a place of intrusion, except at the proper time, it is a *pācattika* offense."
In this regard, these are the appropriate occasions: the occasion of wind, the occasion of rain, and the occasion of suspicion regarding persons; these are the occasions here.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"Eating together" means a man's meal with a woman, or a woman's meal with a man.
"Family" refers to a brahmin family, up to a royal family, or whatever other families there may be.
"Intruding" means entering where husband and wife are moving about.
"Arranging a bed" means placing one's side [against theirs].
"Except in the case of an occasion"—this term was withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense.
An occasion refers to the occasion of wind, the occasion of rain, or the occasion of suspicion regarding a man.
Among these, the occasion of wind is neither past nor future.
Rather, it is precisely while it is currently raining, at such a time of rain,
at what is called a time suspicious of men, [that he stays], lest there be an obstacle to his holy life.
Thus, this time suspected by a person is neither past nor future;
rather, it is precisely the present.
It is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).

It is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī, knowing it to be a family where she shares meals, to take up residence by intruding upon them. However, if it is known that this person is faithful or familiar, even if she takes up residence by intruding, provided she does not actually intrude, there is no offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, knowing it to be a family where food is shared, should lie down in an intrusive manner, except at the proper time, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Herein, this is the proper time: the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of apprehension regarding men.
This is the proper time in this case.
Pācattika Dharma 118:
On the Road 232. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, the monks who had spent the rainy season retreat in Vaiśālī set out for Śrāvastī in order to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
The nuns heard that the monks were indeed going to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One;
they went to their courtyard and said:
"I pay homage, Noble One; let us listen, Noble Sirs. They are going to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. They said, "Yes; what should be done?"
They said,
"We too shall go.
They said:
The Blessed One has prescribed a training rule: it is not permissible for a nun to travel along a road together [with a monk]. They then said, "When, O Noble Ones, will you depart?"
They said,
"On such-and-such a day.
They counted the days one by two, thinking, "We shall go on that day."
Now, those women, having already finished their meal by nature, put on their lower garments and upper robes, took up their bowls and outer robes, and stood on the road.
At that time, those monks set out;
seeing them, they said:
"Venerable ones, these sisters are going very quickly;
those bhikṣuṇīs are also going very quickly. Then those bhikṣus ran after them.
Those nuns also ran forth;
then, among them, those nuns who were young and strong pursued those monks.
But those who were there—those weakened by old age, those weakened by illness, and those naturally delicate—they were left behind and trampled.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"How can you indeed set out across foreign kingdoms and across foreign districts without a caravan?"
Therefore, it is not permissible for a nun to set out on a journey across a foreign kingdom or across a foreign district without a caravan,
until she has become fully purified [in her training].
If a nun should set out on a journey across a foreign kingdom or across a foreign district without a caravan, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Beyond the kingdom" means another's kingdom. "Beyond the district" means another's district.
"Without a caravan" means that a caravan—whether a householders' caravan, a monastics' caravan, or a wagon caravan—must be sought out.
"On a journey" means she sets out elsewhere.
It is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*), up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If this nun sets out on a journey without a caravan,
when she has completed the road, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Now, if she travels together with a caravan:

Those who set out on level ground but enter uneven ground incur an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. Those who set out on uneven ground but enter level ground incur an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. Those who set out on level ground and enter level ground are without offense.
If they set out on a dangerous path and enter a dangerous place, they incur a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk travels alone on a road that is considered dangerous, fearful, and full of apprehension, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should travel on a journey across a foreign kingdom or across a foreign district without being accompanied by a caravan, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). Thus it was said.
Pācattika Dharma 119:
Udyāna 233. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, some bhikṣuṇīs went out to a park together with women; there the women were eating and drinking,
while the bhikṣuṇīs, in female attire, wandered about gazing at the pleasure-houses, the forest-houses, and the painted pavilions.
Now, having been harassed by men in a secluded place,
those nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
[the matter was then conveyed] until the Blessed One said:
"Within a kingdom" means even within one's own country.
If a nun should go there to see pleasure-houses, forest-houses, or picture galleries, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Even within a kingdom" means within one's own realm.
"Even within one's own country" means in one's own kingdom.
And therein, "monastery dwellings" refers to these:
they may be *caṃpaka* groves, or *panasa* groves, or *atimuktaka* groves.
"Forest dwellings" refers to these:
groves of *nyagrodha* trees, or vineyards, or plantain groves, or groves of pomegranates, or groves of citron trees.
"Variegated dwellings" refers to these: assembly halls or gabled houses.
"She should go for the sake of seeing" means for the sake of looking.
It is an offense of expiation (pācattika),
as defined in the formal rule (prājñapti).
It is not permitted to go to see a pleasure-house, a forest-house, or a picture-gallery.
If she goes, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
when she has arrived there, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
Now, if he wanders about right there with women, there is no offense.
However, if a monk goes to see a pleasure-house, a forest-house, or a picture-gallery where those who indulge in sensual pleasures sport, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:

If a nun should go to see the inner apartments of a king or the inner quarters of a kingdom, whether they be palace residences, forest dwellings, or painted chambers, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). //8//
Pācattika Dharma 120: In Secret.
234. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
A certain bhikṣuṇī named Sujātā was formerly the second wife of the venerable Udāyin.
She then sent a messenger to him with this message: "Come; it will be your turn for the shared lodging;
we shall stay together."

When those bhikṣuṇīs had entered the alms-round, the venerable Udāyin, having dressed and put on his robes at the very time [of their arrival], took his bowl and outer robe and entered there. Now, they were sitting behind the monastery in a storeroom with lustful minds, gazing at one another’s private parts with their own supple organs. At that time, another bhikṣuṇī, an elderly woman, went to the area behind the monastery for the purpose of voiding excrement or urine.
She was seen by her;
she then became ashamed and withdrew.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
It is a misdeed for you, Sujātī, until [your offenses] have been fully purified.
Furthermore, if a nun should sit in private with a monk, one-on-one, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Furthermore, if a nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"One with one" means that she is there and another is also there;
[the other] may be asleep, intoxicated, insane, deranged in mind, afflicted by intense pain, lying on his back, a non-human being, or one belonging to the animal realm—
even in such cases, this is "one with one."
"In private" means secretly. "He prepares a seat" means they should sit together.
An offense of expiation (pācattika);
[the] usual formula; up to the formal rule (prajñapti).
If this nun sits together with a monk even for a single time and remains seated for the entire day, she incurs one *pācattika* offense.
If, however, she rises and sits down again and again, she incurs a *pācattika* offense for each instance.
Now, if there are two people and one enters the dwelling for some purpose, the nun must rise quickly.
Nor should he think, "Now she intends to harass me by force";
rather, he should perceive:
"I shall rise."
He asked: "For what purpose?
It should be stated."
To stand alone with one [woman]:
if that novice (śrāmaṇera) is less than seven years old,
to what extent of an interval does an offense (āpatti) arise for the purpose of seduction rather than release?
If alms are given in a place that is not intentionally prepared for that purpose,
and if the nuns' dwelling is crowded with people where carpenters, joiners, and painters are coming and going— even if they are there as preparers of allowable items—
there is no offense.
Now, if the gateway to the street is the door and women and men pass through it, even though those who perform the ritual service (*kalpiyakāra*) are present, there is no offense.
But if the interval between them is severed, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
If the ritual server is sleeping, he should be awakened by snapping one's fingers.
Now, if two [weavers] are present in a place where there are no [other] authorized persons (*kalpiyakāra*), and one sees any one of the three [objects], there is no offense.
Or, if one sees any one of the three through the opening of the shuttle (*vema*), there is no offense.
There is the range of vision (*darśanopavicāra*) but not the range of the ascetic (*śramaṇopavicāra*).

There is that which is the sphere of activity of a recluse but not the sphere of activity of seeing; there is that which is both the sphere of activity of seeing and the sphere of activity of a recluse;
and there is that which is neither the sphere of activity of seeing nor the sphere of activity of a recluse.

Now, what is the case where there is the range of vision but not the range of hearing? A monk sees with his ordinary eye that "this person is sitting here" as either a monk or a nun, yet he does not hear their voice with his ordinary ear.
In this way, the fourfold permutation is to be applied.
As far as this offense extends—
whether in a village or in a forest, by night or by day, in a concealed place or in the open air, for one person and not before a great multitude, neither in their presence nor at a distance—
the Blessed One has said:
If a nun should sit in private alone with a monk, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Pācattika Dharma 121, [Section on] Men 235. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī, having gone to her family home, was staying alone with each of her brothers, nephews, maternal uncles, and their sons.
When the bhikṣuṇīs, while wandering for alms, saw this, they complained:
"How can this woman who has gone forth sit in private, alone with a man?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
... [the report continued] until the Blessed One said:
"Call Bhadrā before me."
She was then summoned; she was questioned on all of those very matters, to which she replied,
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible for one woman to sit in private with one man," up to the point where the Blessed One said.
Furthermore, if a nun should sit in private with a man, one-on-one, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Furthermore, if a nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"With a man, one-on-one" means that she is indeed alone with him in this manner.

"Secretly" means falsely. "Should sit down together" means they should sit together. It is an offense of expiation (pācattika) as far as the rule has been prescribed. If that nun sits down during the day in the company of a man, she incurs one offense of expiation.
Thus it was detailed just as in the case of the monk.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should sit in private with a man, alone with one person, it is a *pācattika* offense. (Pāc 56)
Pācattika Dharma 122:
Upakarṇaka 236. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī had gone to her family home;
she stood within arm’s reach of her brothers, sisters, sons, and nephews, conversing with them and whispering into their ears.
The bhikṣuṇīs then complained.
"What is the use of whispering into the ear of this woman who has gone forth?
She is certainly speaking for our benefit.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on.
If a nun should stand within arm's reach of a man, or converse with him, or speak into his ear, it is a *pācattika*.
"If a nun" means one who has received full ordination.
"Together with a man" means with either a householder or one who has gone forth.
"Within arm's reach" means he should stand within the range of physical exertion.
"Converses" means he should say something;
"speaks into the ear" means he should speak in a manner suitable for the ear.
This is a *pācattika* offense, as far as the formal rule is concerned:
it is not permissible for a nun to stand within arm’s reach of a man, nor to converse with him, nor to speak into his ear.
Now, if there is something that must be said, [she should speak] from a distance.
However, one may speak with [a man] while standing within arm's reach.
But if it becomes necessary to speak in private, one must speak after placing a wall, a partition, a pillar, a tree, or a curtain between oneself and him.
If a nun stands within arm's reach of a man, or converses with him, or speaks into his ear, it is a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk stands within arm’s reach of a woman, or converses with her, or whispers into her ear, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun stands within arm’s reach of a man, or converses with him, or whispers into his ear, it is a *pācattika*. [1] Summary verse:
An umbrella [1(112)], a couch [2(113)], and a single-layered rug [3(114)];
he steps forward [4(115)], he enters [5(116)].
[6(117)] Together with people; [7(118)] on the road; [8(119)] in a garden; [9(120)] in secret; [10(121)] a man;
[11(122)] whispering into the ear.
The twelfth chapter.
Pācattika Dharma 123:
Approaching.
237. The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī.

Now, Bhadrā Kāpileyī, having gone to her family home, would suddenly enter by force while her sons, brothers, and nephews were in private in the dark and unaware. They would then raise a clamor there. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Thus, knowing this, you approach a dwelling with a man in the dark without a lamp.
Therefore, it is not permissible [to do so]. This rule shall remain as it is until it is fully purified:
Should any bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a dwelling contains a man, approach it in the dark without a lamp, it is a pācattika offense."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another. "With a man" means where there is a man. "In the dark without a lamp" means where there would be neither an oil lamp nor a torch.
"To enter" means to go inside; it is a *pācattika* offense, as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) is concerned.
It is not permissible for a nun to enter a dwelling containing a man in the dark without a lamp.
However, if there is some business to be done and there is a loud noise there, she may enter; there is no offense.
Now, if there is no fire, one should make it known;
one should either snap one's fingers or clear one's throat.
If he says, "Enter," one should enter.
If that nun approaches without even perceiving [the danger] or making a snapping sound, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk also approaches a dwelling containing women in the dark without having made himself known, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, knowing that a dwelling contains a man, should enter it in the dark without a lamp, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika Dharma 124, Viśoka 238. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.

Now those six group of bhikṣuṇīs went to a mountain-top festival. Having gone there, they each took separate seats; a dancer performed with laughter, and when the performance was completed according to the script, all the people laughed.
Then they stand silent like practitioners of yoga;
when the drama has become tranquil and concluded,
they let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
Then everyone became happy;
however, the people now complained,
"There is excessive laughter among these female ascetics."
Now, having been deprived of their sight, they did not offer the *nelāṭika* (forehead-mark) and complained:
"We do not receive the *bāhanelāṭika* from these female ascetics."

The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She reported it to the Buddha,] and so on until: "Yes, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "In that case, it is not permissible to go to see Viśoka."
Then indeed, the Blessed One said: "Up until they become completely purified:
whatever nun should go for the sake of seeing a spectacle, it is a *pācattika*.
'Whatever nun' means one who has received full ordination."

"Regarding 'free from sorrow' (viśoka): if one goes to see performances by actors, dancers, wrestlers, boxers, musicians, or those who play with jars and earth—even if it is only a place where as few as four people have gathered for the sake of amusement—it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule.
From now on, it is not permitted to go to see such 'free-from-sorrow' spectacles."
Now, if a bhikṣuṇī is walking for alms and sees the royal harem departing by way of the divine carriage, she may close her eyes; even if she sees [them], there is no offense.
But if she then makes a deliberate effort, thinking, "I shall look at these," or "I shall look from here," it is a pācattika offense.

Now, when there was an offering of garlands for the Blessed One, the male and female lay followers said, "The noble ladies must prepare the decorations; the assembly must be provided. It is permitted to provide the assembly.
Now, if at that time some alteration of the mind arises, it is not permissible to remain.
Even if a monk goes for the sake of seeing Viśoka, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun goes to see a performance for amusement, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika Dharma 125:
Quarreling 239. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.

Then indeed, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, acting like a bull among the bhikṣuṇīs who were engaged in quarreling, brawling, and fallen into disputes and contention as they lived together, did not settle their legal cases herself, nor did she cause them to be settled, nor did she exert herself toward their settlement.
The nuns reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One questioned them about everything, and they replied, “Yes, Blessed One.”

The Blessed One said: "Is it true, as you say, that when the bhikṣuṇīs have fallen into quarreling, brawling, and disputes, you, acting like a bull, neither settle those legal cases yourself nor cause them to be settled,
nor do you exert yourself toward their settlement?"
Therefore, it is not permissible.
Rather, [the instruction] shall remain until they have become completely purified.
Furthermore, if a nun [should provide] for nuns who have fallen into quarreling, into brawling, or into strife and dispute...

If a *vṛṣabhī* who lives together with [other nuns] should not settle legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) among those who are quarreling, nor cause them to be settled, nor exert herself toward their settlement, there is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
"A nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*) refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"Among those who have become quarrelsome" means those who engage in verbal strife, such as saying, "My position is correct," "Your position is incorrect," and so forth.
"Among those who have become quarrelsome" means among those who are engaging with one another, saying "It is mine.
"Living while fallen into strife and dispute" means, for example: "This is the Dharma, that is not the Dharma; this is the Vinaya, that is not the Vinaya."
For those living [in the community], there are offenses and non-offenses; grave and light; with remediation and without remediation; with remainder and without remainder;
legal action and illegal action; united action and divided action; and so on, up to action that is fit for its basis.
"Being like a bull" means being powerful;
"one would not settle legal disputes oneself" means one would not resolve them personally, while "one would not cause others to settle them" means one would not have others resolve them.
One should not fail to make an effort toward pacification; [if one does so], it is a *pācattika* offense, as established by the rule.
Now, when these nuns live having fallen into quarreling, strife, and disputes, it is no longer permissible to neglect them;
rather, they must be pacified and brought to reconciliation.
Zeal must be exerted for the sake of pacification; one should place hope in it, mutually ask for forgiveness, admonish each other as the occasion requires, and bring about harmony.
Now, if she is unable [to do so], another nun should be requested, or laymen, laywomen, monks, or nuns should be encouraged.
If those legal disputes are harsh and difficult to settle, she waits for the right time for those very disputes, waits for the proper occasion, and waits for their ripening.

If, having considered the time, the occasion, and the ripening [of the situation], he brings about pacification, there is no offense. Furthermore, if a monk, acting as a bull among monks who are engaged in quarreling, brawling, and fallen into strife and dispute,
does not himself pacify those legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), nor causes them to be pacified, nor makes an effort toward their pacification, [there is no offense].
She incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, if a nun [should] [interfere] with nuns who have fallen into quarreling, brawling, or entered into strife and dispute..."
If one who is dwelling like a bull among cows should not settle a legal dispute, nor cause it to be settled, nor exert effort toward settling it, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika). //3//
Pācattika Dharma 126:
Anointing. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.

Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī was being led to her kinsmen's home for anointment and bathing; she was being taken by the housewives who said, "We shall anoint the Noble Lady and we shall bathe her; there will be merit for us.
Some did so out of faith, while others desired to see her slender limbs.
Now she was gracious and beautiful to behold; women, by their very nature curious and fond of fine colors,
anointed her with *kāleyaka*, *tuṅgeyaka*, *svaṅgaka*, and *padmaka* powders and fragrant scents.
She then consented; now the nuns complained, "See, noble ladies, even now this woman who has gone forth still has great desire!"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ... "Yes, Blessed One," they replied.
The Blessed One said:
"In this way, you have indeed had yourself rubbed with unguents, massaged, and bathed by householders in exchange for [services].
Therefore, it is not permissible.
Now, the Blessed One [spoke] until they became completely purified."

Furthermore, whatever items are approved for householders for the purpose of rubbing, massaging, or bathing—with such things as these, a nun who is not ill should not have herself rubbed or massaged; it is a *pācattika*.
"Whatever items are approved for householders" refers to the daughters of Kṣatriyas, the daughters of Brāhmaṇas, and the daughters of Gṛhapatis.
"Approved for rubbing, massaging, or bathing" refers to *kāleyaka*, *tuṅgeyaka*, or *cikkasa* [unguents].

If a single one among those nuns, being not ill, should have herself massaged, what then is intended by "illness" here? If she is weak from old age or weak from disease and has herself massaged, there is no offense.
"Should have herself massaged" means she should have herself rubbed; [if she does so], it is a *pācattika*.
Now, if there is an abscess or a carbuncle, it is permitted to have it treated with medicinal ointments and massages.

If there is an agitation of bile (*pitta*), it is permitted to smear it with chickpea paste (*cikkasa*). If there is an agitation of wind (*vāta*), it is permitted to smear it with wheat paste (*godhūma-cikkasa*).
Now, when there is a gathering, one should have her anointed, massaged, and smeared with compounded medicines.
Having been smeared, she must not stand in a place where people pass by;
rather, she should stay in a secluded spot.
When it becomes soiled, one should then have it rubbed and go out [to bathe].
If a monk who is not ill should have himself rubbed or massaged with clay paste, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should have herself rubbed, massaged, or bathed by householders with substances intended for rubbing, massaging, or bathing, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika Dharma 127,
Bhikṣuṇī 241. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.

Now, a training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One: "It is not permissible for nuns to have themselves massaged or rubbed by those who are authorized to perform massage, rubbing, bathing, and grooming for householders.
Yet Bhadrā nun continued to have herself massaged and rubbed by the other nuns.
The nuns then began to complain.
... [as before] ... up to where the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill should have herself rubbed or massaged by another nun, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "To a nun" means to one who is fully ordained.
"Not ill": what, then, is intended here by illness? Is it being weak from old age or weak from disease?
The Blessed One has withdrawn [the rule], so there is no offense for one who is ill.
To have herself rubbed or massaged [by a nun] constitutes a *pācattika* offense, up to the point where the rule was established.
If that nun, when not ill, has herself rubbed by a nun but does not have herself massaged, it is a transgression of the Vinaya.
If she causes [a woman] to be massaged but does not cause her to be rubbed with unguents, it is a transgression of the Vinaya.
If she does both, it is a *pācattika* offense. If she does neither, there is no offense.
If a monk who is not ill causes a monk to rub his body or massage him, there is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill causes a nun to rub her body or massage her, it is a Pācittika. (Phu)
Pācattika Dharma 128:
It is exactly the same for a female novice; there is no difference.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill should have a female novice scrub her body or massage her, it is an offense of expiation. *phu*.
Pācattika Dharma 129: This very same rule applies to a *śikṣamāṇā*.
A *śikṣamāṇā* is one who trains for two years according to the eighteen rules. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, when not ill, causes a *śikṣamāṇā* to have her body rubbed or massaged, it is a *pācattika* offense. [End of section]
Pācattika Dharma 130:
This very [rule] applies to a female householder.
There is no difference;
"gṛhiṇī" means a householder. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun who is not ill should have herself rubbed or massaged by a laywoman, it is a *pācattika* offense. HRĀ.
Pācattika Dharma 131:
Regarding Living Together in Purity.
242. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now the bhikṣuṇīs had assembled for the poṣadha ceremony;
there was a bhikṣuṇī named Jetā,
and she did not come.
She sent a messenger [saying], "Noble lady, please come; the nuns have assembled for the *poṣadha* ceremony.
She then said:
The Blessed One has prescribed the *viśuddhi-poṣadha* for those who are pure.
Since I am one who is pure, I do not go to any of those [assemblies].
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. ... [peyālam] ...
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “It is a transgression for you, Jeta.”
And yet you do not honor the Poṣadha;
who else will honor it? And what is the honoring of the Poṣadha? One should approach [the assembly] when not ill.
A formal consent (chanda) must be given by one who is ill;
indeed, the Blessed One has said that this shall continue until they have become completely purified.
Furthermore, if a nun who is not ill does not attend the half-monthly ceremony for pure association (viśuddhi-saṃvāsa), it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

"Any nun" refers to one who is fully ordained. "Every half-month for the sake of pure association" means that on the fourteenth day she attends the fourteenth-day ceremony, or on the fifteenth day she attends the fifteenth-day ceremony. "If, not being ill, she does not honor the Poṣadha" means she does not attend it.
What, then, is intended here by "illness"?
It is this: she is either weakened by old age, or weakened by disease, or her veins have been pierced; or she has taken unpalatable medicine, or she has taken ghee.
Consent must be given.
If that nun, being not ill, does not go to the Poṣadha ceremony,
or if she is ill and does not give her consent, it is a pācattika offense.
If a monk who is not ill neither goes to the Poṣadha ceremony nor gives his consent (chandana), he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill does not attend the half-monthly invitation for purity (viśuddhi-saṃvāsa), it is a Pācattika offense."
