Approaching [1(123)]; Quarrel [3(124)].
Viśoka [2(125)];
Udvartana [4(126)];
Bhikṣuṇī [5(127)].
The female novice (śrāmaṇerī) [6(128)]; the female trainee (śikṣamāṇā) [7(129)]; the laywoman (gṛhiṇī) [8(130)].
Through dwelling in purity.
The thirteenth chapter is completed.
Pācattika Dharma 132:
Approaching for Exhortation and the Purification Poṣadha.
243. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. The elder monks were exhorting the nuns in turn.
Now, those venerable ones of the group-of-six did not receive their turn for the exhortation.
They then said:
"These people will not give us our turn for instruction; to whom, then, shall we go for our turn of instruction?"
They then said:
"The Venerable Śāriputra is both stubborn and soft;
[this was] in detail until the Blessed One had prescribed the rule of training."
"It is not permitted for a monk who has not been formally authorized to exhort the nuns.
Let us go outside the boundary and authorize one another.
Then, having gone outside the boundary and authorized each other, they dressed and robed themselves at daybreak and went to the nuns' quarters, where they said:
"Sisters, assemble; there will be an exhortation.
Those who belonged to the group of six wished to assemble, but those bhikṣuṇīs who were practitioners of yoga did not assemble.
They said,
"For what purpose shall we go to give instruction to these undisciplined ones?
Then, having spent a short while with them, they departed, breaking away like a flight of crows.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, having dressed at the very time [of departure], took his bowl and robe and set out together with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, in full detail. Eventually he said:
"Gather together, sisters; there will be an exhortation."
Those bhikṣuṇīs who were practitioners of yoga desired to assemble,
but the bhikṣuṇīs of the group of six did not come.
The elder asked:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is indeed complete," they said. "Is there no one who has not come?"
The group of six nuns said:
"A messenger has been sent to them, saying, 'Come, sisters; there will be an exhortation.'"
Then they said:
"We will not come;
we have been exhorted by the venerable members of the group-of-six with an improper exhortation."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, thinking that the community of nuns was distracted, rose from his seat and departed.
The Blessed One, knowing full well, asked: "Gautamī’s mother, why have you returned so quickly?
Have the nuns been exhorted?"
He said:

"Lord, having dressed myself at the very time [for the instruction], I entered the nuns' quarters to exhort them. I said, 'Gather together, sisters; there will be an exhortation. Those nuns who were practitioners of yoga (yogācārā) gathered as they wished."
The group-of-six nuns did not assemble.
I said, "The community of nuns is unanimous," and they replied:
"No.
"Who is not coming?
They replied, "The group of six."
A messenger was sent to them, saying:
"Come, sisters; there will be an exhortation.
They replied:
"We will not come; we have been exhorted by the noble ladies of the group-of-six with an improper exhortation.
"I too, Blessed One, thinking 'the community of nuns is busy,' rose from my seat and departed.
The Blessed One said:
"Summon the group of six nuns.
They were then summoned,
and the Blessed One questioned them about all of that in detail.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, members of the group of six, until [your offenses] have been fully purified.”
Whatever nun, moreover, does not honor the approach to the community of monks for exhortation every half-month, that is a *pācattika*.
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Every half-month" means from the fourteenth day to the fourteenth day.

Whether it be on the fifteenth day or during the fifteenth-day ceremony, if one does not show respect by approaching the community of monks for instruction, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika), as defined in the formal rule.
However, if one is now weakened by old age, weakened by illness, or has consumed ghee, it should be said: [I am unable].
"I give my consent for the exhortation three times.
If that nun, being not ill, does not go to the exhortation, or if she is ill and does not give her consent, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
When the *poṣadha* ceremony takes place, the women who are to take the consent must go to the monks' residence and say:
The entire community of nuns bows their heads at the feet of the entire community of monks, receives the *poṣadha*, and requests instruction. This should be requested three times.
If there is someone who serves as the instructor of the nuns, it should be said:
"Sisters, this instructor will come."
Now, if there is no one at all who is endowed with the [required] qualities, then he who possesses them should be appointed.
If there is still no one, it should be said:

"Sisters, there is no instructor of the bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, practice with diligence, attend to your offenses and the poṣadha ceremony, and be respectful toward the elder bhikṣus and those of middle standing."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun does not honor the half-monthly purification *poṣadha*, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*)."
Pācattika Dharma 133:
A Boil or a Carbuncle 244. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.
A boil arose in a private part of the nun Jetā.
While her female disciples had gone out for alms,
a physician who was a chariot-maker arrived.
She then said,
"Long-lived one, are you able to perform a surgical operation on me?
He then replied:
"Certainly. So he tore it open, washed it, applied a bandage, and departed.
Then those bhikṣuṇīs arrived.
Then they saw that place smeared with pus,
and they said,
"Noble lady, what is this?"
He said,
"Surgical treatment was performed.
They replied:
"A rash act has been committed by this noble lady, having had a surgical procedure performed in a cramped place.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...up until: "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"In this way, you indeed cause a surgical procedure to be performed upon the Saṃgha on a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury above the knees and below the armpits, without having first performed the preliminary rites and without having inspected [the patient]."
Therefore, it is not permitted...
[peyāla] ...up to:
if a nun, above the knees and below the armpits, has a boil, a carbuncle, or a wound...
Or if she causes it to be soaked, washed, or dyed by a man without first performing the preliminary duties or without having consulted the Saṃgha, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Again, a bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who has received full ordination.
"Above the two knees" means above the thighs and the navel.
"Below the two armpits" means below the breasts and the abdomen.
"Without having first performed the preliminary rites"—this means that a nun who intends to have surgical treatment performed must say: "A monk should be told.
"Without having looked upon the Saṃgha"—this means that an inquiry must be made in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"May the noble Saṃgha listen to me. If it is the right time for the Saṃgha, may the nun named so-and-so have surgical treatment performed."
"The Noble Saṃgha shall have the nun named so-and-so have surgical treatment performed.
Since there is silence, it is approved by the Saṃgha; thus do I understand this.

"By a man" means by one who is either a householder or a renunciant; "should have it cut, should have it washed, or should have it bandaged"—as in the case of the nun Jetā, it is a *pācattika* offense, according to the formal rule (*prajñapti*).

Now, if there is a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury in a cramped place, it should be reported to a female disciple, a fellow student under the same preceptor, or a fellow student under the same teacher—whichever one she trusts.
It should then be caused to be lanced with a thorn or a fingernail, or smeared with medicinal ointment. Now then...

If there is a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an ulcer below the kneecaps or above the armpits, and a man causes it to be lanced, washed, or treated with poultices; or likewise, if he causes a vein to be pierced—whether it be the temple vein, the arm vein, or the ankle vein—it must be stepped upon by another nun. Therefore the Blessed One said:

If a nun, without having first performed the preliminary treatment and without having had it examined by the Saṃgha, should have a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an ulcer above the knees and below the armpits lanced, washed, or treated with medicinal plasters by means of a man, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Pācattika Dharma 134:
Regarding those who have entered the rains retreat [245]. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Then a nun named Kālī, having entered the rainy-season retreat, departed on a journey after locking the monastic dwelling belonging to the Saṃgha.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...up until: "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Kālī, that you set out on a journey while having entered the rains retreat.
Therefore, it is not permissible for one who has entered the rains retreat to set out on a journey."
Now, indeed, until they have become completely purified:
whatever nun, having entered the rains retreat, should set out on a journey, that is a *pācattika* offense.
"Whatever nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"Rainy season" means the rainy night. "Has entered" means she has entered either the earlier or the later period of the rains-retreat (*varṣopanāyikā*).
"Should set out on a journey" means she should go elsewhere, even to another village; this is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*), as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) extends.
If that nun stays away for even one night, it is a *pācattika* offense.

However, if there should be fear of the king, fear of an army, fear of a foreign army, or if there should be a threat to her life or a threat to her celibacy (*brahmacarya*), she may go even if she does so; there is no offense.

There is no formal act of authorization (*avalokanākarma*) for a nun [to stay away]; however, if a monk, having performed the act of authorization, should remain empowered for seven days and then go, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has entered the rains retreat should set out on a journey, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). //3//
Pācattika Dharma 135:
Having Resided for the Rains. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, the bhikṣuṇīs, having completed the rainy season retreat at Śrāvastī, arrived at Vaiśālī.
They entered the family circle of Bhadrā Kāpileyī’s relatives,
and those women said:
"Where did the noble ladies spend the rains retreat? They replied, "In Śrāvastī."
They asked:
"What is Śrāvastī like? They replied:
Such and such is this very delightful pleasure grove;
even so is the Jeta Grove.
Thus is the Fragrant Chamber;
thus does the Blessed One dwell;
thus do the noble ones Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
"If this is what renunciation is, then as for this noble daughter of ours— born right here and raised right here—
who goes nowhere at all but remains like a frog in a well, unable to go forth; how can she be said to have renounced?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"In that case, a bhikṣuṇī who has completed the rainy-season retreat may set out on a journey."
As far as the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has completed the rains retreat does not go on a journey, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Regarding the phrase "if a nun": she is one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).

"Having spent the rains" means that during the three months of the rainy season, one should not set out on a journey, even as far as to another village; [if one does so], it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If a nun sets out in this manner even at night, it is a *pācattika* offense.
However, if she is now weakened by old age or weakened by illness and is not capable of going, there is no offense even if she goes.
If a monk who has completed the rains retreat does not set out on a journey, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has completed the rains retreat does not set out on a journey, it is a *pācattika*. (Rule 86)
Pācattika Dharma 136:
Udvaheya 247. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.

The nun Jetā, while traveling toward Rājagṛha, was stopped by the nun Sthūlanandā, who said, "The noble lady must observe the rains retreat here. She [Sthūlanandā] then spoke in praise of her among the families:
"The noble lady Jetā is excellent, virtuous, well-behaved, and restrained."

"Exert yourselves in her service. Now she approaches families with a pleasing demeanor—whether in advancing or retreating, looking forward or looking aside, in contracting or extending [her limbs], and in carrying her outer robe, bowl, and monastic garments;
she is disciplined, free from arrogance, not fickle, not talkative, and does not speak in a scattered manner.
She is pleasing; thus gods and humans have faith in her. They perform services for her:
they address her, rise up for her, and invite her with alms-bowls, robes, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

The nun Sthūlanandā was lacking in proper decorum and lacking in proper deportment; she wore robes that were soiled, filthy, torn, and tattered; she had large, protruding breasts hanging down like bags of grain, and she had large buttocks; she was arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, and loose-lipped.
They showed her no respect and did not invite her.
She then pursued her with both body and speech.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Then the Blessed One said, "Summon Nandā. She was then summoned, and everything was questioned of her, until she replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "It is a transgression for you, Nandā," and so forth.

Furthermore, if a nun, having said to another nun, "Noble lady, you must dwell here for the rains," and having spoken thus, subsequently moves away herself or causes [another] to move away, it is a *pācattika*.
"Furthermore, if a nun" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).

"To a nun, saying 'Noble lady, you must dwell here for the rains'" means having spoken thus—having restrained her for three months—and subsequently "moves away herself" means she herself moves away by means of body or speech.
"Or causes [her] to marry" means: by means of another's body or speech, it is a *pācattika* offense.
This is according to the formal rule (*prajñapti*).

It is not permissible to marry her after having previously dissuaded her. However, if she becomes lax, or indulgent, or unwilling to train, or quarrelsome, and [the monk] perceives that if she remains here, she will become a source of trouble...
Thinking, "She will give birth," even if she carries her [to term], there is no offense. However,
if that nun carries another nun [to term], it is a *pācattika* offense.

If she marries a female novice (śrāmaṇerī) or a trainee nun (śikṣamāṇā), there is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. At the very least, if she marries even a householder woman, she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline for one who has entered the vows.
Furthermore, if a nun, having spoken thus and said, "Noble lady, you must dwell here for the rains retreat," should afterwards herself marry or cause another to marry, it is a Pācattika offense. 3.
Pācattika Dharma 137:
Regarding the One Who Arrived First. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now there was a nun named Kālī;
she approached [the assembly],
but those [nuns] had gone to another village for the rainy season retreat.
When the bhikṣuṇīs had arrived and gathered there,
the bhikṣuṇīs assigned the dwellings and the lodgings; then she said:
"Noble lady, please give me a dwelling.
She did not obtain a dwelling. They said:
"Where has the noble lady Varṣopanāyikā gone?
She is quarreling.
Now, there was another nun who was a practitioner of yoga.
She then said,
"Noble lady, this is my dwelling; bring your bedstead here and we shall live together."
She caused a bed to be brought in there;
it was a wooden frame where she would insert the branches.
Then she said:
"Noble lady, do not cause confusion in the monastery.
She then said, "Bhadrāyaṇī, was the monastery built by you? Was it sold by you?"
"Why would one not enter a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha?
She persisted both with her body and with her speech.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call Kālī. She was then summoned.
All of this was questioned of her, to which she replied, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Kālī.

Whatever nun, knowing that another nun has already arrived, should afterwards come and either herself drive her out or cause her to be driven out, whether by body or by speech, it is a *pācattika* offense."
"Whatever nun" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means either she knows it herself or she hears it from another.
"A nun who has already entered [the rains retreat]" means one who has entered during the first *varṣopanāyikā* (the commencement of the rainy season retreat).
"Having come later" means in the western [direction]. "Or should carry away" means either by oneself or by causing another to carry it away.
"Or" means that by means of another's body or speech, it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If she marries a nun, it is a *pācattika*.
If she marries a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*) or a trainee nun (*śikṣamāṇā*), she incurs an offense of transgression of the discipline requiring confession (*deśanāgāmi-vinayātikrama*).
At the very least, if one marries even a householder woman, it is a transgression of the discipline that leads to restraint.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun, knowing that another nun has already arrived [at a residence], should afterwards come and marry her, or cause her to be married, whether by body or by speech, it is a *pācattika* offense. // Phu //
Pācattika-dharma 138:
Vighasa 249. The Blessed One was dwelling in Kāśī.
Now, another nun, having failed to inspect her chamber-pot, discarded it on the street.
At that time, another brahmin, having bathed his head and dressed in fresh garments,
was passing along that street when the chamber-pot fell upon his head.
His head and clothes were ruined,
and the people mocked him, saying, "O Brahmin, you are well-bathed and well-anointed!
He then began to revile them.
She said, "Daughter of Itikitikā, you ascetic woman, do you not see that my head and my clothes have been defiled by excrement?
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [And so on.]
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “It is a transgression for you; indeed, it is improper for you to discard [the refuse] without first examining it.”
Therefore, it is not permissible to discard [anything] without first examining it;
rather, it must be done until they have become completely pure.
Furthermore, if a nun should discard excrement, urine, spittle, snot, food scraps, or refuse behind a wall without having examined it, it is a *pācattika* offense.

"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "Across a wall" means across a fence; [to discharge] feces or urine, or phlegm, or snot, or food scraps, or refuse, or laundry water, or dishwater, or hair, or nails.
"Without having examined" means without having looked. "Should steal" means should discard.
It is an offense of expiation (pācattika), up to the point of the formal rule (prajñapti).
If one wishes to discard something, it should be examined:
if the street is crowded with many people, it should be hidden away;
however, if it is not crowded, there is no offense even if one discards it.
Now, it is not even permissible to throw it out without making a sound; rather, one must snap one's fingers or cough.
If that nun neither inspects the area nor throws it out after snapping her fingers, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk also throws it out without inspecting and without snapping his fingers, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, without first looking, should throw away excrement, urine, spittle, snot, food scraps, or refuse over a wall, it is a *pācattika* offense.
[Pācattika-dharma 139, 140]
250. On green grass and water. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now, King Prasenajit of Kosala had a park named Pūrvakoṣṭhaka, which was well-provided with lotus ponds; it was open to the monks and nuns, but closed to other people. The king then said to the park-keeper:
"O gardener, prepare the eastern enclosure of the park by watering and sweeping it; tomorrow I shall go out there with my harem.
Now, this was overheard by the group of six nuns.
"Tomorrow the king, together with his harem, will go out to the park grounds.
So, having gone there beforehand, they covered the area carpeted with green grass with dried phlegm and dried snot;
then, having bound up packets of excrement in lotus leaves, they floated them into the lotus pond.
Now, having spent the day there breaking up the flight of crows, they entered the city at the time of sunset. Then King Prasenajit of Kośala came out the following day accompanied by his harem.
Those women of the harem, having been somehow released from their confinement, moved about as if they had been liberated from a cauldron;
some sat down, while others lay down.
Some ran here and there, seeking an opening, and wandered about upon the grassy carpet;
their clothes were now ruined by their own ripe phlegm and ripe snot.
They then descended into the lotus pond to bathe.
They saw those flower-baskets floating by.
Thinking, "The noble sons heard that tomorrow the king, together with his harem, will enter the park; they must have sent these baskets of perfumes," they took them.
However, they were soaked by the water and had been nibbled at by excrement, and the lotus petals were naturally delicate.
As soon as it was taken, it melted away.
"Alas! Alas! It has vanished! they cried, and then they approached the king and said, "Great King, such is his condition. The king said, "Summon the monastery attendant."
He was then summoned, and the king said:
"Ho there, my man! Garden-keeper, by whom has the park been laid waste?"
The group of six nuns said, "We have gone away after breaking off our fast for the entire day like crows.
The king laughed and said,
"This shall be the consequence for those ill-behaved women."

The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in turn reported it to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One said: "Whatever nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or nasal mucus upon green grass, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
If a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or nasal mucus into water, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"Excrement" means feces.
"Urine" means urine.
"Spit" (kheṭa) means phlegm;
"snot" (siṃghāṇaka) means dried snot. "On green grass" means on a verdant lawn that has not been cut or mown. "Water" (uda): water is said to be of ten kinds.

One shall not void excrement or urine in a river, in a pond, in a well, in a hole containing water, in a stream, in rainwater that has collected, in a spring, in atmospheric water, in melted snow, or in the sea; [if one does so], it is a *pācattika* offense, as established by the rule.
Now, if during the rainy season the entire ground is covered with a carpet of green grass, one should do it in a place where there is only a very small amount of greenery.
Now, if there is no greenery, one should defecate upon a basin, a brick, a stone, dry grass, a piece of wood, or wherever another has already voided excrement—
whether by an ox or by another person. If none of these are available, one must at least prick one's smallest finger and defecate [upon it].
One should act in such a way that it falls first upon that [spot].
Now, when walking, it is not permissible to discharge phlegm onto green grass;
rather, it should be discharged onto a mat or into a leaf-cup.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or nasal mucus upon green grass, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). If a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or nasal mucus into water, it is an offense of expiation."
Pācattika Dharma 141: Group Gain 251. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now those women of the group of six were seeking consent;
they said, "Prajāpatī, give us your consent; we shall provide a meal for the noble ladies."
Then those women offered [their services], and they said: "Noble lady, on the day you provide a meal for the Saṅgha, please inform us as well;
we too will come as servers."
They then invited the venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, Upavāna, the venerable Rāhula, and the group of six monks. They then prepared two sets of seats.
One [portion] was for the elders and the other for the group of six.
Then, at the very time of the meal, the monks entered after having put on their lower robes and donned their upper robes.
Thereupon, for the Venerable Śāriputra, there was to be given rice boiled with milk, soup of mung beans, ghee, and curd.
For the Venerable Maudgalyāyana there was barley-rice, bean soup, and oil; for others there was sixty-day rice with soup;
and for others there was kodrava-rice.
To some the condiments were given, but no rice;
to others the vegetables were given, but no rice;
to others the thick rice was given, but no condiment.
Then those women, taking various kinds of greens and solid and soft foods, went to the venerable Rāhula and asked,
"Where are those noble ladies?"
Now, having concealed the elder monks, they showed the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks;
then rice porridge was given to them, along with mung bean soup, ghee, fresh butter,
water, sweet things, molasses, curd, white curd, and milk— whatever was required and as much as was required.
Whatever choice food, whether solid, soft, or liquid, was considered excellent, the group of six monks had it served to them.
These venerable monks, having finished their meal and risen from their seats, approached to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
Knowing full well, the Blessed One asked:
"Moreover, Śāriputra, [it was] in the month of Śobhana, whether it was pure, exquisite, or abundant.
The Elder said:
"O Blessed One, the purpose of food has been accomplished."
A second time, a third time,
the Blessed One said;
the Elder said.

"Lord, we have obtained rice from Śāli rice, soup of mung beans, fresh butter, water, sweet side dishes, jaggery, curd, and milk; for whatever purpose these are required, they are given as much as needed, even for the sake of accepting the offerings of sisters who are full of faith and serene.
The Blessed One said:
"Who was the elder of the Saṅgha there? "The Venerable Śāriputra.
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, is it true? “Yes, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, you have misused [the gift]; for you thus remain indifferent while the community of monks is being harassed.
For one whom the Blessed One has declared to have ‘misused’ [the gift], that food would remain for an eon or the remainder of an eon, and it would never undergo digestion.
When the Elder [Mahākāśyapa] gave him a crow’s beak [to vomit], he vomited everything up with a retching sound.”
The Blessed One said,
"Summon the bhikṣuṇīs. They were summoned and questioned on this very matter.
They replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "It is a transgression for you, O bhikṣuṇīs, that knowing this to be so, you divert a communal gain to a specific group."
Therefore, it is not permissible. Furthermore,
until they have become thoroughly purified,
if a nun, knowing that a gain belongs to a group and has been dedicated to a group, should dedicate it to [another] group, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"A group-gain" refers to the gain of a group of monks or a group of nuns.

"Gain" refers to the eight types of gain, from that which is for immediate use (*yāvat-kālika*) to that which is for as long as the world lasts (*yāvat-kalpika*), including what is permissible and what is impermissible. "Dedicated" means fully accomplished. If one should dedicate it to a group, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*); this is the formal rule (*prajñapti*). Now, suppose someone comes wishing to give a gift.
He said:
"Noble lady, if it is desired, it should be accepted as being accepted.
These are the *prātideśanika* dharmas, number 18.

Clarified butter, oil, and so forth [up to] 252. Now those monks of the group-of-six [took] clarified butter from those dealing in clarified butter, oil from those dealing in oil, molasses from those dealing in molasses,
honey from those dealing in honey, fish from those dealing in fish, meat from those dealing in meat, milk from those dealing in milk, and curds from those dealing in curds.
They ate curd after having made a formal request for it.
People then complained, saying, "Look, sirs! The ascetic Gautama praises fewness of desires in many ways, yet he has even laid down a rule of training [that contradicts it]."
Therefore, Gautamī, in this matter the bhikṣuṇīs must train in this very way; this is the origin of the rule. Gautamī, on one occasion the Tathāgata was dwelling among the Śākyas.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs, as many as there are, until they have become thoroughly purified.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, for her own sake should request ghee from families, or cause it to be requested, and then eat it..."
Or if she should eat it, that bhikṣuṇī must confess: "Venerable ladies, I have committed an offense requiring confession; it was not appropriate for me. I confess that offense.
This is an offense requiring confession.
In this way: [1] clarified butter, [2] oil, [3] honey.
[4] Molasses; [5] milk; [6] curds.
[7] Fish; [8] meat. "Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"For her own sake" means with reference to herself, having directed her intention toward herself.
"Not ill" (*agilānā*) is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill. What, then, is intended here by "illness"?
It refers to being weak from old age, or weak from disease, or having drunk a purgative, or having had a vein opened, or suffering from phlegm, or from a disorder of the humors (*sannipāta*).
"From families" means from Kṣatriya families, or Brāhmaṇa families, or whatever other families there may be. "Ghee" refers to the milk-fat of cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, or camels.
"Having requested" means having requested it oneself.
"Having caused to be informed" means having caused another to inform [her]. "Solid food" refers to that which is solid food;
"soft food" refers to that which is soft food.
That nun must confess it, for this rule is one requiring confession (*prātideśanika*).
Now, if there is a disturbance of bile, she is permitted to request ghee; the rest is as before. Furthermore, if while walking for alms she sees ghee being sold, she must not say:
“May there be the attainment of long life, and may it be abundant;

"What is the need for the Noble Lady? "I must go for alms," he replied. Then she said:
If she needs ghee for the sake of a noble person, she should say, "I need it. If she receives even a full bowl, there is no offense.

it is permissible to say, "Give this to her too.
The same applies to oil.
If there is a disorder of the wind (vāta-vikāra), it is permissible to request oil; however, he should not request it from oil-pressers.
Now, if while wandering for alms he sees oil being measured out, he may take as much as fills his bowl without fault.
He may say, using a present application [of speech], "Give me some of this as well."
The same applies to honey: if there is a disorder of phlegm, it is permissible to request honey; however, it is not now allowable to request it from honey-makers. The same applies to molasses.
If she is ill and a physician says, "Noble lady, prepare a preparation with molasses," it is permissible to request molasses. Likewise for milk; it is permissible to drink milk.
Now, while wandering for alms, if he sees cows being milked in the houses, he must not say:
"May there be a great yield; may the cows graze in safety.
They said: [This is the rule].
"What is the need for the Noble One?
"I must say: 'I am going on almsround.'"
They said:

"If a noble lady offers a bowl that is already full of milk, there is no offense in accepting it, provided one may say, according to the application of the present moment, 'Give this [other thing] as well.
Now, if she is training in the white [practice],..."
"There is no [milk] made of white [substance]. Do you desire milk? He replied.
"I wish for it.
If one receives even a full bowl, there is no offense.
Now, if one has a cold, [one may do so].
The physician said, "Prepare some curd. It is permissible to request curd.
Now, if while wandering for alms he sees curd being consumed, it is permissible to request the whey. Then he says:
"If there is no whey, do you want curd? He says, "I want it.
If he accepts even a full bowl, there is no offense.
Now, if a nun wishes to perform emesis or purgation and a physician says, "Noble lady,
take an abundance of fish broth," it is not permissible to request it from fishermen.
However, if she is walking for alms, it is permissible to request sour gruel made from fish.

the physician says:
"Noble lady, please partake of meat broth.
It is permissible to request meat broth;
it is not forbidden for those who raise sheep."
Now, while wandering for alms, it is permissible to request vegetable broth. Then he said:

He said:
"I desire it.
Even if he receives a full bowl, there is no offense.
Now, if one knows that at a certain time there may arise an illness and these medicines will be difficult to obtain, and one requests them beforehand, there is no offense.

If one who is ill requests [medicine] and then, when not ill, consumes it, it is a transgression of the Vinaya. If one who is not ill requests [medicine] and then, while ill, consumes it, there is no offense.
If one who is not ill, having requested [food], eats it while not being ill, it should be confessed.
If what was prepared as unsuitable is eaten as suitable, there is no offense. If it was prepared as suitable...
If it is prepared as unseasoned and he eats it unseasoned, there is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. If it is prepared as seasoned and he eats it seasoned, there is no offense.
There is no offense regarding a livelihood dependent on others.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

If a nun who is not ill, having requested it herself or having caused it to be requested from families, should eat or consume it, that nun must confess:

This is a *prātideśanika* offense:
one should not act in this way with oil,

Furthermore, whatever foods are considered choice, such as meat—if a nun who is not ill should, having requested them herself or having had them requested by another from families, eat or consume such food, that nun must confess it:
"Venerable lady, this was improper for me; it is a matter to be confessed. I confess that transgression."
This, too, is an offense requiring confession.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 1:
Concerning Sitting (niṣadyā), 255. This is the beginning of the Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka of the Noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, those bhikṣuṇīs were sitting in the final meditation session in the svastika cross-legged posture.
Then, a long worm entered through the opening of a wound of another bhikṣuṇī, following the flow [of the body fluids].
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Go and give her such-and-such medicine; then that long worm will emerge.
So she gave him that medicine for him to drink.
The long worm came out with the current, and he did not die.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, you should sit in the auspicious cross-legged posture (svastika-paryaṅka).
Therefore, it is not permissible to sit in the auspicious cross-legged posture."
Concerning the manner of sitting:
it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
Rather, she should bind the lotus posture with only one foot.
The wound-mouth must be covered with another heel-patch.
If that nun sits in the *svastika* cross-legged posture, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called that which is connected to sitting.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 2: Connected with the Kaṭhina. 256. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those nuns, having placed their robes on the *kaṭhina* frame, were sewing them.
Another nun caused a wound to be made by a bamboo splinter, which drew blood.
This is the case.
[The usual formula.

if these bhikṣuṇīs now wish to sit on a robe,

Now, one should sew after having spread out mats in the assembly hall, or in a palace, or in a meditation hall, and having hung up a robe-cloth.
If even this is not possible,
one should sew it after having hung it over a bench or a couch.
If even this does not suffice, she should sew while placing [the cloth] upon her knees.
If that nun sits on a wooden board (kaṭhina), she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section connected with the wooden board. //2//
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 3: Concerning the Veṭhaka. 257. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now the nun Sthūlanandā, having gone with many women to the Ajiravatī River, set aside her robes in a secluded spot and entered the water to bathe. She then emerged first, wrapped her body in a turban, and said to the women,

"Am I beautiful or am I not?
They then said,

"We do this for the sake of honor, so that we may be enjoyed for our desires and become even more beloved by the householders. "Noble lady, what is the use of that?"
The nuns then heard what had been said by those women.
[This is] the case; ... [as before] ... "Is it so, Blessed One? "It is so."

If this nun wraps her body with a turban or a cloth band, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Now, if she wraps her body with a strip of cloth or a metal band,
it is not permitted to wrap it even twice or thrice.
Now, it should indeed be wrapped with a single layer.

Concerning the Ornaments of a Housewife.
260. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, those Śākyan girls, Koliyan girls, and Malla girls who had gone forth from great families took their ornaments with them;

People then began to murmur in complaint.
"This is not the life of renunciation; this is trade.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 7: Concerning Prostitutes 261. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now, those bhikṣuṇīs— daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Koliyas, and daughters of the Mallas who had gone forth from great families— were going forth while taking their maidservants with them;

“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,

Therefore, it is not permissible to maintain a courtesan.
If a bhikṣuṇī maintains a courtesan and makes her livelihood thereby, she commits an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
This is called that which is connected with courtesans. Chapter on Villages.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 8: Concerning the female attendant of the monastery. 262. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, the Blessed One has prescribed this training rule:

The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ... "Yes, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, it is not permissible to maintain a park-keeper as one's own personal attendant."
It is not permitted [to accept] a female monastery attendant;

That nun who keeps a female attendant belonging to an individual incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. This is called the section concerning the female attendant. // hrā //
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 9: Concerning the Saṃkakṣikā. 263. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

When putting on the *saṃkakṣikā*, it must be worn in such a way that the breasts are covered.
If a nun does not provide herself with a *saṃkakṣikā*, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya."
If one does not wear it when it is available, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya; this is called that which pertains to the *saṃkakṣikā*. // 0 //

Concerning the Bathing Robe (dakaśāṭikā) 264. The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 13, 14:

The Blessed One said:

It is not permissible to insert [the organ] too deeply. If one inserts it too deeply and thereby dispels lustful desire, one incurs a *thūl'-accaya* offense. This is called that which is connected with washing and that which is connected with insertion. // ṇka //
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 15, 16, 17: Concerning the *ānicolaka* (menstrual pad). The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, as those bhikṣuṇīs reached their season month after month, the blood ruined their bedding and seats. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Now, it should indeed be inserted into the opening of the wound when it is relaxed.
If that nun inserts it too far or inserts it too deeply such that she experiences sensual desire through that very act, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 16:

269. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

This is the case;

270. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
The Blessed One has prescribed a training rule:

"In the same way, it should be done at a washerman's bathing place.

Now, having taken water in a bowl, a pan, a cup, or a water-jar, it should be washed in a secluded place until it is completely finished.

Concerning the Stream of Water. 272. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

273. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

The Second Chapter.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 21:
Concerning Deformity 274. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those bhikṣuṇīs were inducing ejaculation in various ways, using radish, onion, kebukā, sobhañjanaka, and latikā.
[They reported] this matter to the Blessed One, up until:
the Blessed One said:

Therefore, it is not permissible to release [the food] by means of transformations. That is to say, that nun [is not permitted to do so] with radishes, or onions, or *kebuka* stalks, or *sobhañjanaka* (horseradish), or creepers.
If he causes her to be released by means of a bitter gourd, or a cucumber, or a bottle-gourd, or a kakṣāruka, or by any other such means,
and thereby dispels his lustful passion, he incurs a thūl'-accaya offense. This is called that which is connected with a transformation.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 22:
Connected with Formal Acts (Karma).
275. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepanīya-karman*) was being performed against another monk;
there was no one there skilled in performing such acts,
so the act was performed by a nun.
Then she felt regret, thinking,
"Is it indeed permissible to do this, or is it not permissible?
Because of her regret, she informed the nuns.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"This is the foremost assembly."
It is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to perform a formal act (karman) for a bhikṣu;
it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to perform any formal act connected with the *karman* for a bhikṣu.
However, if there is currently no one at all who is skilled in performing the *karman*, it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to instruct a bhikṣu.
Now, if one who is performing the ritual action forgets, it is permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to assist in providing it.
If that bhikṣuṇī performs the ritual action for a bhikṣu, there is a transgression of the Vinaya;
however, even if a bhikṣu performs the ritual action for a bhikṣuṇī, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with karma.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 23:
Concerning Silk.
276. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī, dressed in a silken robe, was going to her kinsmen’s home when a heavy rain fell. The silken robe became soaked; clinging to her body, her body appeared like crystal polished.
A crowd of people gathered, desiring to see Bhadrā’s slender form.
She was then sitting in a crouching posture, surrounded by her female disciples.
This is the account of the matter, up until:
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible [to wear] silk, nor anything connected with silk."
"Silk" (*kauśeya*) refers to both that which is natural and that which is artificial.
If this nun wears natural silk,
it is an offense of transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*) requiring confession (*deśanāgāmin*).

If one who is observing the restraint wears artificial silk, it is a transgression of the Vinaya; however, even if a monk wears both types [of silk], there is no offense. This is called that which pertains to *kauśeya* (silk). //3//
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 24:
Concerning the Concealment of a Boil.
277. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā was walking back and forth on the open terrace of the monastery wearing only a single upper robe;
as she walked, her large breasts bounced up and down.
People mocked her, saying, "Look, you fellows! This female ascetic is crossing the river like a gourd-vessel!
The nuns heard this matter...
[and so on].
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, one should make what is called the 'covering for the sores' (gaṇḍapraticchādana); it should be connected with the covering for the sores."

It should be drawn over the *saṃkakṣikā* so that the swellings are covered; if that nun does not wear the garment for covering swellings (*gaṇḍapraticchādana-paṭa*), it is an offense against the Vinaya. Now, it is not permitted to sit in an open place wearing only the *saṃkakṣikā*; nor is it permitted to walk about in an open place wearing only the *saṃkakṣikā*.
Now, if she walks in a secluded part of the monastery while wearing only a single shoulder-cloth, there is no offense.
This is called the section concerning the concealment of a tumor.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 25:
Concerning Female Ornaments 278. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now those Śākyan maidens who had gone forth from great families were capable of adorning themselves with supernormal powers. Whenever young girls were being married off, or new brides were being brought home, they would adorn them as they were led from house to house.

They receive food and drink in order to adorn themselves, and by means of that they provide for their livelihood; people now complain, "This is not true renunciation; these women are merely decorators."
The nuns heard this matter...
[as before] ...until the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, it is not permissible to adorn oneself."
Connected with the ornaments of women:
if that nun adorns her head, applies collyrium to her eyes, or powders her face with face-powder, and makes a livelihood by means of that, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Now, if there is pain in the eyes or a headache; [in such cases, it is not an offense].
Or one may obtain *ardhāvabhedaka* [ointment] to apply as collyrium to the eyes or to cleanse the head;
this is called that which is connected with the adornment of women. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 26:
Concerning the Lotus Sower, 279. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, those Śākyan girls, Koliyan girls, and Mallan girls who had gone forth from great families were planting and selling blue lotuses,
and they made their livelihood by that means.
People then began to complain.
"This is not the life of renunciation; this is merely a lotus pond.
This is the context, and so on as before, until the Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permissible to sow blue lotuses in connection with being a lotus-sower.
If a nun sows them and sells them, and makes her livelihood thereby, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
However, if she sows them for the sake of a *caitya* or sows them as an act of worship for the Blessed One, there is no offense.
This is called the account concerning the sower of blue lotuses.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 27: Concerning the planting of *sumana* flowers. 280. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
In this very way, the sowing of *sumana* flowers should be performed; this concludes what is called the section connected with the sowing of *sumana* flowers.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 28:
Concerning Utpalagranthikā, 281. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, the Blessed One has laid down a precept:
"It is not permissible to cultivate *sumana* flowers.
Consequently, those Śākya maidens, Kolita maidens, Malla maidens, and Licchavi maidens now string together blue lotuses and sell them.
Now people were complaining, "This is not true renunciation; this is merely a performance. The nuns heard about this matter.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permissible to string together blue lotuses;
that is, [any practice] connected with the stringing of blue lotuses.
If a nun makes garlands of blue lotuses, or garlands of jasmine, or garlands of *āraṅgaṇa* flowers, and sells them, [she commits an offense].

And if they make their livelihood by means of that, it is a transgression of the Vinaya. Now, if there is an offering of garlands, or a festival for the birth [of the Buddha], or a festival for the Enlightenment, or a festival for the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, or a festival for Ānanda, or a festival for Rāhula, or a Pañcavārṣika festival, or a Mahāpañcavārṣika festival.
Now people said: "The noble ladies should adorn themselves. Even if a nun weaves a garland of blue lotuses, a garland of jasmine, or a garland of *āraṅgaṇa* flowers, there is no offense.
This is called the section connected with the Utpalagranthikā. Hraḥ.
Bhikṣuṇī Prakīrṇaka 29:
Concerning the seller of *sumanā* garlands.
In this very same way, the distinction regarding the seller of *sumanā* garlands is that she makes knots, strings, or flower-enclosures, and then sells them.
If one makes a livelihood by means of that, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section concerning the *sumanā* flower garland-maker. 0.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 30: Concerning Cutting. 282. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those nuns—Śākyan women and others who had gone forth from great families—being conceited, spun thread and sold it.
People then complained:
"This is not the life of a renunciant; this is merely the work of a cotton-carder."
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ...until the Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permitted to engage in weaving or anything connected with weaving.
If a nun weaves wool, cotton, linen, silk, hemp, jute, or any other material, and then sells it to make a living, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
She obtains it.
Now, if a nun’s robe has become worn out or exhausted, it is permissible for her [to obtain another].

"By whom?
He said,
"My brother-in-law is causing me to fall."
Desiring to lead me away, he said:
"Mother, sit down; go."
"We shall protect you," they said. She replied, "I will go to the presence of the Noble Lady; the Noble Lady will protect me.

Then she had her anklets fastened, her earrings put on, and her bracelets slipped onto her wrists; she was adorned and dressed in protective garments dyed red, with her head veiled, and surrounded by four or five female attendants.
Then that man stood at the door and watched; thinking,
"When she goes out, I shall seize her," he saw her as she was departing.
It occurred to him: "This woman deserves to be the wife of a householder;
she is not that nun.
Then, when that nun went to the dwelling place, she was seen by the other nuns.
They said,
"Noble lady, this Sudinnā has run back.
She said:
"I did not run toward him; rather, my brother-in-law wished to run toward me. Out of fear of him and with the intention of protecting myself, I acted in this way.
[The rest is] as before, up to these very words.
The Blessed One asked everything. "Yes, Blessed One," [he replied]. The Blessed One said:
"And yet you violate the proper conduct!
Therefore, it is not permissible to violate the proper conduct.
When that nun violates the proper conduct with a mind that has abandoned her vows, she ceases to be a nun."
Now, if one who intends to protect [herself] violates the proper conduct, it is a transgression of the Vinaya;
yet she does not cease to be a bhikṣuṇī.
Likewise, if a bhikṣu, with a mind that is neither renounced nor liberated, violates the proper conduct for the sake of protection, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with the violation of proper conduct. //1//
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 32: Concerning the Covering of the Alms Bowl. 284. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
The nun Sthūlanandā was wandering for alms;
she had now entered another large household for alms,
where there was a woman with a child in her womb who was restless.
She then said,
"Noble lady, abandon this boy.
She replied:
"Venerable lady, please set it aside;
I will give something to you.
She said:
"I will not abandon him.
She said,
"I will give the noble lady this much and that much."
The greedy woman said,
"Give it here into this bowl.
Having covered it, she went out.
Now the Elder Mahākāśyapa entered for alms. The Elder also had a vow: "Whatever first alms I receive, that I shall offer to either a monk or a nun."
Then she saw her; she said,
"Bring the bowl."
She pulled it back and covered it, not showing it.
The Elder said,
"Bring forth the bowl."
She was addressed by an elder who was of great renown and like a teacher himself;
then, being terrified and trembling, she extended her bowl toward him,
and it was seen by the elder.
He said:
"Alas, the Dharma has declined!
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa informed the monks of this matter.
The monks informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Call Nandā."
She was then summoned and questioned on this very matter; she replied,
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda; this is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya...
and yet you, indeed, cover over your alms bowl."
Therefore, it is not permissible to cover the bowl;
this concerns the covering of the bowl.
It is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to go for alms with an uncovered bowl; she must go having covered it.
When she receives alms, she should receive them with [the bowl] uncovered.
If she sees a monk on the street, she should show him [the bowl] uncovered.
If that nun wanders about with her bowl uncovered, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If, upon seeing a monk, one does not uncover [the bowl] and show it, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya;
this is called that which is connected with the concealment of the bowl.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 33: Concerning the privy. 285. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those nuns were sitting in a latrine with a closed door.
A woman’s miscarried fetus had been thrown into the latrine,
and outcastes were dumping excrement from painted jars.
They saw that boy;
seizing him by one arm, they complained,
"A female ascetic has indeed given birth in a latrine!"
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ...therefore, it is not permissible to sit upon a covered latrine.
Regarding the privy:
it is no longer permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to have a covered privy constructed;
rather, one must have it constructed with open sides.
It is not permissible to have [a latrine] constructed with water flowing into it;
it must be constructed so that there is no boundary for the water. If a nun sits in a covered privy where water flows in, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called that which is connected with the privy.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 34: Concerning the Jentāka (Steam-bath). The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, while that nun was bathing with Śākyan girls, Licchavi girls, and Malla girls in a bathhouse,
she was entered by young men of good family and led astray from the holy life.
The nuns heard about this matter.
[The usual formula applies]... up to: therefore, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to bathe in a steam-bath house (jentāka).
However, if she is now ill, she may bathe after having sweated in a dwelling and having anointed her limbs with oil.
If that nun bathes in a sauna, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya. This is called the section concerning the sauna. //3//
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 35: Concerning Lodgings in the Forest. 287. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
At that time, at that period, forest lodgings for the bhikṣuṇīs had not yet been prohibited, nor had those in the vicinity of villages been established.
Now, at that time, about five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, headed by Mahāprajāpatī, were residing in the Royal Park.
They were daughters of the Śākyas, Licchavis, and Kolitas—graceful and beautiful to behold.
Now those women, having been observed by the sons of good family,
sat down for the meditation session during the first watch of the night, while the sons of good family remained close by, thinking, "We shall seize them."
They rose up into the air;
those sons of good family were filled with hesitation.
Then, during the middle watch and likewise the final watch, they sat down for the practice of meditation.
The sons of good family gathered there, thinking, "We shall seize them.
Then those who were swift in attaining meditative absorption were led away;
and those whom sleep had not overcome rose up into the air.
As many as were in meditative absorption, and those who had fallen into sleep, were seized and harassed by the sons of good family.
This is the account;
[the rest is] as before.
Therefore, it is not permissible to dwell in a forest dwelling (*āraṇyaka-śayanāsana*).
However, if there is a crossroads where laymen and laywomen (*upāsaka-upāsikā*) pass through throughout the entire night, it is permissible to dwell there.
Even in that case, it is not permissible to dwell in a secluded spot.
If this nun takes up residence or dwells for the rains in a forest lodging, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section concerning forest lodgings. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 36, 37: 288. That which is the *āstāra* (formal proclamation) for the bhikṣus is not the *āstāra* for the bhikṣuṇīs.
Whatever is an offense for nuns that is not an offense for monks. [End of section.]
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 38, 39:
Whatever is an offense for monks that is not to be confessed (anuddhāra) is likewise for bhikṣuṇīs. This is the rule.
Whatever constitutes a suspension for nuns that is not a suspension for monks. // 0 //
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 40, 41:
That which is an offense for monks that is not an offense [for them] is likewise for bhikṣuṇīs. (ḷ)
Whatever is an offense for nuns that is not an offense is likewise for monks. (6)
The Fourth Chapter.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 42, 43: 289. Whatever food is unallowable for monks, [it is likewise for nuns].
That is not allowable for the bhikṣuṇīs.
That which is non-permissible food for the bhikṣuṇīs is permissible for the bhikṣus. // 2 //
It is permissible for a monk to accept [gifts] from a nun, with the exception of gold, silver, and things that may be used by fire. // 3 //
It is permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to have [an object] accepted by a bhikṣu, with the exception of gold, silver, and things that may be used with fire. // Nka //
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 46.
290. There are three things that cause one who is a bhikṣu to cease being a bhikṣu.
What are these three?
[1] He renounces the training with a mind that has abandoned and released it;
[2] the Saṃgha no longer resides in that place;
[3] or she manifests as female.
These are the three things that cause a monk to cease being a monk.
That monk must go to the nuns' quarters;
it is not permitted for him to stay even for a single night or for a single watch of the night within the same enclosure as the nuns.
Now, one must dwell where the range of movement has been cut off.
When the marks of a monk appear in him once again, then he should come to the monks' residence;
that itself is his full ordination, and that itself is his seniority in the rains. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 47:
There are three things that cause a bhikṣuṇī to cease being a bhikṣuṇī.
What are these three?
[1] He violates the rules of conduct with a mind that has abandoned and released its restraint;
[2] the Saṃgha no longer dwells in that place;
[3] or his male organ reappears.
These three things cause a nun to cease being a nun, exactly as in the case of a monk. Phu.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 48:
There is no superfluous formal act for a bhikṣuṇī. (Rule)
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 49:
Connected with Jewels 291. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, furthermore, there was a family that had been oppressed by the royal household;
royal guards had surrounded it and were guarding it.
A nun named Sthūlanandā, while wandering for alms, entered there.
That woman said to her:

"Noble lady, this family has been ruined by the royal house; it is in a state of utter disorder. Noble lady, please take this out. If we are released alive, it will be ours; we shall provide for the noble lady's livelihood, and it will belong to you.
She then presented her with the alms-bowl, saying, "Give this to me."
Having filled a bowl with various kinds of jewels—pearls, gems, crystal, musāragalva, and red coral—it was given to her;
she then departed after covering it up. She was seen by the guards, and they said:
"Bring it! What is this?
She hesitated and would not show it;
trembling all over and terrified, she showed it to him.
The bhikṣuṇīs heard this. They reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, until she had her summoned.
That very point is asked:
he replied, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible to conceal a jewel,
nor anything connected with a jewel."
Now, this great family remains unattached to the royal court as long as no written record has been made and no formal agreement has been established;
if they give anything, it is permissible to take it away.

Now, if a document has been drawn up, or if protection has been arranged, or if they are surrounded by soldiers, he says: "This house has been seized by the royal family; if we are released while still alive, it will belong to us, and it will belong to the Noble Lady alone. Therefore, it is not permissible to have them expelled.
It should be said:
"The training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One; it is not permissible to expel [the person]. Then he said:
Whether it is given for a shrine, for the Saṅgha, or "given specifically for a noble lady," it must be accepted.
Having accepted it, one must not take it away after concealing it;
having made it public, it should be taken away.
Then he is asked, "To whom does this belong? [If he says] "It belongs to the shrine," "to the Saṃgha," or "to me," if he is released, it is well;
but if it is cut off [from him], it must be given away.
If that nun conceals a bowl full of jewels, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 50: According to Seniority 292. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
On both banks of the Ajirāvatī River, there was a meal for the Saṅgha;
the monks went there by boat,
but the bhikṣuṇīs were not permitted to board.
The monks said,
"Sisters, do not mount it;
a training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One."

"It is not permissible for a monk to embark upon a single boat together with a nun. Now, as those monks were crossing at a landing place, even a single boat became crowded by one monk; it became crowded by two or three in this manner.

When those monks had crossed over, the nuns were then ferried across by a single boat-load. As they were calculating their seniority according to the date of their rains-retreat (*varṣāgra*), it became out of sequence. Then, at the time of evening, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, with her great limbs exhausted, approached the Blessed One to pay homage at his feet.
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked:
"Gautamī, by what have your great elements become exhausted?
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported all of that to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, eight bhikṣuṇīs should sit according to seniority,
while the remaining ones may sit according to their arrival."
Now, when there is a meal, a refreshment, a drink of gruel, or even a festival lasting more than one year or five years, eight seats must be set out for the eight nuns according to seniority;
or else, having first prepared eight hollowed-out hands [as placeholders], they should depart.
If those nuns sit down after having set out the eight seats, they commit an offense against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"The eight nuns shall sit according to seniority, while the remaining ones shall sit according to their arrival."
